en: The Vow of Non-Action from the Treasury of Buddhist Tantra (following the confession of misdeeds)
Having again undertaken the restraint of non-doing (*akaraṇa-saṃvara*)... (Sā. Mā., p. 55).
Confession of sins and the restraint of non-doing (*pāpa-deśanā-akaraṇa-saṃvara*)... (Sā. Mā., p. 106).
Confession of sins and the restraint of non-doing (*pāpa-deśanā-akaraṇa-saṃvara*)... (Sā. Mā., [p. 106]).
138, 173, 193) Having confessed [the transgression] and undertaken the restraint of not committing it again; (Sā. Mā., p.
201) the letter *a*.
In the midst of these, within the pericarp, resides the Supreme Lord;
the Supreme Lord is indeed encircled by eight groups [of letters].
The letter *A* is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, and the leader of the groups (*varga*).
From it alone have all the mantras of embodied beings arisen. (Vajratilaka, pp. 73–74).

The Blessed Lord *A*, situated in the midst of the vowels and consonants together with the eight groups of letters, exists in the form of all phonemes, words, sentences, great sentences, and so forth.
From that very source these phonemes emerge;
they produce words, and those in turn produce sentences.

Those great statements (*mahāvākya*) as well—as numerous as the infinite distinctions of worldly states, amounting to eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*)—all these originate from the letters and so forth. (Vajrayoginī-ṭīkā, p. 71).
There are fourteen fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) according to the established tradition of other schools.
However, according to the established tradition of his own school, the syllable *A* functions by relying upon the five fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).
Enveloped by the eight classes [of letters], this very syllable *A*, the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), is the cause of all mantras. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, pp. 72; 74–75) The syllable (*akṣara*).

The *bimba* accompanied by *nirvāṇa*, which is of the nature of emptiness, is the unchanging (*akṣara*) uncontaminated great bliss that transcends *saṃsāra*, characterized by perishable pleasure. (Se. Ṭī. p.
70) If the mind is empty of any object of apprehension and so forth, it is called "unshakable" (*akṣobhya*). (A.V.Saṃ., p. 29)
He is unshakeable by all undesirable people, and his gnosis is not disturbed even by false teachers; because his nature is immovable, he is proclaimed as Akṣobhya. (Jñānasiddhi 15.6)
Akṣobhya is said to be the vajra (Saṃvarodaya-tantra 2.7), because Akṣobhya is not agitated by the afflictions (kleśas). (Hevajra-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 19a):
Since the seminal essence (bodhicitta) is fluid, it is considered a substance consisting of the water element.
"Because water is of an unshakeable nature, hatred is indeed the leader Akṣobhya. (Hevajra Tantra 2.2.54).

He whose mind is like space is "Space-Minded" (Ākāśacitta), namely Akṣobhya, because his intrinsic nature is the perfectly pure dharmadhātu. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana, p. 51). He is "Unshakeable" (Akṣobhya) precisely because he is undisturbed by passion and the other afflictions. (Vimalaprabhā-ṭīkā, p. 85).

The three fires— those located in the heart-lotus, the throat, and the navel-lotus, as well as those in the thunderbolt, the sun, and the fire— are manifested in sequence within the bow-shaped, the circular, the daily oblation-vessel, and the triangular sacrificial pit.
Above them is the supreme fire, which possesses shimmering, stainless rays and is the embodiment of knowledge at the end of darkness;
in that [fire], neither the sun, nor lightning, nor the lord of the gods, nor the moon, nor the planets, nor the stars and so forth are found. (Kā.Tantra 2.36) This is the circle of fire.
The fire-mandala resides in the throat-lotus. Upon its arising, a red ray of light emerges and remains for half a watch (*yāma*);
at that time, one should perform subjugation and attraction. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 143)
The Fire [element] likewise resides in the triangular region at the base of the spine;
Aṅgarika [resides] in the two armpits, and Aṅkurika is so called because he generates the sprouts of the eyes. (Vātūlanāthasūtra-vṛtti, p. 61; Vātūlanāthasūtra-ṭīkā, p. 49)

The four limbs are the four components— namely, service (*sevā*), secondary service (*upasevā*), accomplishment (*sādhana*), and great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*)— as stated in the *Hevajra-tantra* (1.1.25). These are immovable.
The thighs and shanks are the "near-meeting" (*upamelāpaka*), because of the meeting of those previously mentioned [the feet] as well.
That itself is the "immovable" (*acalā*), because its conjunction is unavoidable. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 28)
For that gnosis which is inconceivable and effortless is indeed declared to be inconceivable;
for that which is conceived as inconceivable does not truly become inconceivable. (Avataṃsaka-sūtra, p. 20, 30)

What is this inconceivable realm? This inconceivable realm is that realm which is certain, which cannot be traversed by the mind, which cannot be measured by the mind, and which is not to be realized through mental volition.
This is called the inconceivable realm.
Moreover, Blessed One, the mind itself is the inconceivable realm.
For what reason?
For when the mind is no longer mind, no mind is found;
indeed, the mind is ascertained through the realization of the mind's true nature.
And yet, the realm of the Blessed One is inconceivable in all its aspects.
It is said elsewhere:
"O you whose intentions are free from conceptual construction, whose mind is non-abiding!"
Homage be to you, who are beyond mindfulness and mental attention, and free from any object of support.
In the *Catuḥpradīpa*:
"That which is born through conditions is indeed unborn;
for it has no arising by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."
That which is dependent on conditions is said to be empty;
he who understands emptiness is heedful. (Avataṃsaka Sūtra, p. 25).
This is infallible.
That which is the non-differentiation of emptiness and compassion, characterized by oneness, is called the *bodhicitta* that is "unfallen" (*acyuta*);
it is not any other [bodhicitta] produced from the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) or the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*), which is characterized by emission and vibration (*kṣara-spanda*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 70)
Aḍakavatī is outside; by the word "aḍaka" is meant a collection of corpses whose life-force has perished.
Since that [collection] exists in this place, it is called Aḍakavatī, a cremation ground.
...the cessation of twenty-one thousand six hundred minus thirty-six hundred inhalations and exhalations within one *āḍhaka* of time;
because this [cessation] exists in her, she is the stage called Dharmameghā.
[See Āḍhakavatīnivāsī] (Vi. Pra., p. 17).
Non-duality is the ultimate truth; it is called non-dual because its intrinsic nature possesses neither origination nor destruction. (A.Kr. 4)
That knowledge is called non-dual, devoid of all conceptual constructions;
it is completely free from all doubt, beyond dualities, supremely auspicious, equal to space, liberated from imagination, and is indeed termed non-dual. (A.Kr. 12–13, 17–18)
Non-dual knowledge is indeed one, free from all conceptual constructions;
it cuts through the web of imagination, being inconceivable, non-dual, and supreme.
It transcends form, sound, and taste, and is devoid of smell, touch, and the rest.
The supreme, pure, non-dual gnosis consists of the dharmadhātu;
it is liberated from all conceptual constructions and devoid of subject and object.
The abode is pure by its very nature, non-dual, ultimate,
indestructible, unarisen, imperishable, and without foundation.
This Mahāmudrā is the supreme non-dual gnosis, absolutely without duality. (A.K.
30–33) It is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and is free from both the perfected and the generative stages.
When the mind and mentation are relinquished, that is the supreme non-dual gnosis. (A.K. 51–52)
The ultimate truth is called non-dual (a. kra. 78).
Yet all non-dual gnosis is seen and appears as such.
It is non-dual, infused with compassion, and endowed with wisdom and skillful means (a. kra. 93).
The one named "beginningless and non-dual" is established in the form of glorious bliss (*śrīsukhākāra*). (A.K.
118) "Non-dual" means devoid of the appearance of the duality of wisdom and means. (He.T.Ṭī., p.
51b) [This refers to] the intercalary month.
For the sun, an intercalary month occurs every thirty-two months due to the absence of a solar transit on the new moon day. (Viṣṇupurāṇa, p. 78).
This knowledge, which is the sequence of the presiding deities, is self-evident and its scope transcends the path of speech.
"For this is the sequence of empowerment, consisting of the wisdom of the Omniscient One" (Hevajratantra 1.8.51).
"Entreaty" refers to the request:

"May the Blessed Ones, the Perfect Buddhas, and their sons, the Great Bodhisattvas, act for the sake of sentient beings as long as cyclic existence endures; may they remain until my own final nirvāṇa" (Sādhanamālā, p. 56).
"May the Blessed Tathāgatas and their sons remain for as long as saṃsāra lasts to act for the sake of the world, and may they enter parinirvāṇa after me. (Sā.mā., p. 202).
The Empowerment of Authorization (*anujñābhiṣeka*):

The seventh [empowerment], which brings about Buddhahood, is the empowerment of authorization for the purpose of teaching the supreme secret Vajrayāna through the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate, according to the inclinations of the infinite realm of sentient beings.
The application of non-arising is non-arising; it is the ultimate truth.
In that [state], the entry of the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) is the practice of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Regarding *anusmṛti*:
having visualized [the deity] through recollection, one should touch [it] with its very form. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana, p. 31)

"Recollection (*anusmṛti*) is to be known as that wherein an appearance arises" (Se. Ṭī., p. 30). That conventional truth, consisting of the appearances of the three realms, which was cultivated and stabilized through the two limbs of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), should be made to radiate forth in that very form by means of recollection.
One should cause that form— which is the form of conventional truth—
to expand and perceive it as pervading the entire expanse of space;
this should be understood as the recollection (*anusmṛti*) consisting in the vision of the three worlds throughout all times.
"The appearance of the triple world arises therein" occurs during the limb of recollection (*anusmṛti*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 33).

"From the union with recollection, a circle of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*) arises. (Se. Ṭī., p. 31). The union with recollection is the embracing of the image (*bimba*), which is the state of the mind being free from all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). When [this occurs]...
Then a stainless circle of light arises, and five-colored rays of light radiate forth from the pores of the skin. (Se. Ṭī., p.
34) "Recollection" (*anusmṛti*) refers to the subsequent attainment of ultimate truth following the realization of the Buddha-body.
Its mindfulness is the realization of that. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p.
69) Non-abiding nirvāṇa arises from detachment, from the departure of passion; that bliss which resides in the *uṣṇīṣa* is the semen (*śukra*), and that is "abiding."
That which has fallen from the *vajramaṇi* is *nirvāṇa*.
This King of Bliss (*sukharāja*), however, because it pervades the space between the *uṣṇīṣa* and the *vajramaṇi*, is non-abiding *nirvāṇa* (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*).

For this very reason, he is the Great Passion (*mahārāga*) and the Immutable (*akṣara*); by virtue of his preeminence, he is the Lord of the Three Realms (*traidhātukeśvara*) for all Buddhas. (Se. Ṭī., p. 55)
The pure body (*śuddhakāya*) is designated as "non-abiding nirvāṇa" and "great bliss" (Se. Ṭī., pp.
55–56). Non-existence (*abhāva*) is the grasping at annihilation (*ucchedagraha*) (Ta. Saṃ. Ṭī., p. 3).
Non-existence is that which does not come into being; it is non-arising.
And so it was said by the Blessed One in the *Laṅkāvatāra*:
"He who understands existence as non-existence..."
He never forms a conceptual perception regarding any phenomena;
he who never forms a conceptual perception regarding any phenomena touches the signless samādhi. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 5a)
The five superknowledges (abhijñāpañcaka) are the five superknowledges— namely, the divine ear (divyaṃ śrotra), the divine eye (divyaṃ cakṣuḥ), and so forth.
Knowledge of the minds of others, recollection of former abodes, and knowledge of supernatural powers. (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p. 27)
Covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is the longing for the property of another; it is directed toward [that object]. (Guṇasthānakramāroha, 206) It is oriented toward [the object].
The *upacchandoha* is located in the heart and the generative organ,
because of the turning away from them once the meaning has been understood and the food has been digested;
that very same [power] is oriented toward them.
Because it is directed toward the ripening within that very limit. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
28) "Consecrated" refers to the knowledge of all Tathāgatas, which is known as vajra-knowledge.
"By him [the wise one] who has been consecrated, one is said to be 'consecrated'. (*Jñānasiddhi* 1.37).

Having explained the seven consecrations—which consist of the lower conventionalities that serve as the steps to the palace of mundane and supramundane accomplishments—one now explains the threefold consecrations which consist of the conventionalities of the yogi, which are the means for achieving mundane accomplishments and are conducive to the ultimate truth.
He introduces [the topic] with the words "Kumbha," and so forth (*Se. Ṭī.*, p. 21):
"For consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is the perfection of the cultivation [of the deity], common to all yogas...
Consecration is the ocean of gnosis."

For the purpose of washing away all obscurations of the corpse-seat (*śavāsana*), there is the fourfold perfect awakening, characterized by the perfect awakening in a single instant, the five aspects, the twenty aspects, and the net of illusion (*māyājālābhisambodhi*). (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 16b)

In that regard, according to the sequence of birth from the womb, when the two drops of the mother and father have become unified in essence within the secret wheel of the mother, there occurs for the *ālayavijñāna*— which is about to arise— a single moment of pure conventional bliss,
and the body takes on a uniform appearance like a rohita fish; this is the "enlightenment in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisaṃbodhi*).

When, while still within the womb, there is the consciousness of the five cognitions consisting of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of form and so forth, appearing in the shape of five protrusions (*sphoṭaka*) extended like a tortoise, that is the "awakening in five aspects" (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*).

Then, when for each of the five cognitions there is a differentiation of the latencies of the four elements beginning with earth, and the body is also complete with twenty fingers, that is the "awakening in twenty aspects" (*viṃśatyākārābhisaṃbodhi*).
Thereafter, having emerged from the womb, the consciousness of infinite phenomena like a net of illusions (*māyājāla*) is the "awakening as a net of illusions" (*māyājālābhisaṃbodhi*).

By contrast with this, the *bindu*—which consists of pure gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), is imperishable (*acyuta*), and is the *vajrayoga* of the *svābhāvikakāya* and gnosis—is Vajrasattva, the seer of all objects. Because he is perfectly awakened in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisaṃbuddha*) through the exhaustion of the wheel of breaths characterized by twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths, he is the "perfect awakening in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisaṃbodhi*).

He alone is the *dharmakāya*, the *cittavajrayoga*, the Great Being (*mahāsattva*), and the supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*); because he is perfectly awakened in five aspects (*pañcākārābhisaṃbuddha*), he is the "five-aspect perfect awakening" (*pañcākārabhisaṃbodhi*).

Here, she is characterized by the five wisdoms such as the mirror-like and so forth; she consists of the elements beginning with earth and the aggregates beginning with form, having the nature of wisdom and method; and because her essence is the cessation of the five maṇḍalas, she is that very Saṃbhogakāya, the Vajrayoga of Speech, the Bodhisattva whose meaning of truth has twelve aspects, who favors the Bodhisattvas, and who teaches the Dharma through the voices of all sentient beings. She is to be understood here as the presence of the cessation of the twelve transitions—characterized by the removal of obscurations regarding the five sense faculties, the five objects, the five action faculties, and the five actions of the action faculties—due to her being perfectly awakened in twenty aspects.

That very emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is the yoga of the vajra-body, the *samayasattva*. By means of perceiving the reality of the sixteen aspects, it is the primordial benefactor; its body is expanded through infinite nets of illusion (*māyājāla*). Because of its perfect awakening through the net of illusion, it is the "perfect awakening of the net of illusion" (*māyājālābhisaṃbodhi*). Here, it should be understood as characterized by the simultaneous manifestation of infinite and boundless various illusory emanations, resulting from the cessation of the drops (*bindu*) of the sixteen joys (*ānanda*) and so forth. (Se. Ṭī., pp. 6–7) This is the "perfect awakening in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisaṃbodhi*).
The fivefold awakening, the twentyfold awakening, and the awakening through the *māyājāla*.
Here, what is called "awakening in a single moment" refers to the moment of supreme unchanging great bliss (*paramākṣara-mahāsukha*). (Vi.pra., p. 20)

...Thus, he who is perfectly awakened in a single instant is the Wisdom-Vajra (*jñānavajra*), the seer of all objects; he who is perfectly awakened through the five aspects is the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*), the supreme immutable bliss.

He who is perfectly awakened through twenty aspects is the Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*), whose reality-meaning consists of twelve aspects, and who teaches the Dharma through the voices of all sentient beings.

He who is perfectly awakened through the Net of Illusion (*māyājālābhisambuddha*) is the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), the knower of reality in sixteen aspects, whose body is emanated through infinite nets of illusion. (Vi.pra., pp. 44–45)
Because it gives rise to the indestructible nails and teeth, it is "indestructible" (*abhedyā*) on the head. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā,
44) It is non-mental engagement (*amanasikāra*).
Regarding the term *amanasikāra*, many hold differing views. Among them, someone says: "This is a corruption; in a compound, it ought to be *manaskāra*."
To this it is replied: because of the word "bahulam" (variously) in the rule "tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam," when an *aluk* compound is formed according to "saptamyā aluk," we have *amanasikāraḥ*,
*amanaskāraḥ*, and *tvacisāraḥ*.

"Tvaksāraḥ"; O Yudhiṣṭhira, these forms are thus established, and this is not an incorrect word (*apaśabda*). Nor should it be said that [the word] denotes non-existence, because the negative particle (*nañ*) here functions as a prasajya-pratiṣedha (a simple negation).

For in the expression "the king's wives are not sun-seers" (*asūryampaśyā rājadārāḥ*), the absence of the sun is not what is being established; rather, that which is the seeing of the sun by the king's wives—which would otherwise occur—is prohibited.

In the same way, in the case of "non-attention" (*amanasikāra*) as well, it is not the mind that is negated by the negative particle (*nañ*); rather, that which is the mental attention toward the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and so forth—which would otherwise occur—is prohibited.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Even in the case of the *paryudāsa* (exclusion) interpretation, there is no fault;
for when it is said, "Bring a non-Brahmin," the bringing of a Kṣatriya or similar person who resembles a Brahmin occurs.
But not of something of a different class, such as a mat and so forth.
Here too, the establishment of a cognition that is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) has been made.

Alternatively, in the term *akārapradhāno manasikāraḥ*, there is a compound with the middle word elided (*madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ*), similar to the compound *śākapārthiva* (a king who is fond of vegetables).
By this, the meaning is that whatever mental attention there may be, all of it is of the nature of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

The fact that the letter *A* acts as the cause of non-arising is stated in the *Hevajra*: "The letter *A* is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are unarisen from the very beginning," and so forth.
And in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*:
"The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, the supreme syllable;
it is indeed the Great Breath, unarisen, and devoid of verbal expression.
Alternatively: "The letter A here is the seed-syllable of selflessness (nairātmya)."
And so it is said in the *Hevajra*: "The beginning of *ālī* is *nerādi*, [which is] Nairātmyā.

By this it is stated that all mental engagement (*manasikāra*) is selfless and without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Alternatively: "That Wisdom (*dhī*) is conceived by the Buddhas as having the nature of the first vowel (*ā*)."
That very Blessed Lady is [attained] through the yoga of the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*).
Alternatively— "A" is the term for *prabhāsvara* (luminosity),
and "mental engagement" (*manasikāra*) is the term for *svādhiṣṭhāna* (self-consecration). That which is both "A" and mental engagement is "non-mental-engagement" (*amanasikāra*).
By this term "non-mental-attention" (*amanasikāra*), there is the mental-attention to the inconceivable luminosity, which is itself non-mental-attention.

By this term "non-mental-attention," the state of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*)—the inconceivable luminosity—is brought about as the realization that carries the non-dual union of emptiness and compassion, inseparable from one another. (Avaivartacakrasamādhisūtra, pp.
"Non-mental engagement" (*amanasikāra*) means that nothing is brought to mind;
it is non-conceptual, innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*). (Dohākośavyākhyā, p. 62).
Amitābha.
"Non-abiding nirvāṇa is unstained by both existence and cessation;
because of its union with innumerable qualities, it is called Amitābha. (Jñānasiddhi 15.8) "Amitābha is indeed the lotus. (Sādhanasamuccaya 2.7)

"Indeed, fire is always produced from the friction and conjunction of two [substances]. Passion is Amitavajra; passion arises within fire. (Hevajra Tantra 2.2.55) "The phenomena are dissolved in the lotus; their foremost is Amitābha, whose nature is the wisdom of discernment. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 51)

He is Amitāyu because an immeasurable and infinite lifespan is obtained from him; he is Amitābha because his nature consists of the wisdom that contemplates the equality of non-duality (*Guhyasamāja-pradīpa*, p.
52). Because he abides between the eyebrows and sets in motion an infinite garland of bones, he is Amitābha, consisting of that very essence (*Vajratilaka-ṭīkā*, p.
48). He is Amitābha because he possesses immeasurable radiances consisting of wisdom (*Vajratilaka-ṭīkā*, p. 85).
Amṛta, amṛta, and śuktra—thus it is said; from that the three worlds are produced. (Guhyasiddhiprakaraṇa, p. 56). Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
Vighnāntaka is Amṛtakuṇḍalī; his gaze is directed toward the place of nectar, located at the forehead. (Se. Ṭī., pp.
36–37) But at the time of the *upasādhana*, the image (*bimba*) is Amṛtakuṇḍalī. (Se. Ṭī., p.
39) Therefore, by the designation "the image of Amṛtakuṇḍalī," it is stated that [the deity] is Vāyu according to the terminology of the *sandhyābhāṣā*.
And that is of five kinds.
Thus the Blessed One said in the *Samājottara*: "The breath consists of the five jewels and is presided over by the five Buddhas."
"Having emitted [it] in the form of a drop, one should visualize it at the tip of the nose.

Here, by the term "five jewels," there are the five elements—earth and so forth—which possess the nature of the five maṇḍalas of the *rasanā* [channel]; the breath consisting of these is "consisting of the five jewels" in the right nostril.
Likewise, the five Buddhas are the five aggregates—consciousness and so forth—which possess the nature of the five maṇḍalas of the *lalanā* [channel].
The breath presided over by them is [inhaled] through the left nostril.
"Having expelled it in the form of a *piṇḍa*"—
here, the *piṇḍa* refers to the state of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) within the central channel (*avadhūtī*), which is not composed of the [left and right] maṇḍalas of the left and right [nostrils].

Having expelled that vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), one should visualize it in the form of a mass (*piṇḍa*) at the tip of the nose—from the pericarp to the middle of the pericarp, not upon the petals of the left or right lotus.
Thus, the vital breath is restrained in the form of a mass at the location of the *bindu*;
by that very means, its concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is described.
Thus, by means of these two limbs, there is the *upasādhana* (subsidiary accomplishment), which is the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalī. (Se. Ṭī., pp.
41–42) "Amogha" [means] unfailing, because of performing the welfare of the world in all its aspects. (He. Ta. Ṭī., p. 19b)
Amoghasiddhi is in the *kakkolaka*; that which is the mind has the nature of wind (*samīraṇa*).
For envy is Amoghasiddhi, and the unerring (*amogha*) arises from wind. (HeTa 2.2.56)

That great gnosis which personally accomplishes all activities for the benefit of sentient beings is called Amoghasiddhi; its activity is said to be unfailing. One should thus summarize these families as "Amogha" (the Unfailing).

The wondrous ones who act for the benefit of the entire world; their station is the foundation, and Amoghasiddhi is the nature of the performance of activities. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 51)
Because all accomplishments are achieved through the performance of activities for the benefit of sentient beings, he is Amoghasiddhi. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
85) The procedure for requesting [permission] consists of taking [the object] oneself, or describing it by means of one's own conventions or those of others.
Where that [darkness] does not exist, the wise call that very state the "unasked" (ayācita) rite. (Sā. Mā., p. 334).
In the Arciṣmatī [bhūmi], the "subsidiary field" (upakṣetra) is at the tip of the navel and the nose.
Because it carries the *bindu* and the *siṃhānaka*, that very [channel] is the Arciṣmatī, due to its illuminating the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*). (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 28)
*Arbuda*:

By means of these two—the messenger of vowels and the messenger of consonants—through the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of the three mudrās, one awakens to the experience of non-conceptual bliss (*avikalpasukha*) due to the piercing of the staff of the Lord of the Karmic Winds; thus it is *arbuda*, meaning "the back of the head" (*pṛṣṭhaṃ śirasaḥ*). (Vimalaprabhā-ṭīkā, p.
Arbuda is the region of the back. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 32) At Arbuda, however, resides the great-nosed Ḍākinī Piśitāśinī. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 42) Avadhūtī.
She is called *avadhūtī* because she shakes off (*dhunoti*) the evils such as the afflictions (*kleśa*) through non-conceptualization (*avahelā*) and effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*).

The literal meaning of the word is: she by whom the root—the primary stalk—is made into an *avadhūtī*; thus, the cause for making the root-stalk into an *avadhūtī* is the syllable of the word. (Do. Ko. Vyā., p. 150)
“The *avadhūtī* is in the middle region, devoid of the grasped and the grasper. Here,
the grasped is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and the grasper is the cognition (*jñāna*).
It is devoid of those two. (Do. Ko. Vyā., p.
151): In the center of the navel is the great wheel, woven with sixteen threads, joined with the letter *A* through the yoga of encapsulation (*saṃpuṭīkāra*).
"Established there in the center as the very nature of the support of all, that Great Queen, acting as a pillar, is celebrated as the Avadhūtī. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 20).

Thus, by means of the central channel, the Avadhūtī, whose essence is Vajravārāhī, this entire collection of channels arises and returns to dissolve into that very place. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. [21]).
Regarding the three stages,
there are three stages therein:
the stage of the cause (hetvavasthā) refers to the period from the generation of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) until the arrival at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

The state of fruition (*phalāvasthā*) is the state in which, upon the arising of the knowledge of perfect awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), there is the attainment of the abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*) and the acquisition of all virtues. The state of performing the welfare of sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyāvasthā*) begins from the first turning of the wheel of Dharma until the disappearance of the teaching.
Within that, the causal state (*hetvavasthā*) is threefold: the state of intention (*āśayāvasthā*),...
The stage of application and the stage of mastery.
Among these, the stage of intention is the vow not to abandon sentient beings.
There are four causes for that:
namely, the causes of lineage, a virtuous friend, compassion, and fearlessness toward suffering.
By these four conditions, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is produced. Thus it is said.

In that regard, the stage of application (prayogāvasthā) is twofold: the seven perfections (pāramitās) of one whose mind is characterized by resolute conviction (adhimukticitta), and the ten perfections of one who practices with resolute conviction (adhimukticarita).

For the sake of the mind endowed with the four prosperities (sampad) of one who has attained the stages (bhūmi), there are these seven perfections: generosity (dāna), ethical discipline (śīla), patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditative concentration (dhyāna), wisdom (prajñā), and skillful means (upāya).
For one who practices the conduct of resolute belief, there are ten perfections:
generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge; these are considered the ten perfections.

In that regard, there are five states of mastery (*vasitāvasthā*), known as the states of afflictions (*kleśa*), rebirth (*upapatti*), action (*karman*), means (*upāya*), and the maturation of sentient beings (*sattvaparipāka*).
Among these, one who abides in the state of the cause (*hetvavasthā*) must perform all preliminary activities (*ādikarman*).

Furthermore, for one who abides in the state of the fruit (*phalāvasthā*) and the state of performing deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, preliminary activity proceeds spontaneously (*anābhogena*), just like that of Śākyamuni. (Avatamsaka-sūtra-vyākhyāna, pp. 11–12)
The impure [practitioner] is the beginner in the impure stage. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
54b) The meditation on the foul.
The body consists of a collection of feces, urine, semen, blood, phlegm, intestines, mucus, grease, exhaustion, the spleen, the liver, and so forth. As it has been said:
"First, separate this skin-sack from your own intellect;
with the sword of wisdom, strip the flesh away from the skeleton."
Having even separated the bones, look at the marrow within;
consider for yourself whether there is any essence here.
Thus it is said (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā, p. 15): What is the path of no-more-learning? What is the path of no-more-learning?
The final moment of the last [moment] among the knowledges of the path (*mārgajñāna*). (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p. 51).
The eight accomplishments (*siddhi*) consist of five: the sword, the wheel, the jewel, the vajra, and the lotus, along with the accomplishment of the knowledge-holder (*vidyādhara*).
Because the sword serves as an illustration:
that by which one becomes invisible is the second, the accomplishment of ointment (*añjana-siddhi*);
that by which one traverses hundreds of thousands of *yojanas* in a mere moment is the third, the accomplishment of foot-ointment (*pādalepa-siddhi*).
That by which one sees treasures buried in the earth, or enters the openings of caves and draws forth asura maidens, is the fourth siddhi, that of Pātāla.

The fifth is the accomplishment of the yakṣa-woman (*yakṣāṅganā-siddhi*), by which one enjoys yakṣiṇīs of most enchanting form. The sixth is the accomplishment of the pill (*guṭikā-siddhi*), by which, having cast it into the mouth, one travels through all the Buddha-fields and hears the Dharma from the Buddhas.
That by which one accomplishes the eight activities, beginning with pacification (śānti), is the seventh siddhi, which resides within the belly of the three worlds.
By that [eighth], one turns stones, copper, and so forth into gold.
She effects the accomplishment of longevity; thus, there are eight great accomplishments (*mahāsiddhi*). (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, p.
74) Ākāśagarbha: He is Ākāśagarbha because, by means of his two shanks, he causes the emission of sweat that pervades the pores of the skin. (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, p. 49)
The application of the term "space" (*ākāśapadayoga*): space is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*),
and the term is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
The union of these two is their oneness. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 33) There is nothing superior to the Ācārya, who is like a jewel within the three realms.
"By his grace, various kinds of perfections are attained by the wise.
(Guṇasāra 9.11) "There is nothing higher than the Teacher in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile;
by his grace, various kinds of perfections are attained by the wise."
He should indeed be known as Vajrasattva, saluted by all the Buddhas;
the teacher is the supreme deity, who must be worshipped with diligent effort.
He, whose nature is suchness (*tathatā*), for the sake of favoring the world, relies upon form by way of conventional truth and is established upon the seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*). (A.S.
33–35) One is called an *ācārya* because one moves far away (*ārāt*) from evil states (*pāpakadharmāḥ*). (He.Ta.Ṭī., p. 7a)
The Master, however, is the King of Mind by virtue of being the presiding authority over the maṇḍala (*Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka-tantra*, p.

69). This very holder of the Vajra of Mind, who—as previously stated—perceives the maṇḍalas as non-different from his own self-cognizable nature, is the Master (*ācārya*). He is called a Master because he performs [his duties] with distinction (*saviśeṣācaraṇāt*) (*Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka-tantra-ṭīkā*, pp. 68–69).
The Master Initiation (ācāryābhiṣeka) is the demonstration of the nature of the four moments and the four joys by means of the action-seal (karmamudrā).
One is said to be "initiated" by the Master Initiation merely through obtaining the irreversible initiation common to the Kriyātantra and other systems.
First of all, in order to render one fit for the hearing, reflection, and meditation upon the Yoginī Tantras such as the *Hevajra*, one is consecrated with the Master’s Empowerment (*ācāryābhiṣeka*).
Having ascertained the inclination of those who have received this Master’s Empowerment and possess dull faculties, instruction in meditation by means of the Action Seal (*karmamudrā*) is given.
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 7a-b)
Ānanda, this is the master initiation (ācāryābhiṣeka).
...In some Kriyātantras, there is laughter indicating the passion of the male and female deities;
through the purification of that [laughter], one is a Master—thus is the master initiation.
(He. Ta. Ṭī., p.
50a-b) The word *āḍhaka* refers to a corpse-pile in the external [sense], as in the case of one residing in Āḍhakavatī.
Because of its association with them, the cremation ground is called Āḍhakavatī.
In that place, there are always yakṣas who harass sentient beings and create many obstacles.
Their oppressor is the great yakṣa lord residing in Āḍhakavatī, like a king of beasts in the forest.
The cessation of twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths and exhalations—diminished by three hundred and sixty—in the internal self is the *āḍhaka*.
That which possesses this is the *āḍhakavatī*, the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghabhūmi*).

One who dwells therein is a resident of the *āḍhakavatī*; he is the Lord of Yakṣas, the harasser of the Yakṣas who are the obscurations of the Māras, the afflictions, the objects of knowledge, and the meditative attainments. (Se. Ṭī., p. 1)
"The self is the deity; therefore, the self alone is the deity. (Pratyabhijñā-vimarśinī, 5.33) "Through union with one's own presiding deity, one should worship one's own self. (Jñānasiddhi, p. 144)
Self-surrender:
seeing those who are terrified and suffering, one should offer one’s own body. (Sūtrālaṃkāra, p. 169) Self-protection.
Taking a single flower, one should perform self-protection by casting the flower upon the region of one’s own head while reciting: *oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa rakṣa māṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Again, *oṃ āḥ hūṃ* is the mantra for self-protection and so forth. (Sādhanamālā, p. 102).
This is the preliminary rite (*ādikarma*).
The beginner's practice as it has been taught should be performed by all yogins;
that which is intended as the wisdom regarding enlightenment is the inseparability of emptiness and compassion.
... The five perfections are proclaimed under the designation of "beginner's practice."
And the intrinsic nature of these is not held to be the perfection of wisdom. ...
By constantly and respectfully practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom, the wise person becomes happy and remains in a state of well-being.

Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and meditative concentration are the causes for the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) and the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*); wisdom is the cause of the Dharma Body (*dharma-kāya*), while vigor is considered the cause for both. (Avataṃsaka-sūtra, p.
2) Ādibuddha.
The word "ādi" signifies that which is without beginning or end.
He is called "Buddha" because he has awakened to all phenomena (*dharmas*) without error.
Since he is both the "Ādi" and the "Buddha," he is the Ādibuddha.
It is devoid of arising and ceasing;
the meaning is that he is omniscient.
And in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*:
"The Buddha is without beginning or end, the primordial Buddha, and without causal succession" (Sevaka-ṭīkā, p.
7). The relationship of container and contained is such that fire has earth as its womb, whereas earth and wind do not have space as their womb...
O Lord of Men, from wind arises space; indeed, such is the relationship between the support and the supported.
For the support of the aggregates is material in the excellent body; the channels [are the support] of the collection of elements;
and the supporter and support of those two is the all-pervading Unstruck (*anāhata*), saluted by the three worlds. (Kālacakratantra 2.18–19) [This is] immediate succession (*ānantarya*).

The five actions—namely, matricide, patricide, killing an arhat, causing schism in the Saṅgha, and rejecting the true Dharma—are called "ānantarya" because they cause one to fall into hell immediately after death.

Here, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), the term *ānantarya* refers to those who commit such acts. By the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), the near-ānantaryas (*upānantarya*) are included.
Defiling an Arhat mother, killing one established in the certainty [of liberation], and causing immediate harm to a Bodhisattva or a Śaikṣa constitute immediate transgressions.
The five actions similar to the immediate [sins] are the fifth: the destruction of a stūpa.
These are the near-immediate [sins], committed by those who have performed great evil. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, pp. 46–47).
The four joys.

From the center of the four-petaled *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus, the arrival of the semen (*śukra*)—consisting of the five digits known as Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā—into the center of the sixteen-petaled forehead-lotus, which is the pervasion of both, is the first bliss (*ānanda*).
From the thirty-two-petaled throat-lotus, the pervasion into the eight-petaled heart-lotus as before is the supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).
... From the sixty-four-petaled navel-lotus, the pervasion into the thirty-two-petaled secret-lotus is the cessation-bliss (*viramānanda*).
In that context, "various kinds of dalliance" (vividharamaṇa)—characterized by firm embraces, the sound *śīt*, moaning from the throat, and so forth—occurs at the navel;

however, in the secret place (*guhya*), there is merely the experience of bliss characterized by the thought, "Bliss is being enjoyed by me," which is turned away from external delineation (*ullekha*).
It is not, however, a bliss in which the act of dalliance has ceased.
Then, from the secret lotus, as long as the moon of sixteen digits arrives within the lotus situated inside the eight-petaled vajra-jewel, there is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
Due to the power of retention (*dhāraṇā*), because of the absence of external movement, it is unemitted (*acyuta*). (Se. Ṭī., pp.
54–55) Therein, the joys (*ānanda*) arise, differentiated according to the distinctions of the moments (*kṣaṇa*).
From the knowledge of the moments, the knowledge of bliss is established in the syllable E-Vaṃ.
In the *vicitra* [stage] there is the first bliss (*ānanda*); supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) is in that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Cessation-bliss (*viramānanda*) is in the *vimarda* [stage], and innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is in the *vilakṣaṇa* [stage]. (Do. Ko. Vyā., p. 68).
There are four joys (*ānandas*): joy (*ānanda*),...
Supreme bliss,
the bliss of cessation,
and innate bliss. (Hevajra Tantra 1.1.28)
Blisses: there are four blisses— bliss, supreme bliss, [viramānanda, and sahajānanda].
Innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) and the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*).
Otherwise, as it has been said: "Having perceived the target between the supreme (*para*) and the cessation (*virama*), make it firm."
That is not associated with it. (*Abhayapaddhati-vṛtti*, p.
32). *Āyāma* is the movement of the prāṇa and apāna winds through the six channels, such as the lalanā and others, in the sequence to be described; thus, it is called *āyāma*.

From the root *yama*, meaning "to restrain": *āyāma* is the complete restraint (*ā-yamana*), which is the entry of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths into the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 4).
*Ārolik*.
"Ā" signifies saṃsāra because it arises (*ā-rohati*) from all sides; "ārolik" is one who goes (*eti*) from that [saṃsāra], which is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
"Ro" refers to the three types of gnosis.
Therefore, because he has gone to the ultimate truth, it is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (Gośṛṅgaparvata-prakaraṇa, p. 24) [This is] the Noble Path.
The manifestation, as it truly is, of objects past and so forth is the Noble Path (*āryapatha*).

The Four Noble Truths (*caturāryasatya*)—the four noble truths—are suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 171; Hevajratantra 1.1.26)
Regarding the Noble Eightfold Path,
within that path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), the wisdom that realizes the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) is devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) is right view (samyagdṛṣṭi),
as is the view of the existence of the next world.
Right resolve has as its object selflessness, even though it is not yet attained through that vision.
Right speech is the teaching for the sake of sentient beings that illuminates the meaning seen by oneself.
Right action is bodily activity that is exclusively wholesome.

Terrorizing others for the sake of disciplining them through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and so forth is right action (*samyakkarmānta*). Seeking robes and other requisites with moderation, sustained solely by the nourishment of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), is right livelihood (*samyagājīva*).
The application of one’s own mind, body, and speech toward their respective activities in all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) is right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*).
On the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) is the non-forgetting of the object of focus;

the one-pointedness of mind is the immovable vajra-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), which emerges as the interval leading to the stage of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhāsā bhūmiḥ*). (Vasubandhu’s *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p. 56). *Āliḥ*.
*Āli* refers to knowledge of the world (*lokajñāna*). (Candrakīrti’s *Pradīpoddyotana*, p.
24) The sixteen vowels beginning with *a* are *āli*. (Kṛṣṇācārya’s *Hevajratantra-ṭīkā*, fol. 6a) *Āli* is the wind arising from the left nostril. (Kṛṣṇācārya’s *Hevajratantra-ṭīkā*, fol. 9b)
The fifteen vowels beginning with *a* are the *āli*. ... The *āli* is the moon. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
15a) The *āli* abides in the form of the moon. (Hevajra Tantra 1.8.5)
Wisdom is *āli*. (HeTa 1.8.11) *Āli* and *kāli* are themselves *lalanā* and *rasanā*, the moon and the sun, wisdom and means. (HeTa Ṭīkā, p. 6a)
The descent (āveśa) occurs in this manner: first the descent itself, then agitation, trembling, and tears;
followed by falling down, the arising of knowledge, and finally conformity [with the deity], in due sequence.
In that regard, there are three kinds of possession: possession of the body, possession of speech,
and possession of the mind.
In that regard, when there is possession of the body, a thrill arises, the hair stands on end, and there may be trembling of the limbs; tears of joy fall, and one falls to the ground and departs.
Upon the possession of the mind, there arises knowledge and the manifestation of one's own true nature occurs spontaneously.

Upon the possession of speech, there is unprecedented eloquence, characterized by conformity and similarity to the exposition of the knowledge of the Omniscient One. (Tattvārthasūtra-saṃgrahaṇī-ṭīkā, pp. 24–25).
This is the consolation.

"From this moment forth, you are liberated from all obscurations and are the pledge (*samaya*) of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas"—this is the encouragement for the sake of awakening. (Ārya-va-jra-saṃgraha, p. 38).
[The Seat]
The seat is the *dharmodayā*. (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p. 5).
That which is most difficult for someone to relinquish is considered their "supreme" (*uttama*). (Jñānasiddhi, 17.15).
"Utpattikrama" means the sequence or method.
Of what is it the sequence? It is the sequence of meditative absorption (samādhi).
"Arising" (*utpatti*) is the accomplishment of the form of the deity through the transformation of the moon-symbol, seed-syllable, and so forth;
the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which that [arising] exists is the "stage of arising" (*utpattikrama*). (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 23a).
The "stage of the arisen" (*utpannakrama*).

Form is indeed of the nature of the arisen (*utpanna-svabhāvika*). That yoga in which one resolves upon and meditates on that very [form] as being the nature of reality (*tattva-rūpa*) is the stage of the arisen (*utpanna-krama*). (He. Ta. Ṭī., p. 23a)

The stage of generation (*utpannakrama*) is the innate (*sahaja*), non-conceptual state, possessing all aspects, yet free from the fabrication of faces, arms, colors, and shapes. (Vi.pra., p. 20) "Utpala, utpala" [is so called] because of floating. (Jñā.si. 15|25)
Regarding the summary (uddeśa) and the detailed exposition (nirdeśa): in every tantra, such as those of the Yogins and Yoginīs, the summary is threefold, and the detailed exposition is likewise.
Among these, the summary is stated by its own name alone.
The second is the *pratyuddeśa*; the third is the *mahoddeśa*. In this way, the *nirdeśa* is also explained by its own name.
The second is the *pratinirdeśa* (detailed exposition);
the third is the *apara-mahānirdeśa* (further great exposition).
These two—the *uddeśa* (brief statement) and the *nirdeśa* (detailed exposition)—constitute the recitation of the tantra.
In that regard, the compilation by way of summary is the entire abbreviated tantra (*laghutantra*),
such as the *Śrī-samāja* consisting of eighteen hundred stanzas.
The compilation by way of detailed exposition is the teaching of the complete King of Root Tantras.

Just as there is the *Śrīsamāja* in twenty-five thousand [verses], so too is there a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Laghu-tantra* for each individual section (*pratyuddeśa*). Here, "explanation" (*nirdeśa*) is intended to mean a detailed exposition (*pratinirdeśa*).
By him [was composed] the *Pañjikā* on the *Mūlatantra*;
likewise, a *Ṭīkā* on the *Laghutantra* by means of the *Mahoddeśa*. Here, "instruction" (*nirdeśa*) is intended as the *Mahānirdeśa*.
The extraction of the root tantra according to the *Mahānirdeśa* commentary (*Se. Ṭī.*, pp.
4–5): the mantra *ṭākki hūṃ jaḥ* is known as the "extraction" (*uddhāra*).
And so it has been said:
"That which possesses neither the word *svāhā* nor the syllable *oṃ* is called *uddhāra*. It is the *upāya*. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 151).

"That which brings about the desired object through favorable means, like a boat [reaching its destination] by way of a favorable current, is proclaimed as the *upāya* (means) because of its constant favorable application. (Pratyabhijñā-vimarśinī 1.16) "The person (*puruṣa*) is traditionally held to be the *upāya*. (Sāṅkhya-sūtra 1.6)
The means (upāya) is also described as fourfold by Bodhivajra:
first, the ritual of service (sevāvidhāna); second, the near-attainment (upasādhana);
third, the attainment (sādhana); and fourth, the great attainment (mahāsādhana).
First is the realization of emptiness; second is the vajra-aggregation;
third is the perfection of the image; and fourth is the placement of the syllable.
By these four vajras, the accomplishment of gnosis is described (*Abhisamayamañjarī*, p.
211): the characteristic of existence is the means (*upāya*).
...the means (*upāya*) characterized by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). (Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Vṛtti, p. 212) What meaning is expressed by the word "means" (*upāya*)?

The illustrious Vajrasattva, who has become saṃsāra and whose intrinsic nature is compassion, is described by the term "skillful means" (*upāya*) because his form possesses the intrinsic nature of a stable reality.
Thus, "the illustrious Vajrasattva is skillful means. (Abhisamayamañjarī, p. 216)
"...The Means (*upāya*) is also the venerable Vajrasattva, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena" (*Abhisamayamañjarī*, p.
217). "The Means is great compassion, the experience of the equality of self and all sentient beings" (*Hevajra Tantra Commentary*, fol. 37b).
The person is known as the means (*upāya*). (Hevajra Tantra 1.8.28) The practitioner (*upāsaka*) is one who is diligent in the worship of the Buddha and who rests in profound tranquility.
One should be endowed with skillful means for the benefit of sentient beings.
One should always avoid evil deeds and refrain from association with the most wicked;
one should turn living beings away from sin and teach them about sin in every situation.
Freed from all superimpositions and well-composed in meditative concentration,
the wise one, always possessing supreme bliss, shall accomplish perfect awakening.
Who always exerts effort, maintains compassion, and—even with difficulty—does not perform what is undesirable, but rather performs the highest service? (Avaśyaka-vṛtti-saṃgrahaṇī, p. 10).
Indifference.
What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
It is the practice of supreme benefit toward sentient beings, whether they are beneficial or harmful, while setting aside the bonds of partiality and attraction. (Sā. Mā., p.
57) Ultimately, the wise person should meditate on equanimity, which consists in the cessation of attachment to what is unreal. (Sā. Mā., p. 97)
"Disregarding one's own task, indifference, and acting for the sake of another" (*Sādhanamālā*, p.

100). What is indifference (*upekṣā*)? It is a spontaneous engagement in the state of reality (*dharmatā*) which is everywhere free from both aversion and attraction (*pratighānunaya*). (*Sādhanamālā*, p. 115).

Indifference is the disregard for the eight worldly concerns (*aṣṭalokadharma*), having resolved to manifest oneself in the form of Mañjughoṣa by means of the seed-syllable itself. (*Sādhanamālā*, p. 138).

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) has the nature of abandoning improper attachment. What is equanimity? Equanimity is the practice of the supreme benefit toward all beings—whether they are harmful or beneficial—having abandoned the bonds of aversion and attraction; or alternatively, it is the spontaneous engagement in the state of the Dharma that benefits others, free from any underlying tendency toward affection. (Sūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya, p. 173)

Alternatively, equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the disregard for all irrelevant activities, foremost among which are the eight worldly concerns: gain and loss, fame and infamy, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. (Sā. Mā., p.

203) One should cultivate equanimity in the form of bringing forth the path that is the antidote to the afflictions (*kleśa*). (Sā. Mā., p. 225) Equanimity is the mental state characterized by the absence of both attraction and aversion toward friends, neutrals, and enemies; it takes the form of [realizing] "this is merely sentient beings" through the equality of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). (Sā. Mā., p. 385)
Equanimity... which has the aspect of bringing about the supreme [state] as the antidote to all primary and secondary afflictions. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
13b) Ulūkāsyā is right livelihood; Ulūkāsyā. (Vajra-tilaka, p. 56)
The "lotus of the uṣṇīṣa" is the lotus of the uṣṇīṣa because great bliss (*mahāsukha*) dwells within it; thus, it is the "abode of great bliss.
Therein lies the "abode of all-emptiness," which is the peak of Mount Meru known as Jālandhara, consisting of the *ḍākinījāla*. (Dohakoṣavyākhyā, p. 151). [The term] *ūṣmā*...
In the stomach, there is heat (*ūṣmā*) because it carries the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*);
in the throat, there is supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), such as the ability to travel through space and so forth. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 45; Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā, p. 47)
The bases of psychic power are four: the basis of psychic power consisting of desire,
and the basis of psychic power consisting of energy.
The basis of psychic power of investigation and the basis of psychic power of mind.
The basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of the abandonment of concentration through desire.

The basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of the exertion of energy and concentration; the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of the exertion of investigation and concentration;
and the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of the exertion of mind and concentration. (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p. 53)

The basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is that which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and transformed by relinquishment; through dissociation from conditioned things, it is endowed with the abandonment of substantial creation. Thus, when the five factors are combined, there are twenty types of the four bases of psychic power. (Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī-ṭīkā, p. 54) Psychic power is half [of the path].

Because the root *ṛdh* is listed in the *Dhātupārāyaṇa* with the meaning "to increase," *ṛddhi* refers to perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), in which all the qualities of a Buddha—such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*)—attain growth.

Since they are like the feet of that [enlightenment], being the causes for its attainment, they are called the "bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*). (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p. 54)
A solitary tree is one whose shade is not overtaken by another tree,
and which does not itself overtake another.
That is the single tree (*ekavṛkṣa*). (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 21b) The letter *e* is said to be the letter *e*, which is the *bhaga*. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 2a)
Among the various designations— *ekāra*, *ekāra-rahasya*, *padma*, *dharmodaya*, *khadhātu*, *mahāsukhāvāsa*, *siṃhāsana*, *bhaga*, and *guhya*— the designation *ekāra* alone is not the primary one,
because all of them equally establish the emptiness of all aspects (*sarvākāraśūnyatā*).

...Thus, because the syllables *eka* and *ra* establish the nature of the bodhicitta as the indivisibility of emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects and non-referential compassion toward all phenomena (*sarvadharmanirālambakaruṇā*) (Vi.

Pra., p. 34). "In the secret place, or in the element of space (*khadhātu*), in the *bhaga*, in the *dharmodaya*, or in the lotus—seated upon the lion-throne, the Vajrī was described by me in another tantra" (Vi. Pra., p. 39). Thus.

By that lord of yogis through whom the syllable *evaṃ*— which has the inseparable nature of emptiness and compassion— is realized, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and so forth are realized.
That very Mahāmudrā is the form of the casket of Dharma, arising from the Dharmakāya.
Therefore, for those Karaṇḍakaṇṭhas, that very [state] is the awakening to the essence, the dress, the ornament, and the adornment of their own Lord Vajradhara— in other words, it is beautiful.
And so it is said in the Hevajra:
That which is divine, shaped like the letter E, adorned in its center with the syllable Vaṃ,
is the abode of all happiness and the jewel-casket of the Buddhas.
It is also stated elsewhere:
"The letter *e* is the Mother, while the letter *va* is the Lord of Rati;
the Bindu is the Unstruck (*anāhata*) Knowledge, and from it all other letters are born. (Dvayopadeśakrama-vyākhyā, p. 68)
Of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma, he is the father and mother who are the support of them all; likewise, the two syllables have been proclaimed.
The letter *e* is the mother, and the letter *va* is remembered as the father;
the *bindu* therein is their union, and that union is most wonderful.
The letter *e* is said to be the lotus, and the letter *va* is the vajra;
the bindu therein is the seed-syllable from which the three worlds are produced.
The letter *e* is wisdom (*prajñā*), and the letter *va* is the Lord of Bliss (*suratādhipa*).
The *bindu* is the unstruck reality (*anāhata-tattva*), and from it all other letters are born. Thus is the syllable *evaṃ*. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 13)

The syllable *Evaṃ* is Vajrasattva, the *bodhicitta*, Kālacakra, the Ādibuddha, the yoga consisting of wisdom and means, the non-dual nature of the object of knowledge and the knowledge itself, beginningless and endless, peaceful, the Assembly (*Samāja*), the Vow (*Saṃvara*), and so forth—by these and many other names, the non-dual yoga consisting of wisdom and means, which is without parts, must be understood by the yogi. Thus the Blessed One said in the *Mūlatantra*: *(Vimalaprabhā, p. 34)*
The letter E is the curved letter Ma, the abode of the bliss of all Buddhas;
in the expanse of space, this Vajrasattva exists through the union of body, speech, and mind. (Vi.pra., p. 35).
Thus by me...
By the syllable *e* is the goddess Locanā; by the syllable *vaṃ*, Māmakī is remembered.
By the syllable *ma*, Pāṇḍarā; and by the syllable *yā*, Tāraṇī is remembered.
(Hevajratantra 1.1.22). The syllable *e* is said to be the *bhaga*; the syllable *vaṃ* is remembered as the *kuliśa*.
"Maya" is said to be movement; it is the characteristic of Vajradhara. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol.
2a) The letter E is to be known as the earth, while Locanā is the action-seal (karmamudrā).
Sixty-four channels are situated in the emanation wheel (nirmāṇacakra).
The syllable *vaṃ* should be known as water; it is Dharmamudrā Māmakī, who is situated at the heart in the eight-petaled lotus of the wheel of dharma.
The letter *ma* is declared to be Fire; she is Mahāmudrā Pāṇḍarā, who resides in the enjoyment wheel (*saṃbhogacakra*) at the throat, upon the eight-petaled lotus.
The letter YĀ is said to be Māruta; her mudrā is Samayatāriṇī.
She resides in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), within the thirty-two-petaled lotus. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
2b) [She is] Airāvatī.
Airāvatī flows with speed like Airāvata. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 47) The faculty of wisdom is Airāvatī. (Vajratilaka, p. 54) Oḍiyāna.
"And likewise, this Oḍiyāna is said to be the right ear" (Vajravatī-tantra, p.
31). By way of the left ear, there is the movement through the sky-farer (*khecarī*) mode of the Caṇḍālī, which is the journey—the exiting outward;
therein, the "flying up" (*uḍḍiyana*) is the right ear (Vajravatī-ṭīkā, p. 31).
In the great seat of Oḍiyāna, Prabhāvatī is established; residing in the right ear, she dwells as the bearer of skin and impurities. (Vajravatī, p. 42). Oḍra.
The two breasts are proclaimed as Oḍra (*Va.
Ti.*, p. 33). Because she moves upward (*ūrdhvagamana*) and accepts (*rāti*) [the essence] from Oḍra, she is Caṇḍālī; thus, the two breasts are Oḍra (*Va. Ti. Ṭī.*, p. 33).
In Oḍra, the channel that carries bile is known as Mahābhairavikā (*Va. Ti.*, p. 44).
*Kakkola* is considered to be the lotus and *kakkolaka*. (*Hevajra Tantra* 2.3.60).
*Kakkola* is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena.
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 52a-b):
*Muṃmuṇi* is the syllable *Aṃ* at the navel; it is the *kakkola*. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 54b):
It is called *kaṅkāla* because, having reached the root of the ear, it impels the impurities of the skin. (Vajragarbha’s Commentary, p. 48).
The skeleton is in the form of a skeletal staff; likewise, O Sumeru, king of mountains, you are the skull. (Vajrāvalī, p.
62) The skull.

*Kapāla* is a lotus vessel (*padmabhājana*). (HeTa 2.3.58) It is called *kapāla* because it protects (*pālayati*) the face (*kaṃ*); thus it is a lotus (*kamala*). (HeTa Ṭīkā, fol. 62a) *Kabandha* [is] the mantra.
"Oṃ, asti, nāsti, praṇava, and kabandha" refer to the conventional bodhicitta according to the guru's oral tradition (Candrakīrti’s *Pradīpoddyotana-ṭīkā*, p.
103). But what is compassion like?
The resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) is: "I shall rescue the infinite realm of sentient beings who have fallen into the midst of the unfathomable and shoreless ocean of saṃsāra. (Sā. Mā., p.

57) Compassion (*dayā*) is the desire to uplift the worlds from suffering and even from the causes of suffering. (Sā. Mā., p. 97) Pity (*kṛpā*) is the desire to rescue [beings] from the cause of suffering and from suffering itself. (Sā. Mā., p. 100)
What is compassion (*karuṇā*)? It is the desire to deliver sentient beings, who are afflicted by the three types of suffering, from the ocean of *saṃsāra*. (Sā. Mā., p.

115) In this context, compassion is characterized by the desire to rescue [beings] from suffering and from the causes of suffering. (Sā. Mā., p. 138) Compassion is the desire to rescue [beings] from suffering and from the causes of suffering. (Sā. Mā., p. 172)
Furthermore, what is compassion (*karuṇā*) like?
It is the desire to rescue [beings] from suffering and the causes of suffering;

or rather, compassion is the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) to rescue those sentient beings who have entered the iron house of cyclic existence, which is ablaze with the great fire of the three types of suffering.
Alternatively, compassion is the desire to rescue from the ocean of saṃsāra those sentient beings who are afflicted by the three types of suffering (*Sā. Mā.*, p. 203);
it is the aspiration to remove the suffering of others (*Sā.
Mā.*, p. 315); it is the activity of destroying the suffering of others, which is compassion (*Sā. Mā.*, p. 385).

Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the correct intention (*samyag-āśaya*) consisting of the thought: "I shall establish all sentient beings in this very King of Gnosis and surround them with all the requisites for happiness. (Jñānasiddhi, p. 135).
Compassion is characterized by the removal of all suffering. (Hevajra-tantra-ṭīkā, fol. 13b).
Compassion is cultivation with an object. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol.
23b) The agent is the moment of the emission of semen, characterized by the *ālayavijñāna*, which is innate bliss according to worldly convention. (Vimalaprabhā, p. 215)
Camphor is considered to be semen (*śukra*); it is known as *karpūraka*. Camphor... [is] born from all the *yoginīs*. (He. Ta. 2.3.59) Camphor... [is] born from all the *yoginīs*.
"Of the nature of innate bliss, imperishable, full, and moving through the sky" (Hevajra Tantra 2.4.27).
"Candor [camphor] itself is Nairātmyā; bliss has the form of Nairātmyā.
Her bliss, Mahāmudrā, resides in the circle of the navel" (Hevajra Tantra 2.4.40).
Action is action; it consists of reflection on body, speech, and mind (*kāyavākcittacintā*).
Conduct is bodily action, and verbal [action] is the teaching of the Dharma.
The mental action of the wise one who is free from conceptual construction is a formal commitment (*samādāna*).
It is said that such action is unfailing (*amogha*) (Sūtrasamuccaya 2.8).
This is the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of action and gnosis.
The action seal (karmamudrā) possesses breasts and hair;
the wisdom seal (jñānamudrā) is imagined by one’s own mind;
the great seal (mahāmudrā) is free from conceptual construction and has the nature of a reflected image.

The accomplishment (*siddhi*) of these is threefold: the accomplishment of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), which belongs to the desire realm; the accomplishment of the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*), which belongs to the form realm and is characterized by the existence of the form-realm birth; and the accomplishment of the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), which is devoid of both existence and non-existence and is endowed with the excellence of all aspects. (Vi.pra., p. 21)

The action seal (karmamudrā) possesses breasts and hair; she is the cause of the bliss of the desire realm (kāmadhātu). "Action" consists of activities such as kissing, embracing, touching the secret parts, and striking with the vajra.
Therefore, the *mudrā* characterized by that [bliss] is the "counter-acting" one (*pratyakāriṇī*).
Here, "conviction" (*pratyaya*) is characterized by the bliss of emission (*kṣarasukha*). It is called *mudrā* because it bestows *muda*—that is, a specific kind of bliss or delight. (Se. Ṭī., p. 56)
Karma refers to the mental activity of body, speech, and mind; the mudrā that is predominant therein has the nature of conceptual construction.
Within that *karmamudrā*—
Blisses arise there, differentiated by the distinctions of moments.
From the knowledge of the moment, the knowledge of bliss is established in the *evaṃkāra*. ...
Therefore, having obtained the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the fruit of quiescence (*niṣpanda*) arises.
The vibration that is similar [to it] is motionless.
...How can knowledge called "the innate" (*sahaja*), which is unconditioned, arise through the artificial "action-seal" (*karmamudrā*)?
...The lotus of the woman who is the instrument of action is a mine of jewels consisting of a mass of blisses.

When that clear abode, through the union of the essences of the *bola* and *kakkola*, becomes contained within the jewel of the *saṃvṛti-bodhicitta* by means of the *avadhūtī*, then a gnosis arises known as "the momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) and also called "the innate" (*sahaja*).
That innate [gnosis] is not motionless (*niṣpanda*).

In the *Abhayapaddhati-saṃgraha* (pp. 32–33), it is stated that in the [water] initiation (*abhiṣeka*), the triad of wisdom, gnosis, and bliss, accompanied by the four moments, exists in its own essential nature;

and in Haṭhayoga, the fruit of the motionless state (*niṣpanda*) is said to arise from the action-seal (*karmamudrā*). In the *Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā* (p. 62), it is said: "By means of the action-seal, there is the state of the pleasure of the 'alkali' (*kṣāra*)."
The vase consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*) consists of six types, characterized by the water, the crown, the vajra, the bell, the name, and the master (*ācārya*).
All of these are designated as "vase consecrations" because they involve the operation of the vase.
And these six consecrations are irreversible because they possess the nature of the six Tathāgatas.
To explain: the water consecration consists of mirror-like gnosis and has Akṣobhya as its nature;
the crown consecration consists of the gnosis of equality and has Ratnasambhava as its nature.

The Vajra initiation consists of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) and has Amitābha as its intrinsic nature. The Lord’s initiation (*adhipatyābhiṣeka*) takes the form of the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) and has Amoghasiddhi as its intrinsic nature. The Name initiation, through the cessation of ignorance, consists of the wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*viśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*) following from knowledge (*vidyā*), and has Vairocana as its essential form.
The master initiation (ācāryābhiṣeka), however, has the nature of vajra-gnosis;
and herein there is the fivefold initiation,
because of the activity of the five vidyās, Locanā and the others.

And here, for the purpose of washing away the impurity of ignorance, the water initiation (salilābhiṣeka) should be conferred by the Vajrācārya in the form of Akṣobhya upon the disciple who assumes the form of Vairocana. Likewise, in every case, the pride [of identity] is the crown initiation (mukuṭābhiṣeka), which is the future state of Buddhahood and serves as the unmanifest uṣṇīṣa. ... One should perform the procedure of the vajra initiation as if it were the planting of the seed of indivisible gnosis (abhedyajñāna).

In this way, the vajra-bell (*vajraghaṇṭā*)—measuring twelve finger-widths (*aṅgula*) according to the previous intention, with its face turned downward—is likewise adorned with two rows of vajras at the top and bottom to signify that it possesses the nature of all phenomena through the non-substantiality of the union of the lotus and the vajra. It serves to awaken one to the fact that the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) is an indestructible seal of gnosis (*abhedya-jñāna-nigada*). Then, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with this resounding vajra-bell.

Because it brings about the awakening to all dharmas without exception, the vajra initiation is bestowed first—transcending even the vajra-bell initiation which, though it serves as a cause for this [awakening], is intended here to demonstrate its preeminence and establish its causal nature.

This is for the purpose of establishing that "all dharmas are by name," and for the purpose of providing the introductory narrative for the name suitable for the future state of a Lord of Munis; thus, by discarding the former name, the name-initiation is performed according to the family and lineage of one's own deity.

And the master initiation (*ācāryābhiṣeka*) is characterized by the commitments of the vajra, the commitments of the bell, the commitments of the mudrā, the authorization regarding fitness, the vow, the prophecy, and the consolation. (*Ārya-Vajrāvalī-saṃgraha*, p. 36–38) Kaliṅga, moreover, is said to be the mouth. (*Vajra-tantra-ṭīkā*, p. 33)

*Kaliṅga* is [the face], so called because it "marks" (*liṅgayati*) or brings about (*gamayati*) *ka*, which is bliss (*sukha*), since joy arises merely by seeing it at the time of service. (Vajravatī-ṭīkā, p.
33). Śyāmādevī, however, is seated at the side in Kaliṅga. (Vajravatī, p. 45).
Regarding the phrase "the time of the Kali age, the time of the Kali age," what is this *kali*? It is the series of consonants beginning with the letter *ka*.
The letter *ka* is the mouth of all consonants because it is taught at the beginning; or alternatively, it should be understood as being of the nature of *rajas*.
Likewise, its *samaya* (convention) is the *asamaya* (non-convention), which is called the "melodious assembly" (*svaramelāpaka*).
Herein, what is the *ali*? *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa; ca, cha, ja, jha, ña; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa; ta, tha, da, dha, na; śa, ṣa, sa, ka*—this *ali* is the series of consonants.
Herein is the *asamaya* (the non-conventional): *a ā i ī ṛ ṝ u ū ḷ ḹ aṃ aḥ*;
*a ā e ai ar ār o au al āl aṃ aḥ*;
*ha hā ya yā ra rā va vā la lā ha haḥ*. This is the *asamaya-svaramelāpaka* (the non-conventional melodic union).
The "time of the Kali age" (*kaliyugasamaya*) refers to that time when one joins with *kali* (conflict/impurity). (Vi. Pra., p.
46) "Conceptualization" (*kalpanā*) is the mental construction, the activity of the transformation of the intellect, and so forth. (Gu. Sa. Pra., p. 211)
The five degenerations are characterized by afflictions, the eon, sentient beings, craving, and lifespan. (Se. Ṭī., p.
3) The five degenerations are: the degeneration of afflictions...
the defilement of views,
the defilement of sentient beings, and the defilement of lifespan.
And the defilement of the aeon (*kalpakaṣāya*).
(From the *Dharmasaṃgraha*, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkārabhāṣya, Vol. 1, p. 335).
Musk.
Urine is known as *kastūrikā*. (He. Ta. 2.3.59) *Kākāsyā* refers to the completion of the ritual; thus, she is *kākāsyā*. (Va. Ti., p. 56)
*Kāñcī* is said to be the heart; (*Vajratilaka*, p.
33). It approaches, goes toward, and rushes to *kaṃ*, which is bliss.

The Heart [Cakra] is so called because it is endowed with a tube for the daughters of Māra, which resembles a plantain flower, hangs downward, drips drops of nectar, and has the form of the syllable *HŪṂ*. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
34). Hayakarṇā, however, residing in the waist, always carries excrement. (Vajratilaka, p. 45). Kātyāyanī.
From the passing of mucus until it reaches the knees of Kātyāyanī (Va.
Ti. Ṭī., p. 46). A Kāpālika is so called because he is capable (*kṣama*) of protecting (*pālitum*) "ka" [which means] happiness (*sukha*); thus, he is a Kāpālika (Ca. Ko. Vyā., p. 36).
One who protects the conventional bodhicitta (*saṃvṛtibodhicitta*) is a *kāpālika* (as stated in the *Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra-koṣavyākhyā*, p.
63). The desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is sixfold:

the Realm of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*), the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*), the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati*), and the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*paranirmitavaśavartin*); thus, the desire realm is sixfold (as stated in the *Guhyasamājapradīpoddyotana*, p. 169).
The Lord of the desire realm is the desire realm itself, which consists of all women; he becomes the Lord who sports with them all. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 59)

Those beings who delight in desire, yet whose sole nature is suchness and who are ever-yoked to the permanence of suchness—they, those beings who delight in desire, would be the most excellent in the supreme accomplishment. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 47)
*Kāmarūpa* is considered to be the two armpits (*kakṣau*). (Vajratilaka, p. 33).
*Kāmarūpa* refers to that whose form (*rūpa*)—meaning its appearance—is desirable (*kāma*); it is the pair of armpits. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 33).
The channel that carries the eye and is situated in Kāmarūpa is renowned as Airāvatī; it is cultivated through the perception of forms. (Vajratārāsādhana, p. 44).
[The objects of] desire.
The gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika and other realms are called *kāma* because they desire and long for form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects]. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana, p.
86). Furthermore, "food of desire" refers to the objects of the senses such as form; they are called *kāma* because they are desired and longed for.

The apprehension of these [objects] by means of the sense-faculties is the nutriment of desire (*kāmāhāra*). Body, mental formations, feeling, perception, form, and consciousness as well. (S.Ṭī., p. 31)
The body consists of the five wisdoms; it is the five Buddhas, the supreme non-duality. (A.Kr.
73) As for the body wheel, within the body wheel are the ḍākinīs who dwell externally and in the subterranean realms. (V.Ti., p. 48)

In the body wheel (*kāyacakra*), there are eight channels (*nāḍī*) residing in the underworld (*pātāla*), known as the *melāpaka*, *upamelāpaka*, *śmaśāna*, and *upaśmaśāna*. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, 46) The four bodies (*kāyacatuṣṭaya*):
the body is fourfold through the division of the *nirmāṇa*, *saṃbhoga*, *dharma*, and *svābhāvika* [bodies]. (Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā, p. 27)
Through the cessation of the waking state, one becomes free from conceptual construction; by the cessation of the *kāyabindu*, the *nirmāṇakāya* [is realized] in the forehead.

This being so, the dissolution of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists in the cessation of the dream state, occurs at the throat through the cessation of the *vāgbindu*; this is the *saṃbhogakāya*.

In the states of waking and dreaming, the mind—constructing objects such as sounds and the like—is flickering, subject to emission, overcome by darkness (*tamas*), and has undergone the transformations of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Its binding is the disappearance of darkness and the destruction of deep sleep (*suṣupta*) through the restraint of the *bindu* of the mind; this is the *dharmakāya* within the heart...
The falling away of the *bindus* of the body and so forth is its binding, which, through innate bliss (*sahajasukha*), is the destruction of the fourth state (*turya*).
Through the restraint of the *bindu* of gnosis that has reached the *svara*, it is the innate body (*sahajakāya*) in the sky; thus it consists of the four bodies. (Se. Ṭī., p. 8)
The Dharma-body (dharmakāya) exists because its nature is that of the unconditioned Tathāgata;
the Enjoyment-body (saṃbhogakāya) exists because it is mere appearance; and the Emanation-body (nirmāṇakāya) exists because it consists of the imagined and the emanated.
The *svābhāvikakāya* (essential body) exists because of the single flavor (*ekarasa*) of the three bodies. As it has been said:
"The unconditioned mind and its phenomena are characterized by enjoyment;
that very [mind] is the manifold emanation, the seed of all intrinsic natures. (Abhisamayālaṃkāravṛtti-saṃgraha, p. 40)
For this very reason, they call the body the support of phenomena the *dharmakāya*.

...Therefore, the *dharmakāya* is precisely the body of union (*yuganaddhakāya*), distinct from both the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogika*) and the essential body (*svābhāvika*), and is to be personally realized by the yogi. (Se. Ṭī., p.
57) In the womb, it is the perfectly pure body; at the time of birth, it is the *dharma*; and during the stage of the teeth, it is the *dharma*. ...
From the teeth up to the limit of death, there arises the external emanation body of the Lord of Jinas.

The tree of the body consists of the five aggregates beginning with form, the six sense faculties, the elements, and the objects; because it is characterized by sprouts consisting of the grasped, the grasper, and the act of grasping, the body is apprehended as a supreme tree. (Candrakīrti’s *Prasannapadā*, p.
The gateway of the body has a single pillar, nine doors, and is gross; it has five presiding deities.
