The gateway situated within the nine streams is proclaimed as the "nine-doored" one.
The inferior bodily door is gross and fashioned by the deity (*daivata*).
Within that [bodily door], there are eight channels (*nāḍī*) beginning with the eyes: four in the right—eye, ear, and nostril—and likewise in the left. (Vajratilaka, pp. 19–20)

Those located in the *samayacakra* at the mouth, anus, and so forth, should be understood as being well-known by those very names, because of the practice of the *samaya* characterized by the enjoyment of sense objects. (Vajra-ṭippaṇī-ṭīkā, p. 46).
This is the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*).

The application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*) is the abiding of the mind in proximity to that mindfulness which [perceives]: "This body is empty because it is devoid of both [subjective and objective] phenomena" (*va. ti.
ṭī.*, p. 52). Kālacakra is called "Time" (*kāla*) because he is the supreme, imperishable, and non-falling moment within the *dharmadhātu*, characterized as space.
That itself is vajra-gnosis.

At that time, the wheel consisting of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases free from obscuration is the oneness of the three realms of existence, which is the object of knowledge free from obscuration.
That very thing is called the great maṇḍala of the vajra-realm.
The body of the Blessed One consists of wisdom and means; it possesses all aspects and all sense faculties, has the form of the *bindu*, and sustains the universal illusion (*viśvamāyā*).
Compassion is the embodiment of emptiness, and time (*kāla*) is that which has the nature of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
Emptiness is said to be the wheel (*cakra*); thus he is Kālacakra. (Se. Ṭī., p. 3)
The two-syllabled [mantra].
Or, according to the number of each individual syllable:
from the letter *kā* (kā), there is the dissolution (*laya*) of the cause (*kāraṇa*) into tranquility (*śānta*);
from the letter *ca* (ca), [the state] of the restless mind; and from the letter *kra* (kra), by means of the bonds of sequential progression (*krama*).
The cause is said to be the body of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). It is peaceful, free from conceptual construction due to the exhaustion of the waking state.
That very Blessed One Kālacakra, who consists of the four bodies and is the nature of wisdom and means, is described through the relationship between knowledge and the object of knowledge.
Skillful means has compassion as its essence and consists of the six superknowledges;
the wheel of the world is the aspect of the knowable,
and the knowable is the triple realm characterized by infinite phenomena.
That very wisdom, whose nature is emptiness and whose nature consists of all aspects—the oneness of these two is called Kālacakra (Se. Ṭī., p.
8). Compassion is the embodiment of emptiness; Kāla is that which has the form of conventional reality.
"Emptiness is said to be the wheel; Kālacakra is considered non-dual" (Vi.pra., p. 8).

"Kāla" is the supreme syllable, characterized by great bliss (*mahāsukha*); that whose body is the wheel consisting of the aggregates, elements, and so forth, which is free from obscurations and produced by that [Kāla], [is Kālacakra].
This is Kālacakra.
Furthermore, by means of each individual syllable:
from the letter *ka* comes the cause (*kāraṇa*) in the peaceful state, and from the letter *la* comes dissolution (*laya*) here indeed.
By the letter *ca* comes the binding of the flickering mind, and by the letter *kra* comes the binding in sequence.
The sequence (*krama*) is the emission of the drops (*bindu*) of the body and so forth;

its binding through innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) is the *Kālacakra*. Thus, that Blessed One, the sole Teacher, is one who maintains the existence of karma (*karmāstivādin*), not a creator (*kartṛ*). (Vi.pra., p. 17)

I pay homage to that Kālacakra, the progenitor of the supreme Victor, who is omniscient, the primordial Buddha, bowed to by the three worlds, the Wheel-Bearer (Kālacakrī), yet not [the mundane] Wheel-Bearer (Cakrī); at the base of whose lotus feet Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra have sought refuge—he who is beyond attributes and free from conceptual construction. (Kālacakratantra 2.92)
The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, whose lotus-like feet are worshipped by gods, asuras, nāgas, and others, is Kālacakra. (Vi.pra., p.
225) Kālacakrakavīra is the cause of the arising and destruction [of all things]; for those in saṃsāra, he is the sole hero, Kālacakrakavīra. (Vi.pra., p. 212)
*Kāli* [is so called] because of the blackness (*kāla*) of the world-appearance. (Candrakīrti’s *Vyākhyā*, p.
24) The thirty-four consonants beginning with the letter *ka* are *kāli*. (Hevajra-tantra-ṭīkā, fol. 6a)
Āli is the wind arising from the left nostril;
the other is kāli. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
9b) Kāli consists of the thirty-four consonants beginning with *ka*.
Kālī is the sun. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
15a) The sun [is present] in the form of Kālī. (Hevajra Tantra 1.8.5) Kālī is the means (*upāya*). (Hevajra Tantra 1.8.11)
"Kāliñjara is considered auspicious; Kāliñjara is regarded as such. (Hevajra Tantra 2.3.57).
"The Kāliñjaras are the initiates. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 54a).
The Kāliñjara wind.
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 54b) For pacification, the sacrificial pit is circular; for nourishment, the pit is square.
A triangle is prescribed for the rite of killing; one should accomplish the remaining rites right here as well.
For the rite of pacification (śāntika), it should be one cubit or one and a half cubits in height;
for the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika), two cubits in height and one cubit in width is considered appropriate.
Twenty-one finger-breadths in length, it is used for killing when directed downward or upward.
It should be white in color for pacification, yellow for enrichment,
black for killing, and red is proclaimed for subjugation.
Just as it is in subjugation, so it is in attraction; as it is in hatred and the like, so it is in killing.
Sesame seeds are for pacification, curd for nourishment, and likewise thorns for killing;
thorns are prescribed for hatred and the like, while the lotus is for subjugation and attraction. (Hevajra Tantra 2.1.6–10).
And the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is the circle of the navel. (Vimalaprabhā, p. 67).
In the *nirmāṇacakra*, the navel region is the fire-pit; [it is so called] because of the casting of the oblation (*havis*) therein. (*Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā*, p.
67) *Kunduru*.
The union of the two organs is *kunduru*. (He. Ta.
2.3.60) *Kula* refers to the moon of the wrong path (*kumārgacandra*) and so forth, which dissolves into that *avadhūtī*.
That Avadhūtī, which is pure by nature, is to be understood by the term *kula*.
"O Great Compassionate One, they say there are five supreme families: Vajra, Padma, Karma, Tathāgata, and Ratna. (Cakrasaṃvaratantra-kalpa-vyākhyā, p. 126)
The banks are of six kinds, but in brief they are fivefold;
subsequently, they become threefold through the division of body, speech, and mind.

"Because by means of this [knowledge], the five families (*kula*)—which consist of the five elements and have the nature of the five aggregates (*skandha*)—are reckoned (*kulyate*) and counted (*gaṇyate*), it is called 'family' (*kula*).
The family is known to be fivefold, distinguished according to the divisions of the castes (*varṇa*). (Hevajra Tantra 1.5.5, 9–10)
Thus, in intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā), there are five Kaulika Buddhas.
The Ḍombī is renowned as belonging to the Vajra family, the Naṭī likewise to the Padma family,
the Caṇḍālī to the Ratna family, and the Dvija is considered to belong to the Tathāgata family.
The washerwoman and the woman of the artisan caste—these mudrās bestow excellent accomplishment.
Their semen is the *vajra*; having worshipped it, the practitioner should drink it. (HeTa 2.3.61–63).
*Kuḥ* means the earth.
Because he takes—that is, accepts—those beings established therein through the gift of jewels, he is the Jewel-Standard (*ratnaketu*) family (*kula*).
The state of being a family (*kulatā*) is called "the birth" (*jānu*). (Ku.sa.pra., p. 68; Va.ti., p. 35)
Because she cuts away false conceptualizations, she is Kulatā at the knees (*va. ti. ṭī.*, p.
35). At Kulatā resides Mahāvīryā, who carries the lion’s milk (*va. ti.*, p. 48).
[He is] the wielder of the vajra (*kuliśadharaḥ*).
This very Great Void of five syllables, consisting of thirty-six aspects, is called the *vajra* by the Victors.
One who bears that is the *Vajradhara*.
The six-syllabled *bindu-śūnya*, the letter *E*, is the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), whose nature is the emptiness of all forms.

... Thus, the six-syllable *dharmodaya* consisting of the *bindu* and the voids is the *ekāra*, the wielder of the vajra; this is emptiness with an object (*sālambā-śūnyatā*), having the nature of a reflected image (*pratisenā*). (Vi.pra., p. 49) "Born of a tortoise" (*kūrmajā*) means it is as indestructible as the back of a tortoise; because it is bound by a garland of bones, it is "born of a tortoise" at the center of the eyebrows. (Va.ti.ṭī., p. 44) Compassion (*kṛpā*).

"Compassion is like a wish-fulfilling gem, accomplishing all that is wholesome. (Pratyabhijñā-vimarśinī 4.10) "The term *kṛpīṭa* is considered to mean a small drum (*ḍamaruka*). (Hevajra-tantra 2.3.57)

*Kośala* refers to the tip of the nose (*nāsikāgra*). (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, p. 33). Because it flows (*śalati*) or carries (*vahati*) the mucus (*siṅghāṇa*), that [tip] is *kośala*. (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p. 33).
"In Kośala, the divine [goddess] who devours wine is filled with a garland of entrails" (Vātūlatantra, p.
44). "That which is Kaulika is the Kaulika, the unsurpassed" (Pratyabhijñā-vimarśinī, 1.23).
The two stages are said to be innate (*sahaja*), yet they are divided into two distinct types:
that which possesses the form of a deity belongs to the side of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) and is characterized by concealment.
The nature of manifest bliss, however, pertains to the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*).
The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon the two truths.
[It concerns] both the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*) and the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*) itself. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 2b)
The teaching of the Vajra-holders is based upon two stages: the stage of generation and the stage of completion. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.

The teaching of the Dharma by the Vajradharas relies upon two stages. The stage of generation has been explained; now I shall explain the stage of completion. (Hevajra Tantra 1.8.24–25) [This concerns] the four moments.
Having attained the four moments— the variegated, the ripened, the crushed, and the characterized— yogins know them in this way.
The manifold and diverse, known as embracing, kissing, and so forth, is the ripening; its reversal is the enjoyment of bliss through gnosis.

Vimarda is said to be the proclamation, "I have experienced bliss," and Vilakṣaṇa is that which is other than the three [preceding moments], being devoid of both passion and its absence. (Dohākośavyākhyā, p. 68).
These are the moments (kṣaṇas).

There are four moments—the wondrous (*vicitra*), the ripening (*vipāka*), the distinctive (*vilakṣaṇa*), and the increasing (*virdā*). In the case of consecration (*seka*), it should be understood that the distinctive moment occurs in the middle.
Furthermore, in Haṭhayoga, it should be understood that the state of abiding occurs at the end of both the innate (*sahaja*) and the distinctive moments.

And this was taught by the Blessed One regarding the yoga of sexual union (*seka-haṭha-yoga*): (Abhidhānavatārasaṃgraha, p. 32) there are four moments—namely, *vicitra*, *vipāka*, *vimarda*, and *vilakṣaṇa*. (Hevajratantra 1.1.24) These are the [four] patiences (*kṣānti*).

And patience (*kṣānti*) consists in enduring blows such as those from cruel, heated saws and the like (*Avalokanāvatārasaṃgraha*, p. 3). She is Khagānanā because her face has the shape of a bird’s beak (*Vajratilakaṭīkā*, p. 48).

Khagānanā is the factor of enlightenment of vigor (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). (Vajratilaka, p. 55). A sword (*khaḍga*) is so called because it cuts through the enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*). (Jñānasiddhi, 15.25).

Khaṇḍakapālī is so called because she "holds" (kalayati), that is, impels, the "fragment" (khaṇḍa)—the *bodhicitta* located in the head—in the form of nails and teeth; thus she is Khaṇḍakapālī. (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, p. 48).
[She is] Khaṇḍarohā.
It is called *khaṇḍa* because it moves by breaking through the space of fire (*teja-ākāśa*);
because it ascends right there through the purification of that [space], it is *Khaṇḍarohā*. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
41) The application of mindfulness to the Dharma is *Khaṇḍarohā*. (Vajratilaka, p. 51)
She is called Khaṇḍarohā because she first breaks apart the Tathāgatalocanā and others, and then causes them to rise again and be generated. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
48) The factor of enlightenment of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) is Khaṇḍarohā. (Vajratilaka, p. 55) The sphere of space (khadhātu).
This supreme reality, peaceful and established as that which is called the space-element (*khadhātu*),
is obtained through the union of the vajra and the lotus and from the oral tradition. (Guhyasiddhi 3.26) Kharvarī.
She is *kharvarī* because she is harsh (*khara*) due to the burning of the three wheels, yet excellent (*varā*) because of being replenished again thereafter. (*Vajratilaka-ṭīkā*, p.
47) The faculty of virility is *kharvarī*. (*Vajratilaka*, p.
54) The sky-farers (*khecaryah*).
The channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) extending from Pullīra to Mālava are the *khecaryas*. (Va. Ti. Ṭī., p. 27).
*Kheṭa* means movement; *kheṭa* [is derived from] *kha* [space/sky]. (He. Ta. 2.3.56).
The eight qualities are:
aṇimā, laghimā, garimā,
lordship, mastery, and agency;
The eight qualities are: being edible, and the absence of desire for one's own wishes; thus [is] the eightfold quality. (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p. 27). [Thus says] the Guru.

The Lord of the World, the Guru who bestows the accomplishment of all aims, is to be venerated. (Prajñāpāramitopadeśa-vṛtti-siddhi 2.26) The Guru is indeed the Buddha, and he is also the Dharma and the Saṅgha; through his grace, the excellent Triple Gem is known.

"He is the guide who reveals the path for those blinded by the darkness of ignorance. Non-dual, infused with compassion, and endowed with wisdom and skillful means, the Guru—who is not divided by the distinctions of emptiness—is composed of all the Buddhas. (Jñānasiddhi 1.24–25; Abhayākaragupta’s *Āmnāyamañjarī* 93–94)
The secret, the secret, the supreme Vajrayāna above the Śrāvakayāna and Pratyekabuddhayāna. (Vimalaprabhā, p. 17). Secret worship.

The worship of the Tathāgata is characterized by the union of the two organs. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 187). Secret Siddhi: Transgressions of the samaya and so forth are known as "Secret Siddhi. (Guhyasiddhi 6.103).
The Lord of Secrets (Guhyādhipati) is the secret; the Vajrayāna is superior to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
He is the Lord (adhipati) by virtue of being the compiler (saṃgītikāraka) of that [Vajrayāna].
Likewise, according to worldly convention, by the word "Guhyaka" [are meant] the Yakṣas;

their lord is the Guhyādhipati. By means of the lion’s roar of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, through the individual languages of all sentient beings, the one who sets forth the Dharma is the Guhyādhipati, Śrī Vajrapāṇi. (Se. Ṭī., pp. 1–2)

The secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*) is the bestowing of the *bodhicitta* produced by both [the master and the consort] at the same time, for the purpose of making the field of wisdom and faith fertile and for the purpose of guarding the commitments (*samaya*).
Its etymological derivation is "that which illuminates through the secrets of wisdom and means" (*prajñopāyaguhyābhyāṃ dīpayati*). (Abhisamayamañjarī, p. 38)

The experience of the fourfold bliss consisting of the four moments by means of the jewel situated in the secret [place], according to the guru’s instruction, is called the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*), because it is not to be revealed to yogins through conceptual meditations (*prapañcabhāvanā*).
In this initiation, the instruction on the meditation upon the pledge-seal (*samayamudrā*) for those of middling faculties is taught. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 7b)
Supreme bliss is the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*).
In some *Caryātantras*, the mutual gazing that indicates the passion between wisdom and means is the secret initiation by virtue of its purification.
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 50a-b)
"Excrement is said to be fourfold and equal. (Hevajra Tantra 2.3.59).
[This refers to] the household deity.
"The anus, however, is the house-deity" (Vajra-tilaka, p. 34).
The deity of the house—that is, of the body—is Vairocana; he is the house-deity as the fecal constituent (*viḍ-dhātu*).
Because it is the support for that [constituent], the anus is the "house-deity" (Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p. 34).
She constantly carries pus and resides as the deity of the house;
she is the renowned Ḍākinī and Supreme Goddess known as Khaṇḍarohā. (Vajra-tantra, p. 46). [She is] Godāvarī.

Likewise, the Godāvarī should be known as having the nature of the left ear. (Vajratārā-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 32) She is called *godā* because she bestows (*dadāti*) the earth (*gām*), that is, the ground (*bhuvam*) or the nature of the earth (*bhūsvarūpam*), which is the *nirmāṇacakra*; and she is called *avarī* because she is chosen (*vriyate*) or covered (*cchādyate*) by it; thus, [the compound] is *godāvarī*, the left ear. (Vajratārā-tantra-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī, p. 32)
The channel located in Mahorusthāna is situated in the Godāvarī;
it is renowned as Vīramatī and remains there with a firm form. (Vajravārāhī-tantra, p. 42).
This is the state of the grasped and the grasper.

The progenitor of the Victors perceives sound as empty; wind [perceives] the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu), fire the odor, water the taste, and earth the tactile sensation. (Kālacakra-tantra 2.20) [The bell].
Wisdom is designated as the bell (*prajñā ghaṇṭā*).

The commitment of the bell (*ghaṇṭāsamaya*) is the commitment of the bell for the purpose of demonstrating that "you are beyond the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma" (*caturaśītidharmaskandhasahasrapara*). (Abhisamayamañjarī, p. 38) (Jñānasiddhi 15.24)

The "woodworm" is so called because it consumes the net of afflictions such as passion, just as a woodworm consumes straw; thus, it is that very [consciousness] which is the woodworm. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 83)
"Cakra" [is so called] because it cuts through ignorance. (Jñānasiddhi 15.24) "Cakra" refers to the assembly known as the *khadhātu*, which is the purification of the sense objects and so forth.
"Through the union of *bola* and *kakkola*, his bliss is realized. (Hevajra Tantra 2.3.28).
Regarding the four wheels (*cakra*):
in the *nirmāṇacakra*, there is a sixty-four-petaled lotus.
The wheel of Dharma has eight petals; the wheel of enjoyment has sixteen petals;
the wheel of great bliss has thirty-two petals. (Hevajra Tantra 1.1.23)
The Dharma-chakra, the Sambhoga-chakra, and the Nirmāṇa-chakra are located respectively in the heart, the throat, and the yoni;
these three wheels are the body, speech, and mind.
The Body-chakra is in the yoni.
The wheel of speech is at the throat;
the wheel of mind is at the heart;
and the wheel of great bliss, whose nature is the thorough knowledge of these three, is to be known at the crown of the head.
Within these very four wheels, there are four mudrās whose intrinsic natures are the elements of earth, water, fire, and air, known as *evam-mayā*.
(HeTaṬī, fol.
6a-b) Likewise, [there are] the Dharma, Sambhoga, Nirmāṇa, and Mahāsukha [bodies].
The three bodies are established in the navel, heart, throat, and head.
Wherever the birth of all sentient beings without exception is proclaimed, there the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) exists; emanation is considered to be stable.
That by which [something] is produced or emanated is considered the *nairmāṇika* (emanation body);
but the *dharmakāya*, whose nature is the mind itself, resides in the heart.
The enjoyment of the six [flavors] in the form of tastes is said to be *saṃbhoga*;
the *saṃbhogacakra* is at the throat, and *mahāsukha* is situated at the head. ...
*Sthāvarī* is in the *nirmāṇacakra*, because emanation (*nirmāṇa*) is stable (*sthāvara*).
The Sarvāstivādin [school] arose at the Wheel of Dharma, and from it the discourse on the Dharma originated.
Because consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the enjoyment wheel (*saṃbhogacakra*) are at the throat, there is perception (*saṃvedana*);
because the Great Assembly (*mahāsaṃghī*) and the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) are situated in the head, there is great bliss (*mahāsukha*). (Hevajra Tantra 2.4.52–55, 59–60) Cakravartinī.
She whose nature it is to move within the wheels is Cakravartinī. (Va. ti. ṭī., p.
48) Right resolve is Cakravartinī. (Va. ti., p. 56) [She is] Cakravarmiṇī.
The wheels themselves are her armor and equipment; thus she is Cakravarmiṇī. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
48) Smṛtisambodhyaṅga is Cakravarmiṇī. (Vajratilaka, p. 55) [She is] Cakravegā.
Because its speed of going and coming is like that of a wheel within wheels, it is called *cakravegā*. (*Vajratilaka-ṭīkā*, p.
48) *Cakravegā* is a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). (*Vajratilaka*, p. 55) [She is] the fivefold eye (*cakṣuḥ-pañcaka*).
Through the sequence of knowledge, the flesh-eye, divine eye, Buddha-eye, wisdom-eye, and knowledge-eye will arise by the power of cultivation. (Se. Ṭī., p.
38) Here, first the beginner yogin perceives the universal image with the flesh-eye, even without the superknowledges;
thereafter, with the divine eye.
By virtue of the range of the superknowledges;
then, by means of the Buddha-eye, by virtue of the range of those free from passion;
then, by means of the wisdom-eye, by virtue of the range of the Bodhisattvas.
Then, by means of the eye of knowledge (*jñānacakṣus*), through the power of the limit of the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) and due to liberation from all substrates (*upadhi*),
the five eyes of the Tathāgata— beginning with the flesh-eye (*māṃsacakṣus*)— are thus described in relation to the vision of emptiness (*śūnyatādarśana*).
Other sentient beings, however, are like those blind from birth regarding the domain of the vision of emptiness.
The five eyes—the flesh eye, the dharma eye, the wisdom eye, [the divine eye, and the buddha eye]—(Se. Ṭī., p. 48/3).
The divine eye and the Buddha-eye. (From the *Dharmasaṃgraha*)
Caṇḍākṣī is so called because her two channels, the left and the other (the right), are fierce (*caṇḍa*), sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), or burning (*dāhaka*). Thus she is Caṇḍākṣī.
Because the two are illuminated by the middle [channel] (Va-ti-ṭī, p. 53):
"Caṇḍālī, having blazed up in the navel, burns the five Tathāgatas."
"And it burns; Locanā and the others have been burned; I am consumed; the moon flows.

(HeTa 1.1.31) Caṇḍā is wisdom (*prajñā*), because its nature is fierce (*caṇḍa*) in cutting through the primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa-upakleśa*). Āli is Vajrasattva; he is expressed by the word *caṇḍālī*. (HeTa Ṭīkā, 9b) Caṇḍā is wisdom, the syllable *Aṃ*.
Āli is Vajrasattva, the syllable *haṃ*.
The syllables *aṃ* and *haṃ* are Caṇḍālī.
Caṇḍā is the red Dharmodayā, and Āli is remembered as the first letter. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 10a)
Fierce wisdom (*caṇḍaprajñā*) is the investigation of the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) and the completion stage (*utpannakrama*).
The garland (*ālī*) is the mind consisting of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Therefore, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) are expressed by the term *caṇḍālī*. (Hevajratantra-ṭīkā, p. 10b)

Caṇḍālī is unsurpassed wisdom (*niruttara-prajñā*). Some say that the fourth empowerment (*caturthābhiṣeka*), characterized by the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*) and possessing the seven limbs of accomplishment, is the goal of the fourth meaning. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 10b)
Others maintain that the fourth meaning is wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) itself, which resembles the sky at the moment an arrow is released.

Others maintain that the fourth meaning is wisdom-knowledge itself, which is the nature of the primordial (*prakṛti*), the nature of transformation (*vikāra*), consisting of the arising from the primordial, and possessing a perfectly pure intrinsic nature that flows as the non-duality of the unified pair (*yuganaddha*).
Other alternative positions are not stated here for fear of prolixity. (Abhisamayamañjarī, p. 39)
That empowerment by which one perceives or is established in the nature of suchness (*tathatā-svabhāva*) is as follows:

when, through the external mudrā and according to the guru’s instruction, one takes as an object— by means of the yoga of non-objectification— the perfection of characteristics defined by the delimitation of a specific location, that is called the fourth empowerment.
However, it is not the case that the fourth consecration occurs merely through the teacher’s oral instruction.
Rather, it is at the very moment of that fourth consecration that the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā arises for those beings of the highest capacity. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 8a-b)
The fourth consecration is coemergent bliss (*sahajānanda*). ...In some [tantras], such as the *Anuttara*, the coupling of wisdom and means— the union of the couple (*dvandvasamāpatti*)—
and its purification is the fourth consecration.

The four divine abidings consist of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which takes the form of affection for all sentient beings as if they were one's only son; [compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity]. (He. Ta. Ṭī., p. 50a-b)

Having cultivated compassion, whose nature is the desire to rescue [beings] from the ocean of saṃsāra—the cause of suffering and non-suffering; joy, which arises from a mind overflowing with the taking of refuge in the Three Jewels; and equanimity, characterized by the absence of attachment... (Avatārasaṃgraha, pp. 4–5).
The cultivation of the four divine abodes:
(having performed the sevenfold or elevenfold worship,) one should practice the cultivation of the four divine abodes, beginning with loving-kindness and compassion. (Sā. Mā., p. 43)
One should cultivate the four divine abodes (*caturbrahmavihāra*), namely loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). (Sā. Mā., p.
115) Then, once the continuum of the mind has become stainless, one should cultivate compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. (Sa. Mā., p.

138) Immediately thereafter, one should cultivate the four divine abodes—designated as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—in the sequence to be described hereafter. (Sā. Mā., p. 202)
One should cultivate the four divine abodes (*caturbrahmavihāra*).

First, having contemplated loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward sentient beings in the form of affection directed toward one's own beneficial son, and then, through the awakening [realized] regarding a sick only child, one should subsequently cultivate compassion (*karuṇā*) toward all sentient beings. (Sā. Mā., p. 385)

Beholding that abundance of the perfection of happiness, one who is exceedingly joyful should meditate upon equanimity—free from weariness and voidness regarding the thought of what is harmful or beneficial toward all sentient beings—who is the singular embodiment of the true welfare of others.
Compassion is the act of uprooting their suffering. (Sūtrālaṃkāra, p. 389)
Loving-kindness is the establishment in happiness; sympathetic joy is through the state of stable happiness; and equanimity is by way of the nature of suchness. (Sā. mā., p. 405)

Having generated the mind of great awakening (*mahābodhicitta*), one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) which takes the form of bestowing divine happiness upon all sentient beings; compassion (*karuṇā*) which removes all suffering; joy (*muditā*) which takes the form of the resolve never to be separated from that happiness; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) characterized by the non-mental engagement with afflictions, secondary afflictions, the grasped, the grasper, and so forth.

Then, having meditated on emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—which is free from the stains of conceptual constructions regarding phenomena, persons, and the like, resembles the cloudless sky at midday in autumn, and has the singular nature of non-dual gnosis—one should consecrate oneself with the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* ("I am of the nature of the vajra of the gnosis of emptiness").
(The *Sādhanamālā*, p. 474) The fivefold offering (*pañcopacārapūjā*), the confession of misdeeds (*pāpadeśanā*), and so forth up to equanimity (*upekṣā*). (The *Sādhanamālā*, p.
576) The four bodies (*catuḥkāya*).
"The pure, enjoyment, and emanation [bodies]" (Vi.pra., p.
20). "Equal in four parts, it is called 'four-equal' excrement" (He.tan., 2.3.59).
Regarding "the four elders":
here, these four elders are to be propitiated by sentient beings for the sake of this world and the next.

Among them, the one elder who is supreme in knowledge—the Vajrācārya, whether a monk or a householder, who has attained the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and reached the stage of *Muditā* (Joy)—is declared by the Blessed One to be equal to ten monks and thus worthy of worship.

In his absence, one advanced in asceticism who wears the saffron robe is to be honored at all times by those who wear the saffron robe according to the number of years since their ordination, by ministers through the rite of consecration, and by householders because of his seniority in asceticism;
for householders lack such specialized knowledge.
One advanced in learning, a scholar, is worthy of worship as an illuminator of the Teaching and a subduer of adversaries and the hosts of Māra.
"These [deities] are to be propitiated by sentient beings for the sake of the next world;
a king who has increased his wealth is to be propitiated by those seeking enjoyments in this world. (Vi.pra., 54) [The moon].
The moon is the gnosis of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*) (Candrakīrti’s *Pañcakrama-vyākhyā*, p. 49).
The moon:
by the word "moon," the downward-moving wind (*apānavāyu*) is meant (Vimalaprabhā, p. 196).
The *apāna* wind is the lord of the channels of feces, urine, and the moon; it flows downward from the navel.
The lunar channel (*candranāḍī*, i.e., *lalanā*) begins at the throat and extends to the left as the channel belonging to the *saṃbhogakāya*. (Vi.pra., pp. 196–197)
"Resting in the center of the navel, it flows downwards and carries intoxication" (*Vajratilaka*, p.
80). This channel called *lalanā* on the left side, being downward-facing, carries intoxication from the throat down to the center of the navel (*Vajratilaka-ṭīkā*, p. 80).

The moon-maṇḍala, produced from vowels and consonants and possessing the thirty-two marks of a Buddha, which resides in the center of the lotus—that is called the moon-maṇḍala. (Vajra-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 62)

The moon-maṇḍala, which is the special seat of the Blessed One, is the very brain itself, condensed from the thirty-two bodhicittas consisting of the vowels and consonants situated between them. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 79). Regarding the left and right wheels, the moon and sun are the upward and downward flows of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, carrying the white and red elements; these are to be known as abiding in the *lalanā* and *rasanā*, flowing through the upward and downward [channels] of the left and right wheels.

By this it is stated that the external light of the moon and sun is indeed internal. (Vasiṣṭha-tattva-ṭīkā, p. 79) Mounted upon the two gateways and resting respectively below and above, these two known as the Moon and the Sun are proclaimed to be the pair of channels (nāḍī).
The coming and going of the heroes and ḍākinīs are the basis for the meanings of setting and rising, which abide in sleep and awakening respectively. (Vimalaprabhā, pp. 80–81) — *Carca* (Commentary).
Through merit, knowledge, purity, and the bliss that is self-realized, there is purification consisting of self-realization; one is not liberated by any other form of purification.

"Through the application of physicians and medicinal herbs, that is shown to be *caryā*; through the service of attendants, the act of moving about (*carana*) is remembered as *caryā*. (Sūtrasamuccaya 3–4). "The practice of difficult vows by command of the Gurus and Buddhas is *caryā*" (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 21a).
Conduct is also said to be threefold: with elaboration, without elaboration, and utterly without elaboration.
This practice of non-proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*) has been described for those of dull faculties.
For those of superior faculties, however, he will speak of the "practice of absolute non-proliferation" (*atyantaniṣprapañcacaryā*) in the fourteenth chapter.
For those of dull faculties, he will provide a mere indication of the "practice of proliferation" (*prapañcatācaryā*) in the seventh chapter of the second cycle.
The state of conceptual proliferation, and the state free from conceptual proliferation.

The threefold conduct consists of the "utterly non-conceptual" (*atyantaniṣprapañca*). It is called "conduct" (*caryā*) because one conducts oneself by means of it. All forms of conduct are the conceptual (*prapañca*), the non-conceptual (*niṣprapañca*), and the utterly non-conceptual (*atyantaniṣprapañca*) conducts. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, 46)
The foremost practice among them is the practice of Bhusuku. (Guhyasiddhiprakaraṇa, p.

59) Practice free from all conceptual proliferation is the practice of Samantabhadra. (Guhyasiddhiprakaraṇa, p. 73) Practice whose nature consists in removing the affliction of stinginess within the mental continuum of sentient beings is the practice of awakening. (Guhyasiddhiprakaraṇa, p. 81)
In whatever manner the welfare of sentient beings is accomplished— whether by means that are contrary to worldly norms or not contrary—
the engagement of practitioners according to their capacity in those various ways constitutes the conduct of a bodhisattva;
that is to say, what is the practice of mantra is the practice of the Tathāgata.
The gurus are those from whom they explain reality and mantra; these individuals who possess the mantra are "jewel-like persons" (*ratnapudgala*).

Having realized the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), their practice—that which is the proceeding by means of non-meditative yoga—is this very practice of the Tathāgatas. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p.
86) [This is] the mind.

The conception of mind (*cittasaṃjñā*) is twofold: mundane and supramundane. That which is mundane is characterized by conceptual construction (*vikalpalakṣaṇa*) and must be discarded. That which is supramundane is stainless, characterized by the *dharmakāya*, or the innate nature (*sahajasvarūpa*). (Dohākośavyākhyā, p. 92)

The mind, untainted by the conceptualizations of subject and object regarding form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and so forth, and arising from inconceivable conditions, is the state of perfect enlightenment and the state of omniscience. "The Vajra-holder [Buddha] has declared that the mind—overwhelmed by the darkness of manifold conceptual constructions, flickering like lightning driven by a tempestuous wind, and smeared with the stains of passion and other irresistible defilements—is indeed saṃsāra. (Prajñāpāramitopadeśa, 4.22)
Without the mind, the body would never be capable of performing any action;
nor could speech ever exist without it. (Jñānasiddhi 9.6) By the mind alone is the entire world created, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious. (Jñānasiddhi 1.7)
Whatever is cultivated by the mind, that very thing is perceived.
For the mind of all sentient beings is clear, peaceful, and luminous. Indeed, the mind is said to be the substratum of both defects and virtues.
The sequence of the mind... [omitted] ...the four known as the *pīṭhas*.
"Thus, these upapīṭhas are established within the citta-cakra;
they are declared to be the specific locations of the khecarīs. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p.
32) "But in the citta-cakra, the khecarīs are situated in the pīṭhas and upapīṭhas. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 43)

"These eight channels, which are the Khecara goddesses, reside in the primary and secondary seats (*pīṭha* and *upapīṭha*) within the wheel of consciousness (*cittacakra*) along with their means. (*Vajratilaka-ṭīkā*, p.

44) "The application of mindfulness of consciousness (*cittānusmṛtyupasthāna*): because it is not established that [consciousness] exists prior to or subsequent to the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), the application of mindfulness which consists in the recollection that 'consciousness is empty' is the application of mindfulness of consciousness. (*Vajratilaka-ṭīkā*, p. 52)
The *cella* and *cello* consist of the ten precepts (*daśa-śikṣāpada*). (Do. Ko. Vyā., p.
84) Decay.
The defilement of the *bodhicitta* is designated as "emission" (*cyuti*).
For this very reason, detachment arises, according to the scriptural teaching: "From emission arises detachment; from detachment arises suffering."
That alone is suffering which arises from the very falling away from one's state due to karma that brings about transmigration.
And thus it is said: "There is no sin greater than dispassion, and no merit greater than happiness" (Tattvārthasūtra-bhāṣya-ṭīkā, p. 2–3).
"Choma, choma" refers to the communication of the realization through the secret signs (*saṃketa*) of the *mleccha* yoginīs. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
23b) [The world].
The world is inseparable from emptiness and compassion. (Avatāra-alaṃkāra-saṃgraha, p.
26) The world, consisting of cause and effect, is nothing more than the single flavor of existence and nirvāṇa. (Avatāra-alaṃkāra-saṃgraha, p. 42) The Mother.
"Prajñā is called the mother because she gives birth to the world. (Hevajra Tantra 1.5.16).
"She is the mother because she gives birth to the universe in the form of great bliss. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 20a).
This is the relationship between the produced and the producer.

The arising of fragrance occurs even in the earth; of taste in fire; of the sphere of form in water; of touch in wind; and of sound in the tranquil ether; [likewise] of the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu). (Kālacakratantra 2.20) This is the recitation (japa).

"Recitation is called *japa* because it consists of the continuous utterance (*prajalpana*) of the *mālā* and the *ālī*. (Hevajra Tantra 1.5.19) *Jāpa* is the repetition (*āvartana*). (Vimalaprabhā, p. 68)
The repetition of that very mantra (*mantra*) through the sequence beginning with entry and so forth is called *japa*.
By this, it is stated that this is the natural *japa*, common to all the world. And it has been said:

Indeed, those beings within the three realms who, relying on breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), recite the King of Mantras while being ignorant and devoid of meditation and study—[this refers to] Jālandhara. (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, p. 68)
The *śikhā* and likewise *jālandhara*. (Vajravatī-tantra, p.
31) That which is the root of the network of channels (*nāḍījāla*)—the holding of that is *jālandhara*, the *śikhā*. (Vajravatī-ṭīkā, p.
31) In *jālandhara*, however, is Caṇḍākṣī, who likewise carries the hair and body hairs. (Vajravatī-tantra, p. 42)
"Jinajanaka, jinajanaka" refers to Vajrasattva Śākyamuni; he is the "progenitor of the Victors" because he is the progenitor of the aggregates free from obscuration. (Vi.pra., p. 157)
The *jinajik* are the Victors (*jina*), who by nature conquer the Māras;
he conquers them by means of the twelvefold Wheel of Dharma, thus he is *jinajik*. This is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Because he overcomes the four Māras by means of the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*), he is "Victorious" (*jinajik*);
this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). [This refers to] primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 23)
By this designation "knowledge" (*jñāna*), the third void is to be understood.

For example—the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*), the eye, taste, the hand, and movement: the state of being unobstructed, the state of having a single flavor (*samarasa*), and the state of becoming one with the flow (*ekalolībhūta*) of these is "knowledge," the third syllable, the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*).
Its symbolic sign (*saṃjñā-cihna*) consists of two dots (*bindu*) to the right of the central sign of the Unstruck (*anāhata*), which are not to be vocalized. (Vi.pra., p. 47)
The lamp of knowledge (*jñānapradīpa*): knowledge itself is the lamp; this is the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*).
Akṣobhya is the lamp of knowledge, because he produces the light of knowledge within the mental continuums of sentient beings; he is the complete limb.
Knowledge itself appears as the threefold consciousness;
it is like a lamp because it illuminates the ten directions, and thus it is the "lamp" (pradīpa) and the "womb" (garbha).
[The root] *jñā* means "to understand."
The negative particle *na* functions here as a prohibition.
That knowledge in which there is an absence of cognition—what is that? It is the ineffable ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Because it overcomes all splendors without exception by illuminating infinite world-systems, that very [wisdom] is the lamp; this is the ultimate (*kolika*) [meaning]. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p.
23) [This refers to] the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*).
The *jñānamudrā* is that which is mentally constructed by one's own mind (*svacittaparikalpitā*), having the nature of goddesses such as Viśvamātā;
it refers, in short, to what was previously experienced.
Through the *jñānamudrā*, there is the state of the bliss of vibration (*spandasukhāvasthā*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 56)
The term *spandeta* (throbs/moves) also includes the *akṣara* (the immutable) by virtue of its similarity to the flow [of seminal essence].

When these two—the throbbing of the *kṣāra* (seminal essence) and the state of bliss—are directly realized, they serve as the means for attaining mundane accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*) characterized by mastery over the realms of desire and form. (Se. Ṭī., p. 62)
Some [aspects] of it, appearing as mere reflections like images in a mirror, are produced in the mind;
these are indeed to be cultivated by the lords of yogins and practiced by the supreme sons of the Conquerors and the Buddhas.
When that flame of wisdom has fully grown, it burns away the entire host of Māra along with its objects.
And through the yoga of the rains, it also burns away passion and the like within the body, bringing equal bliss to yogins;
[he is] the embodiment of gnosis. (Kālacakratantra 5.113; do. ko. vyā., p. 163)

Because it possesses the nature of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*) at the time of the emission of the seminal essence (*śukra*) of the gnosis-mind (*jñānacitta*), which is the fourth mind, and because it constitutes the arising and ceasing of sentient beings, it is the embodiment of gnosis (*jñānamūrti*). [Vimalaprabhā, p.
216] It is the Gnosis-Vajra (*jñānavajra*).

The wisdom-vajra (*jñānavajra*), characterized by the state of the emission of semen and characterized by innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), should be understood to last until the twelfth year for women, and until the sixteenth year for men. (Vi.pra., p.
165). Through the union with the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*), the Wisdom-Being (*jñānasattva*) is the Tathāgata. (He.tantra 1.1.56).
“The root *ḍai* is here considered to mean ‘moving through the sky.

Because it has been explained by the Blessed One that *ḍākinī* refers to the accomplishment (*siddhi*) that moves through all space, and thus signifies the desire for the *ḍākinīs*, the *ḍākinīs* are the yoginīs of Vajraḍākinī. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 49b).
In that regard, she is called a *ḍākinī* because of her movement (*ḍayana*) upon the earth and in the sky. (Vimalaprabhā Commentary, p. 41).
All ḍākinīs indeed arise from the Vārāhī family. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p.
46) The application of mindfulness to the body is Ḍākinī. (Vajravārāhī-tantra, p. 51) The ḍākinīs are the thirty-six channels. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 67)
In this context, those whose nature is non-conceptual, objectless, and unobstructed are called *ḍākinīs*.

The syllable *ḍai* is conceived as the element of the Buddha in the sense of moving through the air; one who has attained accomplishment (*siddha*) and moves everywhere in space is designated a *ḍākinī*.
And because they move within the great sky of the five wisdoms, those very channels are called *ḍākinīs*. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 60).
The drum (*ḍiṇḍima*) is said to be the drum that is intangible. (Hevajra-tantra 2.3.58).
"Ḍombī, ḍombī"—she who is the completely pure *avadhūtī* is to be understood as Nairātmyā (*Ca. Ko. Vyā.*, p.
35). "Ḍombī" refers to the channel of semen (*śukra-nāḍikā*), the impure *avadhūtī* (*Ca. Ko. Vyā.*, p. 65).
The Ḍombī is the *avadhūtī*, naturally luminous and pure, the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*).
Because the Blessed Lady is intangible, she is therefore called the Ḍombī.
Due to being beyond the range of the sense faculties, she is expressed by the word "Ḍombī. (Candrakīrti’s *Vyākhyā*, p. 66; *Hevajra Tantra* 1.5.18; *Hevajra Tantra Commentary*, fol. 20a).
This reality, free from qualities and defects, is the ultimate truth;
there is no purpose or need for anything else that can be known through self-awareness alone.
For virtues are not to be superimposed there; rather, faults are to be removed from it.
And so it has been said:
"Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added. Reality is to be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated. ... Thus, reality does not come from anywhere.
It goes nowhere;
it does not abide in any place.
And so it is said in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*: “O son of good family! Suchness neither comes nor goes; suchness is immovable.”
"In this very way, noble son! neither the coming nor the going of the Tathāgata is perceived," and so forth.
Even such a reality as this enters the heart through the instruction of the Guru.
The fact that reality is devoid of color (or description) is stated in the *Paramārthastotra*:
"Neither red, nor green, nor madder-colored is the color perceived therein; neither yellow, nor black, nor white. Homage be to You who are colorless.
Thus [it is said]. And he is devoid of form, such as arms, face, and so forth. And it has been said:
"Neither large nor small, neither long nor circular;

having attained the immeasurable state, homage be to You, the Immeasurable. And yet, You are complete in all aspects, according to the statement: "Emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects is held to be suchness. (Dohākośavyākhyā, pp. 69–70).
"Thus, everything is false to the extent that it is conceptualized; that which is not conceptualized is the truth, that which is as-it-is, the reality. To the question "What is that?", he says again:
Its form is considered to be transparent, formless, and stainless;
yet it is not possible for that to be known in any way by those who lack awakening.
Even the Buddha does not know [the nature of things] as this other person knows it;
for he alone truly knows that very dependent origination.
Thus:
"Because it is beyond the range of the intellect, there is no movement of words [therein], much less the introduction of discourse concerning an object renowned for its greatness.
Nevertheless, that [Reality] gradually establishes its own station within the hearts of those possessed of faith, who are purified by qualities such as compassion. (Do. Ko. Vyā., p. 94)
Even regarding conceptual constructions concerning the ultimate truth, the wise person should not become attached;
for what difference is there between a conceptual construction that is wholesome or even unwholesome?
There is no difference in the burning power of fire due to a difference in its substratum;
even when ignited by sandalwood, it still burns when touched. (Dohākośavyākhyā, p.
95) The reality vibrating within the speaker, the listener does not perceive directly.
However, from sound arises its reflection as a conceptual construction.

"Constructing the cultivation of reality through those various hundreds of one's own conceptual constructions, who—possessing a mental continuum agitated by conceptualization—will realize reality? (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 8b).
"The Victors declare that knowledge free from oneness and multiplicity is reality."
That very [reality] appears in four ways and in sixteen aspects to sentient beings, according to the power of their own mental dispositions.
It is fourfold through the divisions of Ānanda, Parama, Virama, and Sahaja.
Then there is the bliss of body, the bliss of speech, the bliss of mind, and the bliss of gnosis.
Likewise, there is the supreme bliss of body, the supreme bliss of speech, the supreme bliss of mind, and the supreme bliss of gnosis.
Likewise, there is the cessation-bliss of body, the cessation-bliss of speech, the cessation-bliss of mind, and the cessation-bliss of gnosis.
Thus there is the innate bliss of body, the innate bliss of speech, the innate bliss of mind, and the innate bliss of gnosis.
When the yogi knows reality in these sixteen aspects, he is called by the Blessed One "one who knows the sixteen-aspected reality."
That very reality is called the sahajakāya;
from that arises the dharmakāya,
and from that the sambhogakāya.
From that arises the nirmāṇakāya;
likewise, the sahajavāk and the sahajacitta.
Innate gnosis; the speech of phenomena,
the mind of phenomena, and the gnosis of phenomena.
the speech of enjoyment,
the mind of enjoyment,
and the gnosis of enjoyment;
The emanated speech, the emanated mind, and the emanated knowledge appear to sentient beings through the power of their mental resolve (*cittādhimukti*). (Vimalaprabhā, p. 45)

The fourfold reality (*tattvacatuṣṭaya*) consists of the four realities— namely, the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), the reality of the mantra (*mantratattva*), the reality of the deity (*devatātattva*), and the reality of knowledge (*jñānatattva*). (HeTa 1.1.27) First, the reality of the self.
The reality (*tattva*) is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the deities such as Hevajra;
the reality is the mantra itself;
the reality is gnosis (*jñāna*) alone—the non-conceptual gnosis of unsurpassed great bliss. (Hevajra-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 8a)
The Tathāgata has gone to suchness, and the Glorious One has come in that very same way; by means of this wisdom and reasoning, he is designated as "Tathāgata. (Hevajra Tantra 1.5.8)
Just as the Tathāgatas have come at the time of birth, so too have they gone at the time of destruction; thus all sentient beings are Tathāgatas. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 219)
"Tantra, tantra" refers to a continuous composition (*prabandha*).
And that is threefold: the causal tantra (*hetutantra*), [the resultant tantra (*phalatantra*), and the method tantra (*upāyatantra*)].
The fruit-tantra and the means-tantra; [thus says] the knower of tantra. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 4a)

He who knows the many variations of these sequences according to the method of expansion (*prastāra*), as well as their synthesis, is indeed a knower of the Tantra (*tantravit*). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 1) — of the Protectors.
*Tāya* is the teaching of the path realized by oneself;
through that connection, the Tathāgatas and others are called *Tāyins*. (Sekanirdeśapañjikā, p. 28) *Tārā*, *tārā*, [and] *tarjanī*. (Sāramañjarī, p. 69)
"Through great compassion, with the constant intention to uplift the world,
and because of her skill in delivering sentient beings, the wisdom of Tārā is revealed. (Jñānasiddhi 15.13) She is called Tārā because she carries [beings] across the ocean of suffering.
She is called Tutturā because she protects (*trāyate*) from affliction (*vyathā*). The root *tud* means "to afflict," and the root *trai* means "to protect."
*Śīghrakaraṇe* means haste; *tur* means in hastening. These three words are used as vocatives. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 145)
*Tāla* refers to the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*). (Sā. Mā., p. 69). *Tilakā*.
Vārāhī, in the form of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), is known as Tilakā;
burning away the afflictions of karma, she blazes within the circle of the navel.
Having attained the spring [of bliss], she is satisfied and established in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
The flame of gnosis (*jñānajvālā*) is called the "tilaka" of Vajravārāhī. Oil. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 38)
Oil is *surā*. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p.
191) Triśakuni is considered to be the navel. (Vimalaprabhā, p. 33)

The "Three Birds" (*triśakuni*) refers to the locus of the navel, where the channels of body, speech, and mind are shaped like birds—resembling fowls with the appearance of bird-beaks. (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, p. 33) The wind-force arising in the Triśakuni is accompanied by the lungs. (Vajrāvalī, p. 44) Taking refuge in the Three Jewels (*triśaraṇagamanam*). (Taking refuge in the Three Jewels.)
"I go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds;
I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost of those free from passion;
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of assemblies"—this is the going for refuge to the Three Jewels. (Sā. Mā., pp. 55–56)

Having understood the infinite streams of the qualities of compassion belonging to the Buddhas existing throughout all three times who pervade the endless directions, and having understood the Noble Ones whose faults have been abandoned together with the True Dharma, I go for refuge with devotion. (Sādhana-mālā, pp.
116–117) I go for refuge to the Buddha until I reach the seat of enlightenment.
I go for refuge to the Dharma until I reach the seat of enlightenment; I go for refuge to the Saṅgha until I reach the seat of enlightenment. (Sā. Mā., pp.
201–202) Here I go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds, until I reach enlightenment.
I go for refuge to the Dharma, the complete Mahāyāna;
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the assembly of irreversible Bodhisattvas. (Sādhana-mālā, p. 225) — *Triśaraṇagāthā* (Verses on the Three Refuges).
Homage to the Buddha, the Teacher; homage to the Dharma, the Protector;
homage to the great Saṅgha—homage perpetually to all three.
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds; I rejoice in the merit of the world; I direct my mind toward the awakening of a Buddha.
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly;
I generate the mind of awakening for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others.
I generate the supreme mind of enlightenment; I invite all sentient beings;
I shall practice the desired, sublime conduct of enlightenment.
May I become a Buddha for the benefit of the world.
Confession of all misdeeds, rejoicing in merits, and having observed the fast, I shall practice the noble eightfold poṣadha. (Avadānaśataka, pp. 5–6).
Knowledge of the staff.
"Because it disciplines through punishment, the knowledge of punishment is that which disciplines sentient beings" (Jñānasiddhi 15.37).
What is the path of vision?
What is the path of vision?
There are seven factors.
Which seven?
The seven factors of enlightenment. (Vasubandhu’s Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa, p. 51)
The path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is the antidote to the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 56).
By the word "petal" (*dala*), the channels (*nāḍī*) characterized by the breath are intended. (Viṣamapada-prabhā, p. 179).
The ten winds are as follows:
the apāna is threefold within the element of gnosis; the prāṇa wind is in the void;
the samāna is in the midst of the wind; furthermore, the udāna is in fire, and the vyāna is indeed in water.
On the earth, the serpent, the tortoise, the *kṛkara* wind, and the god-like *dhanañjaya*—
these four arise from wind and fire in water and earth respectively. (Kālacakra Tantra 2.24) At the end of sixteen years, the bliss-wind (*ānandavāyu*) arises from the space element.
The wind of innate bliss belongs to the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*). (Vi.pra., p.
169): Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna, and the winds nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya reside in the petals of the lotus of the earth.

Thus, in this manner, the ten kinds of vital breaths (pavana) are situated within the wheel of channels (nāḍicakra) according to their various functions; from the heart-lotus of one's own self up to the Śaṅkhinī, they pervade the entire navel-wheel (nābhicakra).

The *prāṇa* makes the breath function as it moves along the paths of the sun and moon; the *apāna* leads all food and drink downward; the *samāna* leads everything toward an equal flavor within the body;
and the *udāna*, vibrating within the body, performs song and dance with the mouth, hands, and feet.
The Vyāna [vāyu] causes disease and likewise brings about a breaking pain in the limbs, according to the influence of its natural qualities.
O King, the *nāga* wind causes belching; the *kūrma* wind contracts the hands and feet;
the *kṛkara* wind produces anger and all agitation; the *devadatta* wind causes yawning;
and the *dhanañjaya* wind alone does not leave the body even when it has reached the state of the five elements.
In this way, all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth do not abandon the qualities inherent in *prakṛti*. (Kā. Ta.

2.42–44) Regarding the ten *vidyās* mentioned in all the *tantras*: once they have been heard and understood along with their commentaries, these ten *vidyās*, which have been taught for the sake of attaining the status of a great sovereign (*mahādhipati*), must be offered by a householder disciple to the Guru in the prescribed order.
In this regard, the Blessed One said in the *Mūlatantra*:
"The sister's daughter, the daughter, the sister, and likewise the mother;
the mother of one's wife, and also the wife of one's maternal uncle."
The wife of one's father or brother, the sister of one's father,
the sister of one's own mother, and one's own wife of excellent form— [these are not to be approached].

The ten vidyās, beginning with Tārā and ending with Dharmadhātu, who are born from oneself as the foremost [consorts], should be bestowed at the time of initiation by the disciple who desires liberation. ... Furthermore, in sequence, they are Śūdrī, Kṣatriṇī, and likewise Brāhmaṇī, beginning with Ayavī.
The Vaiśyā, the Ḍombī, the Kaivartī, the Naṭīkā, and likewise the Rajakī.
The leather-worker, the outcaste woman, and the ten born from the limits of the dharmadhātu—
these are declared to be the great vidyās that bestow the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.

In the sequence thus described, the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the ten masteries (*vaśitā*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the ten powers (*bala*) become purified by these [mudrās]. Therefore, for one who desires the rank of a Maṇḍala Master (*maṇḍalācārya*), the ten mudrās should be bestowed in order to exercise sovereign authority; such is the rule of the Tathāgatas. (Se. Ṭī., p. 23) Divine.
Because it carries the skin-impurity that shines externally, [the goddess] is divine in the left ear. (Vatulanatha-tantra-ṭīkā, p.
44) Dundura is the unmanifest; it is known as *dundura*. (Hevajra-tantra 2.3.57)
The *dundura* are those who do not abide in the [proper] time.
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 54a) The *dundura* are the afflictions, such as passion and so forth. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 54b) Daughter.

Because she milks out the qualities (*guṇa*), wisdom (*prajñā*) is called the "daughter" (*duhitā*). (Hevajra Tantra 1.5.18) She is the "daughter" because she brings to full completion the unsurpassed qualities of a Buddha. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 20a) [This is] the stage *Dūraṅgamā*.
The secret anus is the meeting place (*melāpaka*),
because of the union of wisdom and means and because of the merging of the channels (*nāḍī*) therein;
that itself is the stage "Far-reaching" (*dūraṅgamā*).
Because of the remoteness of the coolness of that channel. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
28) The glances are even and fierce; the glance directed toward the forehead is always said to be the "striking" (pātanā) gaze.
The gaze is fixed on the left for subjugation; the doll and the two [other figures] are also on the left.
The gaze for attracting is on the right side, with two [fingers] above;
the gaze for paralyzing is in the middle, with two [fingers] between the nose and the palate.
One should subjugate by means of the *recaka* (exhalation) alone;
attraction is achieved by the *pūraka* (inhalation) alone; and immobilization is achieved by the *praśāntaka* (retention).
Pātanā is proclaimed for oily trees; Vaśyā for flowers; Ākṛṣṭi for vajra-trees; and Stambhanā for moving grass. (Hevajratantra 1.11.1–4).
These are the four gazes: Pātanā...
Subjugation, attraction, and immobilization.
When the eyebrows are even, straight, and not cruel, and when the wrathful [expression] rests upon the forehead by means of the two forehead-puttalīs, it is *pātanā* (casting down).
When they rest upon the left side and gaze to the left, it is *vaśyā* (subjugation). When they rest upon the upper part and gaze to the right, it is *ākṛṣṭiḥ* (attraction).
That which gazes directly, supported by the two nostrils, is the immobilizing [mudrā] (*stambhanā*). (HeTaṬī p.
42a) Because a deity arises within the body, it is called "deity" (*devatā*). (HeTa 1.5.14)
Regarding deity yoga, the *Vairocanābhisambodhi Tantra* also teaches that deity yoga is twofold: "O Lord of Secrets, the form of the deity is also twofold: the completely pure and the impure.
Among these, the completely pure is the realized form, free from all signs."
All signs, as well as form, color, and shape, are impure.
In this regard, through two kinds of deity-forms, the accomplishment of two kinds of activities occurs:
by means of the form with signs, accomplishment with signs arises.
The supreme Victors have declared that accomplishment is attained through the signless by means of the signless. By always abiding in the signless, indeed, that which possesses signs is perfected.
Therefore, in every respect, the signless is established as the negation of signs.
Thus [it is said]. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 119). Devīkoṭṭa:
Now, the two eyes are Devīkoṭṭa. (Vimalaprabhā, p. 32).
Devīkoṭṭa is so called because it is like a fortress (*koṭṭa*) belonging to that very Goddess; for by means of its support, the two eyes attain her. (Vasudhārā-ṭīkā, p. 32).
"But in Devīkoṭṭa, the channel (*nāḍī*) which is considered soft is known as Laṅkeśvarī."

The *bukka* [vein] carries [the element] constantly; it dwells within the entire body. (Vajratilaka, p. 43) It is called *doṣā* because it is corrupted (*duṣyate*) by its own object and thus undergoes transformation (*vikriyate*). It is the carrier of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) located in the armpits, for the mind is transformed by the sight of the armpits.
And because hatred arises from the thought "this is mine.
Hatred (*dveṣa*) and fault (*doṣa*) are synonyms. (Vajracchedikā-ṭīkā, p. 44) [The shade of a tree] (*drumacchāyā*).
"Like the shade of a tree, it is cool and refreshing; therefore, it is called 'the shade of a tree' (*drumacchāyā*).

The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) is the 'shade of a tree. This is the application of the two faculties. (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p. 47; V. ti., p. 54). The application of the two faculties.
The practice of the two organs (*dvayendriyaprayoga*) consists in the accomplishment of Mahāvajradhara through the non-dualization of the two truths.
Here, the "twelve knots" refer to the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*) inherent in the bodies of living beings, which are designated by the term "knots. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 164)

The divisions of those twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*) are the year, the solstice (*ayana*), the season (*kāla*), the age-cycle (*yuga*), the season (*ṛtu*), the month, the fortnight (*pakṣa*), the day, the *ghaṭikā*, the *pāṇīpala*, and the breath (*śvāsa*). (Vi.

Pra., p. 258) The twelve truths (*satya*)—ignorance (*avidyā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—are the twelve truths that constitute the obscurations for those born from a womb.
"The Buddhas possess the unobscured [states].
Due to the flow of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) through the division of the twelve transits (*saṃkrānti*), those born from a womb possess obscurations;
for the Buddhas, they are unobscured because of the cessation of the twelve links [of dependent origination]. (Vi.pra., p. 20)
"Dveṣarati" means attachment to Akṣobhya, who is hatred; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
"Dveṣarati" means attachment to the purification of the affliction of hatred.
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p.
25) Dharma is so called because it maintains its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); it refers to the transformations of the elements, such as pots, cloths, pillars, and jars.
"In its own nature, it has no form," according to the *Śrīherukatantra-tattvapaṭala* (*Cakrasaṃvara-kosavyākhyā*, p.
17). The *dharmakāya* is the heart-cakra; it is the *dharmakāya*.
Because it withdraws the aggregates, elements, and so forth, which have the form of the syllable *hūṃ* and the rest;
likewise, in the heart as well, there is a lotus endowed with eight petals.
Within that great eight-petaled lotus, the *dharmakāya* proceeds.

The syllable *HŪṂ* is renowned as being at the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*); it is considered the unstruck sound (*anāhata*), joined with the five vowels and adorned with *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 79).
Śrī Heruka himself is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)... he himself is the mantra... he himself is the wood-worm (*ghuṇa*). (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 83).
The perfectly pure great gnosis, which has the nature of all goddesses,
is renowned as Vajrasattva and is declared to be supreme bliss.
This very form of the Self-Existent (svayambhū) is proclaimed as the Dharmakāya. (Vajraṭīkā, p.

85) That which has been previously determined to have the nature of supreme bliss and is independent of causes and conditions is called the Dharmakāya. (Vajraṭīkā-ṭippaṇī, p. 85) It is the reality of phenomena (dharmatattva).
That which can neither be added to nor subtracted from,
and which remains even when that which was set aside for the sake of addition is discarded— that is called the true nature of reality (dharmatattva).
The dharmadhātu is that very same most wonderful abode of all the Buddhas. (Pra.vi.si. 1.18; A.pra.vi.si., p. 214)
"The dharmadhātu is proclaimed as divine, bringing about the highest good and prosperity" (Pravajyā-vinirdeśa-sūtra, 1.21).
"Tathatā, bhūtakoṭi, and dharmadhātu are synonymous" (Hevajra-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 8a).
The wise know the corpse to be of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
For the corpse is indeed selfless (*nirātman*),
and selflessness is the *dharmadhātu*.
The *ḍākas* and *ḍākinīs* have the *dharmadhātu* as their ultimate limit.

The *dharmamudrā*—the *dharmamudrā*—is the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*; she is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcā*), non-conceptual (*nirvikalpā*), uncontrived (*akṛtrimā*), devoid of arising, and has compassion as her intrinsic nature. She is the singular beauty of supreme bliss and serves as the means (*upāya*).
That which is distinct from wisdom (*prajñā*), whose innate nature is eternal by way of its continuous flow, and which arises as the co-emergent (*sahaja*), is designated as the *Dharmamudrā*.

Its other characteristic should be understood as resembling the rays of the sun that dispel the darkness of dense ignorance; it is to be realized through the instruction of the Guru as being devoid of even a blade of grass or a husk’s worth of the thorn of delusion.
It should be understood as the single nature of the three worlds, greatly variegated by all earth, water, wind, and fire, and as indivisible from the waveless emptiness and compassion.
...Lalanā and Rasanā; between these two dwells Avadhūtī.
She alone, through the instruction of a true guru, becomes the Dharmamudrā for one whose single mental state has realized the innate nature (*sahajasvabhāva*) of all phenomena.
It is the cause through its non-differentiation from Mahāmudrā (*Avaivartacakra-samādhi-sūtra*, pp.
33–34). The Dharmameghā [Bhūmi] consists of the thumbs and knees; the *upaśmaśāna* is as before.

That itself is the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*); because it rains down the stable, supreme, and upward-streaming Dharma like a cloud, or because, being free from ailment, it causes the *kunduru* of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) to fall through the application of rain. (Vā. Ti. Ṭī., p.
29) The syllable of Dharma (*dharmākṣara*).

The unstruck syllable (*anāhatākṣara*) itself is the syllable of reality (*dharmākṣara*). ... One should disregard the two, namely supreme cessation (*paramavirama*) and passion-cessation (*rāgavirāga*), which are of the nature of time and non-time (*kāla-vikāla*). Therein, one should perceive in the center the syllable of reality, characterized by liberation and having the form of the sixteenth digit (*ṣoḍaśīkalā*). (Dohākoṣavyākhyā, pp. 160–161)

The application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmānusmṛtyupasthāna*) is the establishment of mindfulness regarding phenomena that are distinguished by various categories such as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, because they are empty as previously described; that which is the establishment of mindfulness is the application of mindfulness to phenomena. (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p. 52). Phenomena (*dharmāḥ*).

The *dharmas* comprised within the side of the wholesome are so called because they are maintained by Bodhisattvas established on the path and fixed in their minds; for they are untainted (*anāśrava*), and the being on the path is exclusively wholesome. (Vasubandhu’s *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p. 52)
The source of phenomena (dharmodaya) is as follows: the Blessed Buddha, the perfectly awakened one, is born from the syllable A.
The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, the supreme syllable;
it is indeed the Great Breath, unarisen, and devoid of verbal expression...
from which arises the birth of the Buddhas and all qualities such as sovereignty.

That is declared to be the *dharmodaya*, supreme and consisting of merit and wisdom (*puṇyajñānamaya*). (Se. Ṭī., pp. 69–70). *Dharmodaya* is, in the language of intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*), the *dharmodaya* of wisdom (*prajñā*). ... Furthermore, that which becomes the place of arising (*udayasthāna*) for the *dharma*—the reality (*bhāva*) as it truly is—through the realization of the true meaning (*sadartha*), that alone is the *dharmodaya*. (Ca. Ko. Vyā., p. 84).
Arising in the form of a triangle, it is known as the *dharmodaya* (source of phenomena).
Filled with moon, sun, and water, it is the embodiment of wisdom (*prajñā*), most brilliantly radiant. (A.K. 98) "Phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*) refers to the noble phenomena (*āryadharma*).
Because their arising (*samudaya*) occurs within this, it is the *dharmodaya*, the *dharmadhātu*.
Here, the lotus of the consort who is its *mudrā* is the *dharmodaya*; [thus] the *dharmodayā*. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 33b)

The nature of the great element of space, known as the Source of Phenomena (*dharmodayā*), having the nature of Mahāvajradhara, white as the autumnal moon, narrow below and wide above, triangular, and having the form of the internal sky—this is the beautiful triangular mandala issued from the *vajrāralli*. (Sā.mā., p. 195)
That which is renowned as Dharmodayā is also called the *bhaga* of women. (Vajravatī, p. 71). The elements: the four elements are the Wisdom Goddesses. (Vajravatī-ṭīkā, p. 67).

Dhāraṇā is the fixing of one’s own mantra in the heart and placing the vital breath within the *bindu*. When the jewel of the senses is restrained, one should maintain that state; this is known as dhāraṇā.
When the mind has entered the vajra of cessation, the apprehension of signs arises;
that sign is fivefold, as taught by the Vajra of Awakening.
The first has the appearance of a mirage, the second the appearance of smoke;
the third has the appearance of fireflies, and the fourth is a blazing lamp.
The fifth, however, is the constant light, resembling a cloudless sky;
one should expand that steady [light] through the path of the vajra into one's own elements. (Se. Ṭī., p.
30) By the power of dhāraṇā, one should constantly enter into Vajrasattva. (Se. Ṭī., p. 31)

Thus, because it serves as a mental protection, one should meditate on one's own mantra— the vital breath— within the heart, from the pericarp into the center of the pericarp, until it reaches the *bindu*; the location of the *bindu* is the forehead, where one should place and restrain it.
One should hold the jewel together with the senses when they have ceased, making it free from coming and going. Holding is known as the limb of retention (*dhāraṇā*).
It is called cessation (*nirodha*) because therein [the senses] are brought to a halt.
This cessation is also the "vajra," thus "cessation-vajra" (nirodhavajra), which is the path of the avadhūtī.
When the mind and the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) have entered therein, the apprehension of signs arises;
that is, the apprehension—the manifestation—of signs such as smoke and so forth, comes into being and is produced.
The explanation of the distinction between the first and second signs is for the purpose of stating dependence upon the Guru.
Having made the "great jewel" (mahāratna) firm—that is, motionless—by means of the limb of *dhāraṇā*, one should raise the *caṇḍālī* from the navel-cakra.

By way of the *vajra*-path through the central channel (*madhyamā*) into the spheres of space (*khadhātu*), she reaches the crown-cakra (*uṣṇīṣacakra*). Having arisen there at the pericarp of the crown-lotus, she causes the syllable *haṃ* to melt; then, by means of the four drops whose nature is body, speech, mind, and gnosis, according to the divisions of bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth—

"One should lead [the breath] to the pericarp of the lotus of the jewel at the tip of the vajra"— this is the instruction of the Guru that immediately following the stage of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), the *caṇḍālī* of one's own sound blazes forth.
By the power of concentration, the objective image of emptiness (*śūnyatābimba*) is invariably (or constantly) grasped, and Vajrasattva— the subjective grasping mind— should enter into it.
By the power of *dhāraṇā*, through the cessation of the coming and going of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), [the mind] becomes one with it. (*Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā*, p.
34). *Dhārā* is the name for *dhārā*. (*Sāramañjarī*, p. 69).
In brief, meditation consists of the five sensual pleasures through the application of the five Buddhas;
conceptualization is called meditation, and that meditation is of five kinds.
Applied thought, sustained thought, joy, as well as bliss,
and one-pointedness of mind— these five are the constituents of dhyāna.
In all the secret tantras, various [methods] have been proclaimed:
reasoning that arises from the three secrets, investigation, and the application thereof.
The third is characterized by joy, the fourth is the gathering of bliss;
one's own mind is to be known as the fifth, wherein the arising and ceasing of both knowledge and the object of knowledge come to rest.
Consisting of all Buddhas, peaceful, and established within all bodies; (Se. Ṭī., p. 30).
Having entered the meditative knowledge (*dhyānajñāna*), one shall attain the state of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*); (Se. Ṭī., p.
31). "The five desires" refers to all entities, both stable and moving.
"By means of the application of the five Buddhas" means by means of the application of all Buddhas.
By their very nature, all phenomena are applied by all Buddhas and consist of all Buddhas.

Regarding those phenomena which consist of all Buddhas, there is a conceptualization and discrimination—free from the delusion of conceptual construction—in the form of a single appearance of the three times and the triple world, to be personally realized by the yogin.
That vision which proceeds as a continuous stream is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
And that meditative concentration is fivefold, distinguished by *vitarka* and the other factors.
It consists of the three secrets—the body, speech, and mind—pertaining to the three times and the three realms.

And its simultaneous arising as the gross form of the *caitya* (the sacred site), consisting solely of the manifestation of the three realms—that realization, that awakening, is the arising of the three secrets.
That itself is *vitarka* (initial inquiry).

... The application of attention (*ābhoga*) toward that object of *vitarka*, the grasping of entities through their specific distinctions such as the stationary and the moving, pots, cloths, and so forth, is *vicāra* (sustained investigation).
Joy (*prīti*) is a state of mental well-being (*saumanasya*) that resembles delight and serves as the cause for directing the mind toward all things within the sphere of investigation.
From all things toward which the mind has been directed, there arises the attainment of bliss, which is the gathering of happiness caused by physical pliancy (*kāyaprasrabdhi*).

The "arising of knowledge and the object of knowledge" (*jñānajñeyodaya*) refers to the emergence of the sixfold active consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, with respect to their objects of knowledge, from form (*rūpa*) up to the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Its destruction is the one-pointedness of mind characterized by the emptiness of the grasped and the grasper; this is what is called "one's own mind.
Such a mind is composed of all Buddhas, because of the pacification of conceptual constructions such as the grasped and so forth.

It is peaceful because it is established solely in emptiness, being nothing more than the manifestation of the three realms. It is "not established in any desires," meaning that all desires—that is, all phenomena—are established and abide herein as a single form, appearing as non-different from itself. (Se. Ṭī., pp. 31–32)
When, through a factor of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*), one's mind becomes steady upon the image and one's eyes become unblinking, then the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) arises.
In this way, the divine ear and so forth arise, whereby one attains the state of possessing the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 34)
And meditation [is characterized] by the effortless, spontaneous flow that accords with the intrinsic nature of all things. (Avatamsaka-sūtra, p.
3) A city is said to be on a finger. (Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra, p. 35)

"Those which do not move are *naga*s, namely the fingers; because they do not extend beyond this point, it is called a city (*nagara*).
