In that city, however, resides the river named Suvīrā, which carries fat and marrow. (Vajratārā-ṭīkā, p. 34) "In the city, however, resides [the river] called Suvīrā, which carries fat and marrow. (Vajratārā, p. 47)
Naraka is Naraka, the hell-guardian;
Mahānaraka is the skull of the twice-born. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 64b) (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 67b)
"O Great Compassionate One, wisdom is called a dancer because of its flickering nature" (Hevajra Tantra 1.5.18).
She is called a dancer because she cannot be stabilized by beginner practitioners (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 20a).
[She is] like the moon that has vanished.
The sixteenth digit of the sun has entered the *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus; that very digit is designated as the "lost moon. (Se. Ṭī., p. 55). The channels (*nāḍī*) are thirty-two channels;
these thirty-two, which carry the *bodhicitta*, flow into the location of the great mouth.
Among them, three channels are primary: lalanā,
rasanā, and avadhūtī.
Lalanā exists by the nature of wisdom (prajñā), while rasanā is established as means (upāya);
avadhūtī is in the middle region, free from the grasped and the grasper.
"Lalanā brings Akṣobhya; rasanā carries blood; avadhūtī is celebrated as the bearer of the moon of wisdom. (Hevajra Tantra 1.1.13–15).
"The 'bearers of bodhicitta' refers to those that carry the innate (*sahaja*). (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 5b).
Above that, in the region of the heart, is situated the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra) within an eight-petaled lotus;
there resides the collection of winds beginning with prāṇa, with the sun, moon, and fire [respectively] in the left, right, and middle.
In the left, the lunar channel indeed flows white; in the right, the solar [channel] flows red;

and in the middle, the Kālāgnirudra flows during the equinox with sixty diminished breaths. Piṅgalā, Sūkṣmā, Iḍā, and the others, having gone upon the threefold path, as well as Rohiṇī and Hastijihvā— (Kālacakra-tantra 2.41).

Pūṣā is the sixth, Jayā has also gone [to the seventh], Vasu is in the ninth, and Alambuṣā is with Śrī and Kuhū; O Lord of Men, Śaṅkhinī, who is numbered as ten, flows the bodhicitta at the end of bliss.
This is the glorious wheel of channels (*nāḍicakra*), which becomes manifold through many different types of junctions. (Kālacakratantra 2.45)
Thus, all thirty-six Kulanāyikās come into being: six having the form of the tastes, six having the form of the elements,
and six having the form of the sense organs.
Six have the nature of the objects of the senses, six have the nature of the organs of action,
and six have the nature of the objects of the organs of action.
In this way, there are six that set form in motion, six that set feeling in motion,
and six that set perception in motion.

There are thirty-six family channels—six that set the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) in motion, six that set consciousness (*vijñāna*) in motion, and six that set gnosis (*jñāna*) in motion—which, through their relationship as support and supported, should be known to be seventy-two. (Vi.pra., pp. 188–189)

Regarding the yoga of the channels (*nāḍīyoga*): from the union of *lalanā* and *rasanā*, one should contemplate the yoga of the channels within the *madhyamā*; [one should contemplate] the *prāṇa* wind [in the *madhyamā*], the *apāna* [in] the *śaṅkhinī*, and the union of the channels of feces and urine [therein]. (Vi.pra., p. 228)
The channels are those that have entered the nine openings, situated at the nine gates;
the tenth, however, is in the middle of the bhaga, and it is the most excellent among them.
Beginning from the location of the forehead, there is the determination of the *haṃ* syllable wheel;
thirty-two streams of bodhicitta flow there day and night. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 26) The channels have the intrinsic nature of Kākāsyā and the others. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 27)
The locations of all the channels have been fully explained everywhere;
in these locations, the *ḍākinīs* reside in the form of the channels. (Vajravārāhī-tantra, p.
36). The names of the thirty-two channels are found in the *Śrīhevajra*.
These thirty-two, together with the four *sandhyā*-nāḍīs, make thirty-six.
Excluding the eight beginning with Trivṛtā and Avadhūtī, the remaining twenty-four beginning with Abhedya and Pracaṇḍā are to be known [as the Yoginīs]. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, 43).
Thus, these Vajrayoginīs abide in the form of the nāḍīs.
The yoginīs of the mind-chakra are said to be thirty-seven.
"For these perfections of wisdom are established within the body" (Vajratilaka, p.
50). "All the channels located within the body, purified as the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, abide by assuming the colors, arms, and forms of the deities" (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 57).
[This is] the *nāda*.
The conceptualization of wisdom as the grasping consciousness is *nāda*. (*Candrakīrtivyākhyā*, p. 146).
*Nāda* is a streak of light. (*Sāramañjarī*, p. 153).
By that very [streak], *nāda* is differentiated by that which brings satisfaction to the fire.

By that, the entire maṇḍala indeed comes into being; there is no doubt about this. For Nāda, which is the single cause of all phonemes—whether they be words or sentences—is established in the region of the navel. (Vajratārā-tantra, p. 63) ...
"Nada, when nourished by this [breath], becomes the locus of contentment;
this is declared to be the Vasantatilaka yoga. (Vasantatilaka-ṭīkā, p. 64). "Nada, moreover, is said to be mantra. (Vasantatilaka, p. 68).

That very vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) which was previously mentioned as being prior to the utterance from the navel-center is called "mantra" because it is the cause of all mantras. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 68).
This is the Name Initiation (*nāmābhiṣeka*).

The sixth is the Name Empowerment (*nāmābhiṣeka*). Because one is given a name such as "Amuka-vajra" with the intention that the castes, beginning with the Brahmins, are of a single essence (*ekakalkatva*), there is at all times the purification of passion, hatred, and so forth through the perfection of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*)—loving-kindness and the rest—and by way of being free from obscurations (*nirāvaraṇatva*). (Se. Ṭī., p.
21). [The seventh is] the Nose.
By the word "nose" (nāsikā), the pericarp of the lotuses at the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown of the head is meant. (Se. Ṭī., p. 32, 42).
The fourfold group (nikāyacatuṣṭaya) refers to the four groups (catvāro nikāyāḥ): Sthavari, ... [and so on].
The Sarvāstivādin, the Saṃvidin, and the Mahāsaṃghin. (He. Ta. 1.1.29)

The *nikāya* is the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*). Furthermore, the Blessed One has taught six other signs, beginning with the flame and ending with the drop, in the *Māyājāla* chapter on meditative absorption (*samādhi*). (He. Ta. Ṭī., p. 9a)
Namely: Gaganodbhava (Born from Space), Svayambhū (Self-Existent), the great fire of wisdom,
Vairocana (The All-Illuminating), the great radiance, and the light of gnosis that shines forth.
The lamp of the world, the torch of knowledge, of great splendor and luminous;
the fierce King of Vidyās, the Lord of Mantras, the King of Mantras who accomplishes the great purpose.
Thus, by means of these two verses, the Blessed One has spoken of the subsequent sign (*aparanimitta*) in the *Māyājāla* through the language of intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*).

That which arises from the previously mentioned cloudless sky is the "sky-born self-arisen" (*gaganodbhava-svayambhū*), [meaning it arises] from the mind free of all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Here, "the fire of the wisdom-knowledge" (*prajñājñānānala*) refers to the appearance of flames.
Vairocana, the great radiance, is the reflection of the moon;
he himself is the illumination of the light of gnosis.
Jagatpradīpa, the lamp of the world, is the reflection of the sun.
"The torch of gnosis" (*jñānolkā*) is the appearance of Rāhu;
"of great splendor and luminous" (*mahātejāḥ prabhāsvaraḥ*) is the appearance of lightning;
and "the fierce King of Knowledge, Anteśa" (*vidyārājogramanteśaḥ*) is the appearance of a drop (*bindu*) in the form of a blue-colored lunar disc.

"The King of Mantras, the accomplisher of great purpose"—this refers to the manifestation of all phenomena within the three realms in every aspect, which is seen by the yogin through *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal), that is, by means of the instruments of the eyes and other sense organs, as being equal to the manifestations of illusion and dreams.
Furthermore, the sign (*nimitta*) is also threefold: the initial sign (*ādinimitta*), [the intermediate sign, and the final sign]. (Se. Ṭī., pp. 40–41)
The middle sign and the final sign.
The initial sign consists of the path beginning with smoke, the accomplishment of the image through the six-limbed yoga, and the attainment of the protection of the senses.

The intermediate sign consists of the attainment of the first bhūmi, the manifestation of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), and the realization of previously unseen objects through eighteen hundred moments of supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarakṣaṇa*); it is the attainment of worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*).

The final sign consists of Buddhahood and the state of Vajradhara through twenty-one thousand six hundred moments of supreme unchanging bliss; it is the attainment of the twelfth bhūmi and the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā (*mahāmudrāsiddhi*). (Vi.pra., p.
The ten signs begin with the appearance of emptiness (*śūnyābhāsa*), which has the form of white smoke pervading all external and internal space;
this arises immediately after the appearance of clouds, as it has been said:
"First it appears like a cloud, the second is similar to smoke.
Thus, the appearance of flickering water is like a mirage; the appearances of fireflies and lamps are well known.
These four signs, because they arise from darkness in a windowless room, constitute the yoga of night and the yoga of space.
As it is stated in the *Śrī-samāja* and other texts, in reverse order of the first and second [chapters]:
"When the Vajra of Cessation has occurred... resembling the cloudless sky."
Then, preceded by a manifestation equal to the cloudless sky, there is the form of fire, radiant with the appearance of emptiness.
The appearances of Indra and the sun are well known.
"Darkness" refers to the light of Rāhu, appearing like a black gem.
"Kala" is the appearance like a flash of lightning.
"Mahābindu" is the appearance in the form of a blue lunar disc that illuminates all things moving and stationary.
These six signs arise from the light of the cloudless sky; therefore, they constitute the yoga of day and the yoga of open space. (Se. Ṭī., pp. 47–48)
When the mind has entered the vajra of cessation, the apprehension of signs arises; that sign is fivefold,
as taught by the Vajra of Awakening.
The first has the appearance of a mirage; the second has the appearance of smoke;
the third has the appearance of fireflies; and the fourth is a blazing lamp.
The fifth, however, is "Always-Light" (*sadāloka*), which is like a cloudless sky. (Guhyasiddhi, p. 164; Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā, p.
30) It is called "Cessation" (*nirodha*) because [all phenomena] are ceased herein.
This is both cessation (*nirodha*) and a vajra; thus, "cessation-vajra" (*nirodhavajra*) refers to the path of the *avadhūtī*.

When the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) have entered therein, the apprehension of signs (*nimittodgraha*) arises—the apprehension of the signs beginning with smoke appears and originates within the visionary manifestation (*pratibhāsa*).
The explanation of the first and second signs in reverse order, however, is for the purpose of stating that [this process] is dependent upon the Guru. (Se. Ṭī., p. 33)
The first sign appears in the form of a mirage due to the dissolution of earth into water.
Likewise, the second is in the form of smoke due to the dissolution of water into fire.
The third is in the form of a firefly due to the dissolution of fire into air.
The fourth is of the nature of a mass of light like a lamp, due to the manifestation of the three appearances from the subtle element (*sūkṣmadhātu*).
The fifth becomes mere luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), constantly radiant like a cloudless sky, because the appearance of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) has dissolved.
These five signs lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa.
As it is said in the *Karmāntavibhāga*:
"First the earth goes to the water; the water goes to the fire;
the fire follows the wind; and the wind enters into consciousness."
"Consciousness, having thus attained retention (*dhāraṇā*), should then enter the luminosity. (*Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, p.
118). "The restraint (*niyama*) is the vow of the ten million *śrāvakas*, the restraint of ethical discipline devoid of the enjoyment of the five objects of desire. (*Vimalaprabhā*, p. 15).
That which perishes— that is, decays— is *kṣara*;
that which is other than this is *akṣara*.
That which has emerged from it is without syllables (*nirakṣara*), meaning it is devoid of arising and cessation; it is stainless (*nirajjana*). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 71)
The Sahajakāya is "stainless" (*nirañjana*) because the "ointments" (*añjana*), namely the afflictions such as passion and hatred, have departed from it. (Dohākośavyākhyā, p. 149).
The mantra *praṇava* is "without end" (*niranta*) when it does not contain *svāhā*; that is said to be "without end. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 153).

The mantra beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *phaṭ* is called "without succession" (*niranvaya*). "Succession" (*anvaya*) refers to phenomena characterized by subject and object, whose nature consists of wisdom and means. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 221) It is "without succession" because it is devoid of such [phenomena].
That which has discarded connection is "without connection" (*niranvaya*).
Here, "connection" (*anvaya*) refers to the side of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the side of means (*upāya*).
Since that tantra has discarded such a connection consisting of distinct sides, it is called "without connection. (Viṣṇupurāṇa-ṭīkā, p. 17)
The Yoga Tantra, whose nature consists of wisdom and means, is called non-dual (*Advayavajra*, p.
18). It is without clothing; it is adorned with bone ornaments and is without clothing (*Hevajratantra* 2.3.56).
"Niroduvajra": that in which cessation occurs is "nirodha"; and since it is both cessation and a vajra, it is "niroduvajra," the path of the avadhūtī. (Se. Ṭī., p. 33)
The emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is indeed the sixty-four-petaled [lotus], proclaimed as the emanation [center]. (Vajratilaka, p.
78) The emanation body is the navel wheel (*nābhicakra*).
The forms of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which possess the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*), arise for all sentient beings. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
78) A lotus endowed with sixty-four petals is situated in the center of the navel. (Vajratilaka, p.
78) Within the wheel of emanation (*nirmāṇacakra*), it is encircled by the eight classes [of consonants].
"This letter *a* is the foremost form among all letters, the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*).
Residing within the Blessed One, it is renowned as the 'mustard seed' (*sarṣapa*);
it is declared to be the form of the sun and is called the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*). (Vajratilaka, p. 79; p. 82)
Nirvāṇa is immovable because it does not waver due to the winds of conceptual construction;
it is non-conceptual because it is devoid of any seal (*mudrā*).

It is unchanging because it transcends the senses; being devoid of arising and passing away, this Nirvāṇa is said to resemble the stainless midday sky and to have the nature of space. (Do. Ko. Vyā., 159) Nirvāṇa is the state of Mahāmudrā. (Do. Ko. Vyā., p. 160)
Apart from saṃsāra, nothing else is called nirvāṇa;
yet these very phenomena, through delusion, take the form of saṃsāra, while [in truth] they are nirvāṇa. (Hevajratantra 2.4.32, 34) It is motionless.
Having obtained the action-seal (karmamudrā), the fruit of non-movement arises. Non-movement is a movement that resembles [the original]; however, that is not the innate (sahaja) non-movement.
However, it is similar to the *sahaja*.

In the *Abhayapaddhati-saṃgraha* (pp. 43–43), it is stated that in the initiation (*seka*), the triad of wisdom (*prajñā*), gnosis (*jñāna*), and bliss (*ānanda*) is endowed with four moments (*kṣaṇa*) by way of its own nature; and in *haṭhayoga*, the fruit of the *niṣpanda* is said to result from the *karmamudrā*.

The Yoginī Nairātmyā, having caused [the winds] to enter the three channels and rendered them free from appearance, is herself the perfectly pure Avadhūtī, the Yoginī Nairātmyā. (Cakrasaṃvarapañjikā, p. 14) This is the position.
"Side" (*pakṣa*) refers to conviction regarding the Guru and the deity (*gurudevatā*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 98).
"Side" consists of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
The "interior" (*abhyantara*) of those two is the middle (*madhya*).
What is that? It is the state of abiding through the non-dualization of the two truths. (Guhyasiddhiprakāśa, p. 121).
This is the *Pañcakrama*.
In the beginning, there should be the stage of generation (utpattikrama), which accomplishes the form of the mantra;
the second stage is said to be the mere contemplation of the mind (cittanidhyapti).
The third stage is the delightful vision of the truth within the conventional;
the fourth stage is said to be the purification of the conventional through the truth.
The fifth is called "Yuganaddha" (the Union), which is the conjunction of the two truths;
this is the sixth branch of practice (*sādhanāṅga*), which summarizes the meaning of all tantras. (Guhyasiddhiprakāśa, p.
1). The five gnoses (*pañcajñānāni*).

The characteristics of the perfectly pure dharmadhātu consist of the mirror-like, the equalizing, the discerning, the accomplishing-of-what-is-to-be-done, and [the nature of] the dharmadhātu itself. (Avatamsaka Sūtra, p.
37) The wisdom of the five Tathāgatas is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) because it reflects the manifold wheel of objects of knowledge.
Because it is the oneness of the stateless and so forth, that itself is the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*).
Because it is the discernment of what has been revealed, that itself is the knowledge of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
Because the welfare of the world proceeds from that very source, that itself is the knowledge of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).
Because it has the nature of *dharmatā*, this is the *dharmadhātu-jñāna*. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, pp.

84–85). The five Tathāgatas, having prepared on a consecrated ground any desired square mandala or other shape from among the four [types], [visualize] in its center, upon a solar disc at the heart of a multicolored eight-petaled lotus, the blue syllable *HŪṂ* fully perfected.
Akṣobhya, black in color, holding the earth-touching mudrā;
following that, on the eastern petal, Vairocana, white in color, produced from the white syllable Oṃ, holding the bodhyaṅgī mudrā;
then, on the southern petal, Ratnasambhava, yellow in color, born from the yellow syllable Trāṃ, holding the boon-granting mudrā.

Then, having visualized Amitābha, red in color, arisen from a red syllable *hrīṃ* on the western petal, holding the *samādhi-mudrā*; and Amoghasiddhi, green in color, born from a green syllable *khaṃ* on the northern petal, holding the *abhaya-mudrā*...
these five Tathāgatas are clothed in saffron-colored robes, possess uṣṇīṣas, have shaved heads and faces, and abide upon solar discs.
Vairocana is the supreme moon-disk;
from him proceed four [deities] facing Akṣobhya, while Akṣobhya faces the practitioner. (Ārya-va-jra-saṃgraha, p. 5)
The five element-ḍākinīs are as follows: Pātanī is the earth element, and Māraṇī is known as the water element.

The fire element is considered to be Ākarṣaṇī, while Vāyu is regarded as Natreśvarī; the space element is said to be Padmajvālinī, who is unagitated. (Vajrāvalī, pp. 16–17). This is the *Pañcapradīpa*.
By the mention of "meat," the inclusion of the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*) is intended. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana, p.
194) "Great meat" (*mahāmāṃsa*) refers to the five lamps. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana, p.
195) The flesh of a cow, a dog, an elephant, a horse, and a human, mixed with fly-saliva and honey, when consumed, constitutes the five lamps and becomes the remover of all diseases.
Furthermore, *makṣikācchardi* is *mādhavī*. (Vi.pra., p.
236). The five arrows (*pañcabāṇa*) are the five shafts known as *mādana*, *mohana*, *nirmohana*, *mūrcchana*, and *niśceṣṭīkaraṇa*. (Gu.sa.pra., p. 197).
"Five-fold prostration" means having performed salutation with the two knees, the two hands, and the head. (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p.
24). "Five paths."
The path of accumulation, the path of preparation,
and the path of seeing.
The path of cultivation and the path of no-more-learning—these are the five paths. (Vasubandhu’s Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa, p.
51) It should be understood that these five paths are subsumed under two: the mundane path and [the supramundane path].
And by means of the supramundane path.
In that regard, how many factors are there in the mundane path?
There are twenty-two factors.
Which are the applications of mindfulness?
[They are] those named the right exertions, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, and the powers.
How many factors are there in the supramundane path? Fifteen.
Which are they? The seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path. (Vasubandhu’s *Triśatikāyāḥ Prajñāpāramitāyāḥ Kārikāsaptati*, p. 52). These are the five jewels.
The five jewels are coral, pearl, lapis lazuli, gold, and silver. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
40a) The five rays are the five seed-syllables of air, fire, and so forth, namely ya, ra, la, va, and ha. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana, p. 218)

The great jewel of five colors refers to the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) that flows solely through the central channel by means of the cessation of both the left and right channels; it is called the "great jewel of five colors" (Sevārthabodhinī-ṭīkā, p.
33). [These are] the Buddhas of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Form is the Buddha Vairocana, while feeling is Vajrasūrya;
perception is Padmanarteśvara, and likewise, mental formations are Vajrarāja.
Consciousness is Vajrasattva... (Vajrāvalī, p. 14–15). The five aggregates are, in brief, proclaimed as the five Buddhas (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, p. 15).
The five aggregates.
The five aggregates are the five *ḍākas*. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.

67) The fivefold realization (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*) consists of the moon possessing mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), and the one possessing the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) who has twenty-one [deities].
The examination of one's own deity by means of seed-syllables and signs is thus described.
The performance by all [Bodhisattvas] as one, its accomplishment, and its nature as pure dharma— (1.8.6–7)—
that [wisdom] has the form of mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), it arises from the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*),
it is the correct analytical investigation (*sadbhūtapratyavekṣā*), and it is indeed the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*).
That is the perfectly pure dharmadhātu (Hevajra Tantra 2.4.46–47).
Regarding the "great emptiness of five syllables," here the five syllables are known as vowels and are unutterable.
That is to say: in the center is the form of a curved knife (kartikā) empty of the vowel *a*;
on the right are two dots (*bindu*) empty of the vowel *ṛ*;
on the left is a single dot empty of the vowel *u*.
In the east is the form of a staff, empty of the syllable *hra*;
in the west is the shape of a plow, empty of the syllable *ḷ*.
In this way, the modifications consisting of the long vowels, the *guṇa*, the *vṛddhi*, and the *yaṇ*-substitutions are to be understood.

Thus, the syllable *vaṃ* consists of five vowels, is the great emptiness (*mahāśūnya*), has as its nature non-referential compassion, transcends the reality of atoms, resembles a reflected image (*pratisenā*), and is accessible only to the yogi. (Vi.pra., p.
48). "With the five nectars" means with curd, milk, ghee, cow urine, and cow dung.
"With the five nectars" refers to that which is internal (*adhyātmika*).
By the mention of feces and urine, the inclusion of the five nectars is intended. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 194)
Feces and urine are the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotanaṭīkā, p. 195).
Regarding the application of the five nectars here, it is said: "As it is externally, so it is within the body" (p. 47).
According to this statement, there are five substances externally;
internally, by unifying the five substances, there is the yoga of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
Therefore, the consumption of the five nectars shall be the bestower of longevity for yogins.
Externally, by the word *viṭ* (feces), Vairocana’s son Bali is meant; because of his power (*vaśāt*), sulphur (*gandhaka*) is called *viṭ*.
Internally, it is simply feces.
Of these two, there is an equal portion.
Externally, urine is King Viṣṇu and the juice of the king of bees;
internally, it is simply urine.
Externally it is red mica; internally it is the female menses; these are in equal parts.
Śukra is mercury externally,
and in the inner self it is indeed semen;
these two are in equal proportion.
Human flesh externally is the three myrobalans (triphalā), and internally it is the marrow; these two are also to be taken in equal parts.
Thus, there is one part of feces,
three-quarters of a part of flesh,
and half a part of blood.
Take one part of *śukra* (semen) and one part of this [the aforementioned substance], combine them, and saturate the mixture with urine seven times.
Dry it repeatedly in the sun; then, if one consumes one *karṣa* daily with ghee and honey for a period of six months, it will grant longevity.
"By the avoidance of vegetables, sour things, oil, and salt"—this is the rule for the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). (Viṣṇupurāṇa, p. 236).
The heroes of the five abodes:
the eye is called Mohavajra, and the ear is named Dveṣavajra.
The nose is the envy-vajra, and the mouth is known as the passion-vajra;
the body is the stinginess-vajra—these five are the gross deities. (Vajravārāhī-tantra, pp. 15–16).
The five-fold offering worship.
The five offerings are flowers and so forth;
that worship is the "five-offering worship" (*pañcopahāra-pūjā*) (Guṇasāgarapraśnottara, p. 77). The five offerings are the five sense objects (Guṇasāgarapraśnottara, p. 219).
Just as a cloth (*paṭa*) or curtain (*paṭala*) wards off disturbances such as gadflies and mosquitoes,
so too this meaning of the tantra is called a "cloth" (*paṭa*) because it wards off disturbances such as afflictions, karma, and birth, like a cloth.
That which takes up or grasps it is the "holder" (*dhāraka*); thus, a *paṭala* is a collection of texts. (Guhyasiddhiprakāśa, p. 29).
Because it is unstained by the defects of existence (*bhava*), it is knowledge (*jñāna*); that is called the "lotus" (*padma*). (Jñānasiddhi, 15–25).
The letter E is said to be the lotus (*padma*);
[it is] Padmanarteśvara. (A.P.V.S., p. 238)
Padmanarteśvara is so called because from the back of the foot of Padmanarteśvara, who is the nature of outflow-free *bodhicitta*, [the dance] proceeds.
(Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p. 49) He is Padmanarteśvara because he prevails there like a lord over the dancing of the lotus (*padmanartana*). (Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p. 82) [He is also] Padmaprakāśa.

The self-arisen one (svayambhū) is called *padmaprakāśa* because he shines and is beautiful within a lotus (*padme prakāśate śobhate*). (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 82). A lotus-vessel (*padmabhājana*) is a skull-cup (*kapāla*). (Hevajra-tantra-ṭīkā, fol. 64a).

Padmāntaka gladdens the world, does not grasp at anything, and discerns all things; being untainted by worldly existences and possessing perfect awakening, he is therefore known as Padmāntaka. (Jñānasiddhi 15.17)

*Padmāntakṛt* (the Destroyer of the Lotus): Just as a lotus, though smeared with water, destroys that very water by which it is smeared, so too does he destroy those very afflictions (*kleśa*) by means of them; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
*Padma* (lotus) refers to the womb (*yoni*).

Because he brings about—that is, produces—the bliss of supreme joy (*paramānanda*) by means of the method of union of the two organs within that [lotus], he is called *Padmāntakṛt* (the Maker of the End of the Lotus);
this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 26).
Those who delight in the substance of another...

The wisdom of the perfectly awakened one is designated as "substance" (*dravya*); those whose nature it is to seize that [wisdom] are considered to be "delighting in the substance of others. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 47).
This is the supreme delight (*paramarati*).
Supreme delight is supreme wisdom, the knowledge characterized by luminosity.

The Supreme Ādibuddha is the supreme, immutable bliss, characterized by the awakening through a single moment, the five aspects, the twenty aspects, and the Net of Illusion (*māyājāla*). (He. Ta. Ṭī., p. 40b)
Therefore, he is the Ādibuddha, the Paramādibuddha;
he is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara),
the Sovereign Lord (Parameśvara), the Wheel-turner (Cakravartin) who is the master of those phonemes whose nature is that of the supreme Vīras and Yoginīs.
For instance, by excluding the four neuter seed-syllables (*bīja*), the twelve letters beginning with *a* constitute the twelve-armed Bhagavān.
The four burnt seeds are Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī.
The consonants from *ka* to *ha*, marked with the bindu of the letter *ma*, are the heroes and heroines of the three wheels.
The letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *ha* are Kākāsyā and the others;
the letter *kṣa* is Kṣayaḍāka;
and in the center is the letter *a*, which is Vajravārāhī. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 73)
Dwelling in Pātāla, beginning from Pretapurī up to Kulatā, they dwell in Pātāla. (Vajratārā-ṭīkā, p. 27).
Drinking.
"Compassion is constantly drunk for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings;
the yogi, delighting in the drink of yoga, does not sink through any other drink. (Hevajra Tantra 1.6.26).
Compassion is cultivation with an object.

The tasting of the essence of great bliss is the drink; that very [essence] is drunk perpetually, day and night, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the world.... Yoga is meditative absorption (samādhi).
That itself is the drink; therein alone lies delight and joy. Therefore, one should not perform immersion through the yoga of conduct by means of drinking other intoxicants such as wine.
Due to the predominance of delusion (*moha*), there would be a great obstacle to yoga. (He. Ta. Ṭī., p.

23b) The instruction on confession is as follows: "Whatever evil karma has been committed, caused to be committed, or approved while being committed by me—through body, speech, or even mind—while wandering through this beginningless and endless cycle of births in various types of existences."
"I confess all that before the Blessed Ones, the Great Festivals of the Three Worlds, the Gurus, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas. (Sādhana-mālā, p.

55) "Whatever evil has been committed, caused to be committed, or even approved by me—whether through hatred, attachment, or delusion, and whether by body, speech, mind, or otherwise—I confess all that before the Victors. (Sādhana-mālā, p. 116)
The practitioner should perform the confession of sins for the sake of increasing auspiciousness:

"Whatever sinful karma has been committed by me—while wandering through beginningless saṃsāra—whether by body, speech, or even mind, whether performed by myself, caused to be performed by others, or even rejoiced in while being performed, all that I confess. (Sādhanamālā, p. 169; Sādhanamālā, p. 201)

"I confess all my own evil deeds" (Sādhana-mālā, p. 225). "Whatever sinful action has been committed, caused to be committed, or approved by me—that I now confess in the presence of the Blessed One, all of it" (Sādhana-mālā, p. 373). The ten perfections.

Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and primordial knowledge are considered the ten perfections (*pāramitā*). (Avataṃsaka-sūtra, p. 12). Pāvakī.
Because of the burning of the face with tears or of grief, [the deity] is Pāvakī on the back of the foot. (Vāmakeśvarī-tantra-ṭīkā, p.
46). The seats (pīṭha), the minor seats (upapīṭha), the fields (kṣetra), and the minor fields (upakṣetra).
Likewise, there is the Chandoha, and also the Upachandoha.

Likewise, the *melāpaka* and the *upamelāpaka*, as well as the *śmaśāna* and *upaśmaśāna*—these ten stages, beginning with the *pīṭhas*, [are attained] through the dedication of merit (*puṇyapariṇāmanā*). (Vajrāvalī, p. 30)
"Whatever root of merit has arisen through the sevenfold unsurpassed worship, I dedicate that very thing toward perfect enlightenment. (Sādhana-mālā, p.
56) "I dedicate all that root of merit which has been produced through the sevenfold unsurpassed worship and the confession of misdeeds toward perfect, complete enlightenment. (Sādhana-mālā, p.
202) "And I dedicate all my own roots of merit toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment. (Sādhana-mālā, p. 225)
Rejoicing in merit:

"I rejoice in all that is wholesome—whether it belongs to the perfectly awakened ones, the pratyekabuddhas, and the śrāvakabuddhas, as well as to their sons, the bodhisattvas, and even to the beings dwelling within the belly of the three worlds. (Sādhana-mālā, p.

And whatever merit belongs to all the Tathāgatas, as well as to others who rely upon perfect enlightenment, to the Pratyekabuddhas, to the true gurus, and to all the Victors—that I rejoice in with my own heart. (Sādhana-mālā, p.
116) Having thus rejoiced in the merit of the assembly of the Perfect Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,

"The entire merit of sentient beings, such as those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), by its very nature" (Sā. Mā., p. 169). "Whatever is wholesome for the Sugatas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and Jinas, as well as for their sons, the Bodhisattvas, and for the world including the gods and Brahmā—I rejoice in all that" (Sā. Mā., p. 201). "I rejoice in all the wholesome [deeds] of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Noble Ones, and ordinary persons" (Sā. Mā., p. 225).
The *pudgala* is filled by karmas and flows away through their very exhaustion. (*Hevaja Tantra Commentary*,
folio 38a) Pullīra.
In Pullīra, however, she is known as Pracaṇḍā, who carries the nails and teeth; (Vajrāvalī-nāma-maṇḍalopāyikā, p. 42).
Here, the word "flower" (*puṣpa*) refers to [the letter] *ḍa* (or *dra*).
The substance of the female form is called *puṣpanasya*;
*puṣpa* is the female discharge (*strīrajas*). (Vi.pra., p. 240)

Externally, *keśarājikā* is *bhṛṅgarāja*; its juice, equal to the flower of a woman, is the "flower-snuff" (*puṣpanasya*) at the time of twilight. (Vi.pra., p. 236) Worship (*pūjā*) consists of the various offerings—flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, flags, and so forth—which have emerged from its very rays; and the worship of these through both external and internal modes of worship is "worship. (Sā.mā., #)
(116) Having mentally performed various kinds of worship with flowers and other offerings to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and leaders residing in the ten directions, (Sā. Mā., p. 169).

Thereafter, one should perform a great worship with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, flags, and so forth, toward those Great Compassionate Ones—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—residing in the space before them. (Sādhana-mālā, p.

201) Within one’s own heart, situated upon a moon disc produced from the primordial vowel (*ādisvara*), is the eighth seed-syllable; accompanied by the five-fold offerings arising therefrom, one should worship with various goddesses through the emanation of clouds of diverse offerings. This is the worship (*pūjā*).
(Sā. Mā., p.
373) Specifically regarding the six sense-bases, the elements, the aggregates, and so forth.
In the same way, the union with those ḍākinīs who possess the forms of deities is declared to be worship, because by that they are worshipped.
Through the practice of the state of selflessness, there arises the meditative cultivation of the form of the deity. (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, p. 67)
That is considered the great worship which propitiates all Buddhas (*Vajratilaka-ṭīkā*, p.
67). The word "full" (*pūrṇa*) designates the very removal or departure of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the obscurations of afflictions, cognizable objects, and meditative attainments.
There is neither an interruption of knowledge nor its fulfillment for that [state].
As it is said in the Āgama:
"But for the Buddhas, [knowledge] is eternally manifest, whereas for those whose minds are afflicted by ignorance, it is not. (Se. Ṭī., p. 62)
And by the venerable Saraha:
"Victorious is the one King of Bliss, devoid of cause, eternally arisen for the worlds;
at the time of whose description even the Omniscient One became poor in words. (Sevaka-ṭīkā, p. 63)
That which is the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) of the bodhicitta is called *pūrṇā*.
This very [state] must be stabilized by the practitioners of yoga.
For if this moon of bliss is not stabilized during the *pūrṇā* [phase], it arises again and again and perishes as well. (Se. Ṭī., p. 64)
The earth-maṇḍala in the heart is the earth itself, square on all sides. (Vajrāvalī, p.
62) This is the offering of the poṣadha.
First is the granting of the *poṣadha*:
"Pay heed, Venerable Teacher! I, [name], a lay follower named [so-and-so], go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, until I reach the seat of enlightenment.
Thus a second and a third time.

"Thus, may they hold me in mind as one who has gone for refuge to the Three. Pay heed, O Preceptor! I, the lay follower named [so-and-so], from this moment until tomorrow at sunrise, in the interval between now and then, shall refrain from killing any living being and from taking what belongs to others.
From unchastity,
from divisiveness of speech, and from the production of faults consisting of falsehood;
From drinking [intoxicants], from eating at improper times, and from [using] garlands, perfumes, dance, song, and ornaments;
"I shall abstain from high beds and seats; for that duration, I shall practice according to these eight qualities. These are the verses on the *poṣadha* (Avaivartacakrasūtra, pp. 3–4):
"The confession of all misdeeds and the rejoicing in merits..."
"I shall practice the fast, the noble eightfold poṣadha. (Avataṃsakasūtra, p. 6).
Nature is nature; it is conventional truth.

(From the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, p. 33; verse 71): Nature (*prakṛti*) consists of twenty-four elements and possesses the quality of being the object for the person (*puruṣa*), who possesses the quality of being the subject.
However, there exists another, luminous nature that is innate and devoid of the quality of being an object. (From the *Vimalaprabhā*, p. 173).
In this body, first of all, there is an eightfold *prakṛti*, consisting of earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṃkāra*).
... Furthermore, *prakṛti* is threefold according to the distinction of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and possesses the characteristics of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
... Another is the fourth *prakṛti*, which is the source of knowledge (*jñānamūrti*). (Viṣṇupurāṇa, p. 216)

The first five are voids; Prakṛti is neither an evolute nor an evolvent. [Then there are] Śrī, Kalā, Bindu, Nāda, Kāla, Citta, and Buddhi; likewise, Prakṛti and the other vowels beginning with Māruta.
The gross forms are the letters of the consonant groups; the ten multiplied by three (thirty) and the other sixteen are the evolutes.

Among them, the Vajrin is neither nature nor transformation; he is all-pervasive and devoid of intrinsic nature. (Kālacakra Tantra 2.87) O Lord of Men, immortality occurs when the state is quiescent; hellishness in the *tāmasa*; animality in the *rājasa*; and humanity on this excellent earth-plane in the *miśra* [state].

The state of being real is threefold—pertaining to *rajas*, *tamas*, and indeed *sattva*—which are mutually mixed; whatever state a living being remembers with the mind at the time of death, there its rebirth occurs. (Kā. Ta. 2.93).
*Pracaṇḍā*.
She whose ferocity (*caṇḍatva*) has been stilled is *Pracaṇḍā*;
that is to say, having attained the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 46). *Pracaṇḍā* is the production of desire. (Vajratilaka, p. 53).
Wisdom is characterized by the image of wisdom; it is the realization of all aspects, the emptiness of all phenomena. (Se. Ṭī., p.
71) Wisdom is the cognition of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, devoid of the grasped and the grasper. (Se. Ṭī., p. 47)
And wisdom (*prajñā*) is characterized by the realization that all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-apprehendable.

In this context, the intellect (*buddhi*) which maintains the forms of the grasped and the grasper—consisting of the four elements, the five aggregates, the six objects, and the nature of the woman—is wisdom (*prajñā*). Wisdom is the variegated, the ripened, the crushed, and the distinct. (Avaivartacakrasamādhisūtra, p. 3; p. 39)
Therefore, know its true nature, by which you are the sovereign lord of the world.
Wisdom is existence, and it is equal; it is the three bodies and the three vehicles.
That itself is the wheel, the blissful means for yogins—that, I say, is supreme.
Mañjuvajra, Mahāmāyā, Vajraḍāka, and others—wisdom alone appears through its various manifestations; that very liberation is the essence of the Victors.
Having realized that the mind has departed, it is without support and unsurpassed.
Peaceful, pure, and without appearance—this is known as the cognition of wisdom.
(Wisdom is the lotus. (Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 52) Wisdom is the lotus. (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p.
9) Through the application of thorough investigation, [one realizes] the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
"Through the distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge, that is called the reality of wisdom (*prajñātattva*).

Having a form like a lotus fiber, established below and above, she is renowned by all the Buddhas as the Mother named Wisdom (*prajñā*). (Prajñāpāramitā-viniścaya-siddhi 1.14; Abhidhānottara-tantra 108–109)
Wisdom (*prajñā*) characterized by the non-discrimination of phenomena, consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, is twofold: investigative and that which is not [investigative].
It investigates each [phenomenon] individually.
That which is sought,
known,
and grasped by the vajra-eye is the wisdom of discerning observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*).
That by which one penetrates is "penetrating" (*nairvedhikī*); that analytical observation is penetrating wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is wisdom characterized by non-existence;
it is wisdom characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
(From the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*, p. 212): Wisdom is designated as the lotus.

...By that nature of the lotus, wisdom—whose intrinsic nature consists of the five goddesses Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, Tārā, and Samantabhadrā, who are themselves the nature of emptiness—is said to be the intrinsic nature [of the lotus].
(a. pra. vi. si., pṛ.
216) A woman, for her part, is *prajñā*. (He. Ta.
1.8.28) The emptiness of all phenomena is *prajñā*. (He. Ta. Ṭī., p. 37b)

Regarding the term *prajñājñānābhiṣeka*, there are two etymological derivations for the word *prajñājñāna*: knowledge by means of wisdom (*prajñayā jñānam*), and external knowledge within that very [wisdom].

In this context, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the intellect (*buddhi*) that maintains the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender; it has as its nature the four elements, the five aggregates, the six objects, and the female consort (*aṅganā*).
Regarding that [wisdom] which serves as the causal sign (*nimitta*), "the knowledge of the mind of awakening" (*bodhicittajñāna*) is one etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*).
That same [wisdom], when empty of the two aspects (*ākāra*), is "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); this is the other etymological derivation. (Abhisamayamañjarī, pp. 38–39)
Superior knowledge (*prajñā*) is the knowledge that all phenomena are nothing but one's own mind;
the consecration for the purpose of realizing that is the consecration of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*).
That knowledge of wisdom is to be understood through the external consort (*mudrā*).

When one has been consecrated in that consecration, the instruction on the *dharmamudrā*—the illusion-like samādhi for those of superior faculties—is explained. Wisdom (*prajñā*) is that which holds wisdom and is characterized by great compassion. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
7b) Wisdom (*prajñā*), [is] the holder of wisdom, characterized by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
"He who holds that [wisdom]" is *prajñādhṛk*; this is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Wisdom is the radiance of the moon;
he who holds it by means of the subtle element (*sūkṣmadhātu*) is *prajñādhṛk*.
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana, p.
24): "Prajñāntaka [swiftly extinguishes] false knowledge as it is manifested by deluded beings."
"Because of his union with the self characterized by perfect knowledge, he is remembered as the 'Ender of Wisdom' (*prajñāntaka*) (Jñānasiddhi 15.16).
He is the 'Maker of the End of Wisdom' (*prajñāntakṛt*), meaning that he destroys the afflictions (*kleśa*) through wisdom; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*)."
Wisdom consists of conceptual construction;

by entering its luminosity, one brings it to an end—thus he is "the one who has brought wisdom to an end" (*prajñāntakṛt*), which is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana, 26)
The Prajñāpāramitā who is the goddess Samantabhadrā, whose essence is the nature of emptiness— that Prajñāpāramitā,

whose nature consists of the gnosis of the four goddesses, is established through the intrinsic nature of emanation and reabsorption; she, whose nature is the transformation of the gnosis of the form of Śrī Mahāvairocana, is called Samantabhadrā by the term "Prajñāpāramitā."

That which is the Samantabhadra Prajñāpāramitā is of the nature of non-existence; by virtue of having the characteristic of space, it has the aspect of emptiness, is secluded, naturally luminous, devoid of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, and has the characteristic of being without intrinsic nature.
Being transformed into the Dharmakāya, when it is established for the sake of those to be trained, it manifests as the Nirmāṇakāya and so forth. (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-vyākhyāna, p. 216)
Wisdom is light. ...The attainments of wisdom and skillful means are intended by the term "wisdom. Their "pāra" is the limit.
The Perfection of Wisdom has gone away...
the ultimate truth. (Guhyasamājapradīpoddyotana, p. 70) The wisdom initiation.
The joy of cessation (*viramānanda*) is the wisdom initiation (*prajñābhiṣeka*).
...In some Yoga Tantras, it is the mutual embracing of wisdom and means;
its purification is the wisdom initiation.

The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is that which investigates, through the discernment of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*), those phenomena produced by the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*); this is the faculty of wisdom. (He. Ta. Ṭī., fol. 50a-b; Va. Ti. Ṭī., pp. 54–55)
The union of both wisdom and means, which is like that of water and milk,
is called "wisdom and means" through its connection with the non-dual form. (Prajñāpāramitā-vinaya-siddhi 1.17)
Buddhahood does not arise through wisdom alone, nor through skillful means alone;
rather, it occurs when both wisdom and skillful means possess the nature of equality.
When these two become of non-different form, then there is both enjoyment and liberation.
And so it has been said:
That which brings about the desired object by way of favorability, like a boat [carrying one] according to the current,
is proclaimed as the "method" (upāya) through its favorable application.
(a. pra. vi. si., pṛ. 214) "Wisdom and means" (*prajñopāya*) means means generated by wisdom; that is, means produced by wisdom.
(a. pra. vi. si., pṛ. 216) The verse of salutation:
"In infinite world-systems, as many Victors as there are, together with their Sons..."
"With body, mind, and speech, I bow down to them all. (Sādhanamālā, p. 2).
"Pratiṣṭhā" refers to the installation, that is, the formal establishment of the deities within the cloth [painting] and other such supports. (Hevajratantra-ṭīkā, p. 42b).

*Pratisenā* is defined by the term *pratisenā* as the object visualized by the practitioner appearing in mirrors and other such surfaces. (Se. Ṭī., p. 49). "The vision of *pratisenā* is like that of a young girl. (Se. Ṭī., pp. 31, 38).

In the *Pratisenāvatāra-tantra*, it is said that the manifestation of a *pratisenā* occurs in non-substantial things such as a mirror, a sword, the thumb, a lamp, the moon, the sun, water, a vessel, and the eyes.

For in the case of a *pratisenā*—that is, a body perceived in a mirror and so forth—there is no characteristic of form (*rūpalakṣaṇa*), because there is no aggregation of substantial atoms (*paramāṇudravyasaṃroha*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 49)
It does not have the characteristic of formlessness, because that which is being perceived is difficult to set aside. (Se. Ṭī., p. 71).
[This is] the condition (*pratyaya*).

In this system of Mantra, the Blessed One has taught three kinds of conviction: first, conviction in the tantra; then, conviction in the guru; and finally, conviction in oneself. (Viṣṇu-prakaraṇa, p. 35)
Certainty arises from scripture, and likewise certainty from the teacher;
certainty arises from oneself, and likewise certainty from another.
"It is to be grasped by means of four conditions...
This statement from the *Guhyatattvaprakāśa* is cited in the *Vasantatilakaṭīkā* (10.10).
Pratyāhāra is said to be the withdrawal, from every direction, of the ten senses from their respective functions, toward the withdrawal of desire. (Se. Ṭī., p. 30)
"Having attained the state of *prathāhāra*, one is empowered by all mantras" (*Sevaka-ṭīkā*, p.
31). "The senses and the objects of the senses are the 'senses' (*indriya*).
The "own-functioning" (*svavṛtti*) of those ten senses—the subjects and their objects—is their persistence or operation within their own self (*ātman*).
The function of its own nature is mere existence (*sattāmātratā*).
The meaning is that the function of its own nature is the cessation of the activity of grasping objects— that is, the transition of the object and the subject into the state of being an object.
Established therein means established in its own functioning;
however, "own functioning" does not refer to activity in the form of subject and object.
Objects such as forms and so forth are called "desires" (kāmāḥ) because they are desired and longed for.
The apprehension of objects by their respective sense faculties is "the nutriment of desire" (*kāmāhāra*).

With reference to that nutriment of desire, the withdrawal [of the mind] by means of the sense faculties, such as the eyes, having focused on the grasping of objects like forms, is declared to be "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*). (Se. Ṭī., p.
31). Having attained this withdrawal, one stabilizes the vision of the images of the three realms through the sequence of the ten signs, beginning with smoke, by means of the limb of withdrawal.
And when the vision of the *bimba* has been stabilized through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), then the yogin is empowered by all mantras and bestows boons and so forth by means of speech. (Se. Ṭī., p.
34) Here, for those in saṃsāra, "food" (*āhāra*) consists of the grasping of objects such as form by the sense organs, beginning with the eyes.
The renunciation of that is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal). (Se. Ṭī., p.
43) The *prabhākarī* [cakra] is the field (*kṣetra*) of the armpits and breasts.
Because the *bodhicitta* is sprinkled under the guise of sweat and milk, that very [stage] is Prabhākarī;
for from observing that, there arises a light of bliss in the mind. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 28)

Prabhāvatī is so called because she is endowed with the radiance of the color of fire (*prabhāvatī agnivarṇaprabhāyuktatvāt prabhāvatī*). (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 47) Prabhāvatī is the production of the supernatural power of investigation (*mīmāṃsarddhyutpādaḥ prabhāvatī*). (Vajratilaka, p. 53)
Luminous, luminous, luminous is the ultimate truth. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana, p. 33, 71)
There, Pramuditā is located at the head, the crown lock, and the back of the right ear; the seat is the locus of bodhicitta,
and she herself is Pramuditā.
Because it generates the threefold bliss through the sequence beginning with dissolution (*laya*), [it is the path of application].
What is the path of application? What is the path of application?
There are ten dharmas. Which ten? They are the five faculties and the five powers. (Vasubandhu’s Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa, p. 51)

In that regard, on the path of preparation (prayogamārga), there are four factors conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya): those that have reached the stage of heat (ūṣmagata), those that have reached the stage of the summit (mūrdhagata), and those that have reached the stage of patience (kṣāntigata).
And there are the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
In that regard, with respect to the meaning of the first two levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), faith and the others are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
For it is when faith and the others proceed toward their goal that they come to be designated as "faculties."

When they are not turned back by their opposites—namely, lack of faith, laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, improper mental attention, and the various forms of faulty wisdom—the five powers come into being. (Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī-ṭīkā, pp. 54–55). They are inclined [toward the wholesome].
Because it carries feces, it is *pravaṇā*;
through the transposition of syllables (*varṇavyatyaya*), it becomes *praṇavā*; it flows toward Vairocana in the heart. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 45)

Those who, having cultivated tranquility (*śamatha*), realize that the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth of those who take life are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), they would be takers of life established in the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 47)
Having expelled the breath consisting of the fivefold knowledge and having the nature of the five elements,
one should contemplate it in the form of a sphere at the tip of the nose.
The great jewel of five colors is known as *prāṇāyāma*. (Se. Ṭī., p.
30) By means of *prāṇāyāma*, the Bodhisattva is certainly perceived. (Se. Ṭī., p.
31) The five gnoses are the five Buddhas, Akṣobhya and the rest; they possess the nature of the five maṇḍalas of the lalanā and consist of the five aggregates, consciousness and the rest.
That breath, consisting of those [elements], is in the left nostril.
Here, by the term "five elements," the five constituents—earth and so forth—which possess the nature of the five mandalas of the *rasanā*, are understood.
That breath, which has the nature of those [elements], possesses the nature of the five elements; [in that...]
Having emitted [the breath] from the right nostril in the form of a *piṇḍa* (a mass/cluster);
here, "mass" refers to the nature of the left and right mandalas of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) within the central channel, the *avadhūtī*.
Having emitted that vital wind in the form of a *piṇḍa* at the tip of the nose.
Here, by the word "nose" (*nāsikā*), the pericarp of the lotuses at the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown of the head is meant.
Having emitted that vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), one should project—that is, visualize—it at the tip of the nose;
specifically, within the pericarp, in the center of the pericarp, and not on the petals of the left or right lotus.
This very vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*), which flows solely through the central channel by means of the cessation of both the left and right channels, is called the "great jewel of five colors.
It should be recited as *prāṇāyāma* and as *vajrajāpa*, being recited with the central channel as its inseparable limb. (Se. Ṭī., pp.
32–33) When the yogin is free from the affliction of the moon and sun, he always becomes a carrier of the central channel.
Then, being purified by *prāṇāyāma*, one is beheld by the Bodhisattvas and praised. (*Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā*, p. 34).
*Prāṇāyāma* is the cessation of the flow in the left and right channels, *lalanā* and *rasanā*;
it is the constant movement of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) within the central channel, the *avadhūtī*.

By means of the yoga of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*), the yogi performs inhalation through the *avadhūtī* with the syllable *oṃ*, retention with the syllable *hūṃ*, and exhalation with the syllable *āḥ*, having the nature of the moon, sun, and Rāhu; this is the limb of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
This is the swinging (*preṅkhaṇa*).
"Āgati" is said to mean "swinging" (He.
Ta. 2.3.57); "Pretapurī" refers to the abode of the *pretas* located at the *liṅga* (Va. Ti., p. 34).
The city of the pretas, like a city of five voids, is the City of Pretas; it possesses a pair of banners. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
34) It is the abode of the inhabitants of the City of Pretas, characterized by phlegm, and swift as a wheel. (Vajratilaka, p.
46) It is beloved.
*Premāṇī* refers to the thighs because they generate love through the spring flowers carried by the red vehicle (*lohitavāhana*). (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 46).
*Phaṭ phaṭ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) indicating killing. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpa, p. 164).
The fourfold fruit (*phalacatuṣṭaya*).

In the syllable *Evaṃ*, there is the outflow (*niṣyanda*); from the wheel of Dharma, the ripening (*vipāka*); in the enjoyment wheel (*sambhogacakra*), the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra*); and in the wheel of bliss (*sukhacakra*), purity (*vaimalya*).
The fruit is said to be fourfold, distinguished by its outflow and so forth;
the Blessed Wisdom, impelled by the wind of karma, is the enjoyer of karma.
As it was performed, so it is experienced; this is designated as "outflow" (*niṣyanda*). Its opposite is "maturation" (*vipāka*), wherein even from a small action there is a great fruit.
"Human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) is acquisition, while "purity" (*vaimalya*) arises from the purification of yoga. (HeTa 2.4.56–58)
The syllable *evaṃ* is the *yonicakra*;
therein is the flow-result (*niṣyandaphala*). In the *dharmacakra* is the ripening-result (*vipākaphala*).
In the enjoyment wheel (*saṃbhogacakra*) is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*);
in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) is the fruit of purification (*vaimalyaphala*).

... Through the cultivation of the action seal (*karmamudrā*), which is characterized by conceptual elaboration (*prapañca*), one attains conformity with that [nature] by means of the aforementioned conduct of conceptual elaboration—through processes such as withdrawal and radiation—so that one's own body as the Vajra-holder acts for the benefit of the world.
Likewise, this attainment of enjoyment is called "outflow" (*niṣyanda*),
because it is said that an outflow resembles its cause;
whereas "maturation" (*vipāka*) is the opposite of that.
The opposite of the similar [case] is as follows:
let that characteristic be in the *dharmamudrā*.

For instance, while abiding in the practice free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcacaryā*) through the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopamasamādhi*) within the *dharmamudrā*, one may attain my fruit—the state of Vajradhara—even through a very slight action.
In Mahāmudrā and in Saṃbhoga, moreover, there is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
For indeed, through the practice that is utterly free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), the fruit to be accomplished is one’s own human exertion;
therefore, it is the fruit of human effort.
Because those of inferior vigor have no entitlement to it. "Purity" refers to yoga, which is the yoga of Mahāmudrā.

Its purification is the attainment of Mahāmudrā immediately following the [attainment of] Senā. For instance, for those of superior faculties whose intellects have been purified through meditation over incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), the attainment of Mahāmudrā occurs independently of further meditation.
The fruit resides in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*). (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol.
58a–59a) *Vimalaprabhā* (or *Bījalaprabhā*)?
*Bala* means flesh (*māṃsa*). (He. Ta. 2.3.56) *Bālabuddhiḥ* refers to the youth Mañjughoṣa.
The practitioner who possesses the intellect and thought directed toward that is one of "childish intellect" (*bālabuddhi*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p.
197). The *bindu* is the long *hūṃ* syllable; it is called *bindu* because it is the conceptualization of the knowledge that grasps the means (*upāya*). (Caryāmelāpakapradīpa-vyākhyā, p. 149).

By this designation "Bindu," the fourth void is to be understood. For example: the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the water element (*toyadhātu*), the tongue, form (*rūpa*), and grasping (*ādāna*)—the state of these being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*), their state of having a single flavor (*samarasatva*), and their state of being unified into one (*ekalolībhūtatva*) is the "Bindu," the great void of the fourth syllable.
Its symbolic sign is a single Bindu to the left of the central sign, which is not to be vocalized. (Vi. Pra., p. 48)
"In its center, however, is the syllable *haṃ*, in the form of a drop (*bindu*), which is indeed the Unstruck (*anāhata*).
It stands in the form of that seed, flowing in the form of nectar... (*Vajratārāsādhana*, pp. 62–63).

"In the center of the brain is the syllable *haṃ*, the Unstruck; because it flows with spreading nectar, it is called a 'drop' (*bindu*) due to its nature of dripping (*vedana*). (*Vajratārāsādhana-ṭīkā*, p. 63).
In the form of the Bindu and Indu, he brings delight to the world;
in the Mahāsukha-cakra, he assumes the form of the unstruck syllable (anāhatākṣara). This is the perfection of the Bimba. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 64)

By means of that seed-syllable (*bīja*), there is the manifestation of the deity’s body—seated upon a corpse atop a sun and other mandalas located in the pericarp of a thousand-petaled lotus, performing the *tāṇḍava* dance in the *arthaparyaṅka* posture; this is the manifestation of the image (*bimbaniṣpatti*).
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 14a).
This is the seed-syllable.
In this context, that which has fallen from the union of the two organs—the semen and blood within the secret lotus—is called the seed (*bīja*).
This collection of seeds occurs within that very luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) of the mind. (Vi.pra., p. 159)

Having visualized the seed-syllable of the deity garlanded with rays of light above the solar and other mandalas as appropriate, and having accomplished the welfare of the world through the infinite emanations of the family of Yoginīs from that seed-syllable, its reabsorption back into that very same seed-syllable is the "collection of seeds" (*bījasaṃgraha*).
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 13b–14a)

A Buddha is indeed called "non-dual" because he has arisen from the exhaustion of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*). Sentient beings are actually Buddhas themselves, but they are obscured by adventitious stains.

By removing that [obscuration], sentient beings are indeed Buddhas; of this there is no doubt. (Hevajra Tantra 2.4.69) A Buddha is not found anywhere else in other world-systems; for the mind alone is the Perfectly Awakened One, and no Buddha is shown apart from it. (Hevajra Tantra 2.4.75)
"Objects" refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*); "Buddha" refers to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñāna*). By means of that knowledge, I am a Buddha. (He. Ta. Ṭī., p.
46a) "Buddha" is the mind free from stains. (Vi. Pra., p. 23) Buddhahood (*buddhatva*).

Buddhahood consists of the splendors of the qualities such as omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). (Vi.pra., p.
16) Buddhahood is the mind free from the latencies (*vāsanā*) of saṃsāra;
a Buddha is the mind devoid of stains. (Vi.pra., p. 23)
Buddhahood (*buddhatva*) is the state of being awakened through the realization of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*);
that is established and situated within one's very own body.
For this very reason, that alone is the Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*).

Because the naturally accomplished, co-emergent Buddha abides right here: "Buddha-worship consists of form, sound, smell, taste, tangible objects, and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). (Vimalaprabhā-ṭīkā, p. 29)
Having realized that [the offering] is devoid of intrinsic nature, that would be the supreme worship of the Buddha.

Through these, known as the five offerings—arising from the cognitions of the eye and so forth, and adorned by the five superknowledges—one shall swiftly attain Buddhahood. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p.
54) [This is] the Jewel Casket of the Buddhas.

The Buddha-jewel is the supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*), the casket (*karaṇḍaka*) consisting of the vajra, the jewel, and the lotus; thus it is the "Buddha-jewel casket" (*buddharatnakaraṇḍaka*). (Vi.pra., p. 20).
The Buddhas are the Buddhas such as Akṣobhya and others. (Gu.sa.pra., p. 93).
The Buddhas are the Victors existing in the three times (*tryadhvavartin*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpa-ṭīkā, p.
101) Awakening (*bodha*) is the realization [of reality] in the form of the apprehended and the apprehender. (Hevajra-tantra-ṭīkā, fol. 33a)
Enlightenment (*bodhi*) is so called because it awakens sentient beings to its own true nature;
enlightenment is non-abiding nirvāṇa.

Enlightenment (*bodhi*) is precisely the thorough knowledge of one’s own true nature (*svarūpa*). It is called *bodhi* because by means of it, all things are understood as being one's own self-nature.
Enlightenment characterized by the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) is the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas; it is partial (*prādeśikī*).
Because they accept phenomena as having substantial reality,
while being liberated by that [wisdom], they would fall into the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas;
since that enlightenment prioritizes only one's own self-interest, it is called "partial" due to its lack of purity.

Enlightenment, which has the characteristic of the selflessness of both [person and phenomena], is the perfect awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*); because it is all-pervasive, it is pervasive, since it abides as the true nature (*tattvabhāva*) of all phenomena. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, pp. 51–52) Bodhicitta.
Bodhicitta is the semen, which has the nature of the conventional vibration. (Do. Ko.
Vyā., p. 150) Bodhicitta is traditionally defined as the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion.
(Sā. Mā., p. 111) Bodhicitta is the moon, consisting of fifteen digits.

The form of Āli is great bliss; the Yoginīs are its portions. (Hevajra Tantra 2.4.26) By means of the mandala circle and so forth, and through the sequence of self-consecration, one should generate the *bodhicitta* which has the nature of both the absolute (*vivṛti*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Closed, it resembles a kunda flower; opened, it has the form of bliss.
It is the nature of the syllable Evaṃ in the Sukhāvatī of the woman’s kakkola.
It is called "Sukhāvatī" precisely because of the protection of bliss.
(Hevajra Tantra 2.4.29–31) Bodhicitta has the nature of the non-duality of emptiness and compassion.
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 9a) Bodhicitta is great bliss.
Bodhicitta is great bliss; it is characterized by the joy that arises from the exhaustion of all suffering produced by the primary and secondary afflictions. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
52a) The generation of the thought of awakening is expressed as:
"I generate the mind for perfect enlightenment for the sake of the awakening of embodied beings."
"I shall practice the *Bhadracaryā*, which brings about the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings. (*Sādhana-mālā*, p.
3) "Thus, from the mass of merit acquired by me, I generate this sublime mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). (*Sādhana-mālā*, p.
117) "O, may I indeed fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake, benefit, and happiness of all sentient beings, until the very end of existence!"

And for the sake of establishing [beings] in the ultimate realm of nirvāṇa and in the awakening of a Buddha—thinking, "I shall generate the supreme Vajra-mind in order to rescue those sentient beings fallen into the ocean of existence"—this is the generation of the bodhicitta. (Sādhana-mālā, p. 225; p.
373) [He is thus called] a Bodhisattva.
Through the arising of this [insight], the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) is generated, and one is called a bodhisattva. (Sā. Mā., p.
111) Briefly stated, one who practices the conduct of awakening (bodhicaryā) is designated a bodhisattva. (He. Ta.
1.1.5a) [Thus,] they are bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattvas are Maitreya and others. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p.
93) *Bodhi* is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and *sattva* is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

He whose self is the body is "one whose self is a bodhisattva" (*bodhisattvātmā*). ... Form (*rūpa*) embraced by the two truths is the bodhisattva. (*Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, pp. 100–101). Awakening (*bodhi*) is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Sentient beings are conventional truth. He who abides in the non-dual nature of these two is the Bodhisattva Mahāvajradhara. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 109). The factors of enlightenment.

The limbs of that awakening (*bodhi*) are the means; they are the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*). "Limbs," "means," "wings," and "causes of manifestation" are synonyms. (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p. 52) Awakening is unobscured knowledge (*nirāvaraṇa-jñāna*).

That by which the vision of truth is concentrated in the mind is the factor of enlightenment of concentration; that by which there is enthusiasm for that very [vision] is the factor of enlightenment of energy.
That is the factor of enlightenment called vigor;
that by which one makes the mind free from doubt regarding that very [object] is the factor of enlightenment called joy.
Through that very joy, because of the pliancy of body, speech, and mind, and due to the abandonment of the heat of the afflictions, it becomes exceedingly cool;
that is the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*prasrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The thorough knowledge of the true nature of reality is the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
In that very state, the non-forgetfulness of this [mind] is the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Equanimity toward both attachment and non-attachment within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*). (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, p. 55–56). *Bolaḥ*.

"Vajra is known as *bolaka*. (*Hevajra Tantra* 2.3.60) "Bola is the mind-vajra consisting of great compassion. (*Hevajra Tantra Commentary*, fol. 52a) "Bola is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) situated at Kollagiri, which is the head. (*Hevajra Tantra Commentary*, fol. 54b)
Since the Buddha-knowledge itself experiences the sense-bases such as form and so forth, the Tathāgatas therefore describe that Buddha-knowledge as six-armed. (Jñānasiddhi 15.23)
The fourfold abode of Brahma refers to the four sublime abodes (brahmavihāra): loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), [sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā)].
Sympathetic joy and equanimity.
(Dharmasaṃgraha)
Compassion is characterized by the increase of passion, while loving-kindness consists in the destruction of hatred.
Joy (*muditā*) consists in the destruction of delusion (*moha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) consists in imperishable bliss; [this is] the fire of Brahman (*brahmāgni*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 66)
"Shaken by the wind of karma, the fire of Brahmā resides in the *trikaṭa*. (Vasiṣṭha-tārāvalī, p. 67).

Through the union of the churning stick and the churning base, that which is produced from karma—the blazing fire consisting of the reality (*tattva*) of Brahmā—resides by its own nature, burning in the *trikaṭa*, which is the triangle below that in the secret place (*guhya*).
Even the deep fire of Brahmā is praised for rites of pacification (*śāntika*);
and that [fire] arises from the friction of the kindling sticks (*araṇi*). (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, p. 67).
[This is] the consumption.
Food is to be understood as that which produces satisfaction. (HeTa 2.3.58) Bhaga is the heart, knowledge... that very thing is bhaga.
Because it shatters all afflictions (*sarvakleśa*),
it is *bhaga*. *Bhaga* is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The Blessed One (Bhagavān) is so called because he possesses the "blessing" (bhaga), which is characterized by qualities such as sovereignty, due to his being composed of the six purified elements.
As it is said in the *Mūlatantra*:
Sovereignty, complete beauty, fame, splendor, wisdom, and the attainment of all goals— these six are traditionally known as *bhaga*.
The thirty-six qualities, such as mastery over the noble vajras of the pure elements beginning with earth, are proclaimed as their six vulvae (*bhaga*). Also, in the *Hevajra*:
"Bhaga is declared to be 'breaking' (*bhañjana*), because of the breaking of the afflictions, Māra, and so forth."
"And those afflictions are carried away by wisdom; therefore, she is called Bhagā. One who possesses the qualities such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and so forth is "Bhagavān.
As it has been said:
"Of complete sovereignty, knowledge, fame, glory, beauty, and the attainment of wealth—these six are known as *bhaga*. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 1b)
"Bhagavān" refers to Vajradhara in the form of Hevajra (*Hevajra-tantra-ṭīkā*, p.
1b). One who possesses *bhaga* is called "Bhagavān" by the Buddha.
They say that *bhaga*s are of six kinds, consisting of all the qualities such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and so forth.

Alternatively, he is called Bhagavān because of his shattering of the Māras of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*). (He. Ta. 1.5.15) He is Bhagavān because of his endowment with good fortune and because of his shattering of all opposing factors (*vipakṣa*). (Gu. Sa. Pra., p. 12) He is Bhagavān because of his possession of the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya*). (Gu. Sa. Pra., p. 18)
"Bhaga" refers to the destruction of Māra and the afflictions (*kleśa*);
it is the collection of qualities such as omniscience and sovereignty.
He who possesses this *bhaga* is the Bhagavān. (Vi.pra., p. 17)

"Like a sister, a sister"—thus wisdom (*prajñā*) should demonstrate the distinction [between the two truths], for she is called "sister" because she explains the distinction between the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*). (Hevajra Tantra Ṭīkā, p. 20a)
The eightfold fear consists of fear from lions, elephants, fire, snakes, thieves, fetters, and water; [this is] existence (*bhava*). (Tattvārthasūtra-bhāṣya-ṭīkā, p. 26)
For conventional bodhicitta is existence (*bhava*). (Candrakīrti’s *Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya*, p.

70) "Existence, which arises from unreal conceptualization and consists of the imagination of things, is described by the wise as that very thing which deludes the foolish. (Pramāṇaviniścaya-siddhi 1.3)

Existence (*bhava*) is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). ... It is called "existence" because it comes into being through the transformation of the marks of the moon and sun; thus, existence is the form of the deity. (*Hevajra Tantra Commentary*, p. 48a). The authorization of fitness (*bhavyatānujñā*).

The reality of the mandala, characterized by the purity of the mandala; the reality of the deity, characterized by the purity of the deity; the preparation of the master; the knowledge for accomplishing the mandala; the five lamps; the consumption of nectar; the reality of fitness;

and the absence of intrinsic nature—these are the characteristics of the generation stage, and they constitute the authorization (*anujñā*) for turning the wheel of Dharma, which is the authorization regarding fitness (*bhavyatā-anujñā*). (Avaśyakasamuccaya, p. 38)
"Every state of being is a grasping at permanence. (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p. 3) "For all those are indeed pure states, since the world consists of the Buddha. (Hevajra-tantra 1.9.4)
The meaning is that it "comes into being" or "arises," [moving] from one state of existence (*gati*) to another state of existence;
[it refers to] the body characterized by the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
4b) Cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The cultivation of body is on the forehead; the cultivation of speech is in the heart; the cultivation of mind is in the secret place.
The collection (*samāhāra*) of the drops (*bindu*) of body and so forth is their unification within the *vajramaṇi*;
therein lies the cultivation of gnosis (*jñānabhāvanā*). (Se.
Ṭī., 62) Cultivation, however, is the manifestation arising from the non-dual union with the mandala. (Va. Ti., p. 68)
Externally, it appears to yogins by taking the body, speech, and mind as objects;
internally, within the four mandalas beginning with the Nirmāṇa, meditation consists precisely in the appearance of the assembly of mudrās and so forth.
Alternatively, the non-dual yoga of the mandala has the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) as its object.
That itself is cultivation (*bhāvanā*). And it has been said: "Non-existence is cultivation; existence is not cultivation at all.
Thus, existence would not be existence, for it is not obtained through cultivation. (Vajravatī-ṭīkā, p. 68)
What is the path of cultivation?
What is the path of cultivation? It is the factors of the path. How many factors of the path are there?
The noble eightfold path. (Vasubandhu’s Commentary on the *Triṃśikā*, p. 51) The path of cultivation is the antidote to the cognitive obscurations. (Vasubandhu’s Commentary on the *Triṃśikā*, p.
56) Phenomenal entities.

"Existents" (*bhāvāḥ*) are those things—such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), whether stable or moving—which arise from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). (Se. Ṭī., p.

59) All existents—whether born from eggs, born from a womb, born spontaneously, or born from moisture, including those of the nature of gods, asuras, and so forth—are by their very nature (*svabhāvena*) completely pure for the lord of yogins. (Ca. Ko. Vyā., p.
32) [The term] "real" (*bhāvikī*)...
"Bhāvikī" means that which flows (*sravati*) as it cultivates (*bhāvayati*) the *vukka*; [it is located] in the two eyes. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 44). [The term] "bhikṣuḥ" [is used].
The monk has ten million precepts (*koṭi-śikṣāpada*). (Do. Ko. Vyā., p.
