84) Those who move upon the earth (*bhūcaryas*) range from Kāmarūpa to the Himālayas. (Va. Ti. Ṭī., p. 27)

The limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is a synonym for the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*), suchness (*tathatā*), and the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 41a) From the perspective of ultimate truth, nirvāṇa is the limit of reality for all things. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 56b)
The space-element is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) is fourfold.
Here, in this world-system, the source of beings is fourfold: here, the source of beings that is earth consists of immobile things externally.
Inwardly, [the source] is hair;
outwardly, those born from eggs have wind as their source;
inwardly, [the source] is lice.

Externally, there are water-born beings such as swarms of worms, and moisture-born beings; internally, within the body as well, there are swarms of worms and the like; externally, there are womb-born beings produced from semen.

Internally it is semen alone; externally, because it is not specifically mentioned, it is the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*). [The beings] are of four kinds as the source of elements (*bhūtayoni*): those who are spontaneously born (*upapāduka*) in the form of essence (*rasa*), and internally, those subtle living beings in the form of eggs (*aṇḍa*). (Viṣṇu Purāṇa, p. 175)
The stages (twelve):
Joyful, Immaculate, Radiant,
Prabhākarī, Sudurjayā,
Abhimukhī,
Dūraṅgamā, Acalā,
Sādhumatī.
Dharmameghā,
Samantabhadrā,
Nirupamā,
And "Jñānavatī" refers to the thirteenth stage, which consists of the realm of non-abiding nirvāṇa. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 25b) Immersion.

In this context, within the mind that is the object of perception (*grāhyacitta*), the entry of the perceiving mind (*grāhakacitta*) into it—characterized by non-engagement with external objects—is called withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), meditation (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and immersion (*majjana*) in the six-limbed [Yoga].
This is the mandala. (Se. Ṭī., p. 46)
"The Maṇḍala is said to be the essence, the great bliss of the bodhicitta.
Because it performs that 'taking' (*ādāna*), the Maṇḍala is considered to be 'grinding' (*malana*). (Hevajra Tantra 2.3.27).
And likewise in the Guṭikātantra:
Transcending the cultivation of all limbs, free from conceptual construction and its fabrications, and endowed with the *mātrā* and the *bindu*—this is the supreme maṇḍala. (Do. Ko. Vyā., p.
158) Transcending the cultivation of all limbs, free from conceptual construction and its fabrications...
"This supreme maṇḍala transcends both measure and the drop" (Jñānasiddhi, p.
141). "The maṇḍala is the footprint; because it is rubbed [or ground], it is called maṇḍala" (Hevajratantra 1.5.19).
It is said that the maṇḍala is the essence (*sāra*).
It is called a *maṇḍala* because it takes—that is, grasps—the gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
What is that? It is the footprint, which is the firm contraction of the two big toes;
because it arises from the mind, it is called a *maṇḍala*.
The verbal root *mala* means "to hold" (*dhāraṇe*).
Because it holds great bliss (*mahāsukha*), it is called a *maṇḍala*. The word *maṇḍala* is a synonym for essence (*sāra*). (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 20b).

...then the ultimate mandala. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 52: *maṇḍa* is essence; that which takes (*lāti*) or grasps (*gṛhṇāti*) that is *maṇḍala*. The mind-mandala. [Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana, 41])

The term *maṇḍala* is derived from the root *maṇḍ*, meaning "essence" (*sāra*), and the prefix *lā*, meaning "to take" or "to grasp"; thus, it is that which grasps the essence, namely conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*)—this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*). Alternatively, *maṇḍala* is that which grasps the essence, namely ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
As stated by the Blessed One in the *Vyākhyātantra*:
"Transcending the cultivation of all limbs, and free from conceptual construction and its products."
This supreme maṇḍala transcends the measure of a single atom (*mātrābindu*); this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
(Gu | Sa | Pra | Pṛ | 45) It is called *maṇḍala* because it takes (*lāti*), that is, grasps and appropriates, the essence (*maṇḍa*). (Gu | Sa)
That very thing is called *maṇḍa*, the supreme essence of all entities. Because it seizes (*gṛhṇāti*) that [essence], it is called *lātā*; thus, the body is considered a *maṇḍala*.
The mandala is indeed considered to be the wheel of the thirty-seven great channels (*mahānādī*).
The great jewel of bodhicitta is the mandala; it is the mandala of reality (*tattvamandala*).
From this mandala arises the manifestation of the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
Thus, this innate nature (*sahajarūpa*) of the Victors consists of the mandala and so forth; [this is] the mandala-circle (*maṇḍalacakra*). (Ti., p. 68)
The mandala circle of the Blessed One Kālacakra consists of deities and goddesses fashioned from the five jewels; it is square, measuring four hundred cubits in extent.
On the outside is the Body Mandala (kāyamaṇḍala), which is square, with four gates, four archways, adorned by the eight cremation grounds, and surrounded by five walls.
...In the center, measuring half the size of the Body Mandala, is the Speech Mandala (vāṅmaṇḍala), which is square, with four gates, adorned by four archways, and surrounded by five walls.
The mind-maṇḍala is half the size of the speech-maṇḍala; it is square, with four doors, adorned with four archways, and encircled by three walls.
Half of that is the wisdom-wheel, beautified by sixteen pillars. Half of that again is the eight-petalled lotus.
The pericarp is one-third of a lotus.

In this manner, the maṇḍalas of body, speech, and mind are complete with all characteristics, adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, provided with jeweled friezes, altars, and *vakulī* railings, and resplendent with mirrors, crescent moons, and bells.
The resident of the maṇḍala is the supreme, all-Tathāgata gnosis that removes all defects;
she is known as the resident of the maṇḍala, intent upon the purification of all things. (Jñānasiddhi 15.12)
Fish after fish are edible foods. (Guṇasāgarapraśna, p. 191) Intoxication.
*Madana* means wine (*madya*). (He. Ta. 2.3.56) *Madhyā* refers to the midday hour (*madhyāhna*) or the fire (*śikhin*). (Sā. Mā., p. 69)
Likewise, because it serves as protection for the mind, *mantra* is also said to be the knowledge of the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*).
And in the *Mūlatantra*:
Since it is the life-force of the elements of body, speech, and mind,
the meaning of "mantra" by the word *mantra* is the imperishable gnosis of emptiness.
The mantra consists of merit and gnosis, and has the nature of emptiness and compassion. (Se. Ṭī., p.
69) It is called a mantra because it protects through reflection;
it is the bodhicitta whose intrinsic nature is the non-duality of emptiness and compassion. (He. Ta. Ṭī., p. 9a)
It is called *mantra* because it is the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and because it protects those born [into cyclic existence].
Ultimate bodhicitta is *mantra*.
Because it is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of mantra. (He. Ta.
Ṭī., p. 11a) It is said that "nāda is mantra" (Va. Ti., p. 68).
This very vital air (*prāṇavāyu*), which was previously mentioned as being articulated from the region of the navel, [is that nāda].

That very [reality] is called "mantra" because it is the cause of all mantras. Whatever flow of speech is produced by living beings, all that is indeed of the nature of mantra; for from that alone is it born. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 68)
"Sound (*nāda*) is indeed said to be mantra... mantra is the supreme Lord of the classes (*vargeśvara*)" (Vajravatī, p. 75).

"Whether it be the sound of great bliss or another [sound], uttered from the region of the navel, that very sound is mantra, because it protects the mind through its secret speech" (Vajravatī-ṭīkā, p. 75).
The intrinsic nature of the class of mantras is the single, supreme syllable;
by the mere thorough knowledge of that, mantras become performers of ritual actions.
For this very reason, we do not accept that mantras consist of the nature of phonemes;
for they are not capable of being the cause for even bending a blade of grass. (Vajrayoginī-tantra-ṭīkā, p.
72) That which women utter at the time when passion arises—
"This *nāda*, whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest, is traditionally known as *mantra*. (*Vijñānabhairava-ṭīkā*, p. 76).
"The recitation of *mantra* (*mantrajāpa*) is indeed the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*). (*Svacchanda-tantra-ṭīkā*, p. 43).
The Mantra system (*mantranaya*)— referred to as "the Mantra system"— is fivefold, distinguished by the divisions of Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, Yogottara, and Yoganiruttara.
That which is whispered and spoken by gurus is called *mantra*.
It is called *naya* because it leads to or brings about that practice which has that [mantra] as its object; thus, it is sevenfold. Namely:

"The mandala, the gaṇa, the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), the offering (*bali*), the sequence of the assembly (*melāpaka*), the reality (*tattva*), and the sevenfold exposition—this is called the *mantranaya*. (Guhyasiddhiprakaraṇa, p. 90)
The discourse on mantra is fourfold— the discourse on mantra being as follows: namely, the designation of mantra, the meaning of mantra, [the syllables of mantra, and the application of mantra].
The interlacing of mantras (*mantravidarbhaṇa*) and the adamantine speech devoid of vowels (*vajravāk svaravarjitā*); this is death. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 90)
Death is liberation, because it is precisely therein that the mind, mental factors, and the characteristics of ignorance set;
that itself is death. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 21a)
"Maru is the big toe; it is called Maru. (Vajratilaka, p. 35).
"Because of the roaring (*ravaṇa*)—that is, the sounding—of *mas*, which is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), [it is] Maru in the big toe of the foot. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 35).
"That which, though parched in the desert, bears [the weight of] exhaustion, is the Cakravartinī" (Vajratilaka, p.
47). "Malayaja is considered to be the meeting with the one born of the Malaya [mountain]" (Hevajra Tantra 2.3.56).
The land of Malaya is the head; indeed, the land of Malaya is [the head]. (Vajratilaka, p.

31). In that context, "Malaya" refers to that wherein the bodhicitta—in which the conventional and the ultimate are non-different, and whose intrinsic nature is great bliss—is dissolved (*līyate*); thus it is Malaya.
The land that has become such is the Malaya country, which is the head, because he exists precisely there. (Vajrayoginī-ṭīkā, p. 31) Mahākaṅkāla.
Mahākālakāla is so called because he "drives away" (kālayati) the great "Ka," which is the sentient being (sattva) situated in the crest-lock (śikhā). (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
48) Mahācitta is the mind whose nature is great bliss; it is the "great mind. (Hevajra-tantra-ṭīkā, fol. 49a)

"Mahādivya" refers to that moment of possession (*āveśakṣaṇa*) in which the great, supramundane, and divine beings, such as Vajrasattva and others, having entered, abide; that is "mahādivya. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 171).
It is "great" (*mahān*).
And she who is the creator of the most wonderful is called "the Great One" (*mahān*).
She whose nose is great— that is, whose nostrils are large in the secret place, the heart, and the mouth— is *Mahānāsā*.
(Va. ti. ṭī., p. 47) He is Mahānāsa because he possesses the miraculous power of the mind. (Va. ti., p. 53) He is Mahābala;
he is called Mahābala because he carries the phlegm (*śleṣman*) which is capable of sustaining the secret body. (Va. ti. ṭī., p. 49)
Mahābalā means she whose power (*bala*) in going and coming is great; she is Mahābalā. (Vajrāvalī-nibandha-ṭīkā, p.
48) Right view is Mahābalā. (Vajrāvalī, p. 56)
Mahābhairavā is the third *ūlī*; she is Mahābhairavā because of the piercing of the knots (*granthibheda*). (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p.
47) Mahābhairavī is the power of faith (*śraddhābala*). (Vajravārāhī-tantra, p. 55)
Mahāmudrā is both great and a seal; thus it is Mahāmudrā.

Mahāmudrā is devoid of intrinsic nature, free from the obscurations of the exhaustion of primordial wisdom and so forth, resembling the stainless autumn sky at midday, the foundation of all prosperity, whose single nature is both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa, and whose body is non-referential compassion.
She whose sole nature is great bliss...

through that Mahāmudrā, whose nature is inconceivable, the fruit called Samayamudrā arises. (Abhayapaddhati-vṛtti on the *Āryāvalokiteśvara-sādhana*, pp. 34–35) It is Mahāmudrā because it is both great (*mahatī*) and a seal (*mudrā*).
Furthermore, its greatness consists in being endowed with the excellence of all aspects, rather than being merely partial.
...The Great Seal (mahāmudrā), however, is the fruit-seal (phalamudrā).
...And its greatness is due to the greatness of abandonment and the greatness of realization.

In this context, the greatness of abandonment (*prahāṇamahattva*) is characterized by the direct realization of the luminosity known as the *svābhāvika-kāya*, which has the characteristic of abandoning all obscurations in every respect.

The greatness of realization (*adhigamamahattva*), however, has as its nature the direct realization of the body known as the "yoked pair" (*yuganaddha*), which consists of all the perfectly pure Buddhas. (Se. Ṭī., pp.

56–57) Furthermore, the cultivation of the unchanging syllable (*niṣpandākṣara*) by means of Mahāmudrā is the means for accomplishing supramundane siddhi, which is characterized by omniscience (*sarvajñatva*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 62)
...the Mahāmudrā is situated in the circle of the navel.
"That which has the nature of the primordial vowel (*ādi-svara*) is designated by the Buddhas as *dhī* (wisdom);
that very same [wisdom] is the Blessed Lady Prajñā through the yoga of the *utpanna-krama* (the stage of completion). This is called *Mahāmudrā*, the supreme *mudrā*. (Hevajra Tantra 2.4.40–41)
"Internal" means up to that point.
(HeTaṬī, p. 57a) In the context of the *utpannakrama*, that very *mudrā* is the *sahaja*. (HeTaṬī, p.

57a) It is called *mahāmudrā* because it flows toward—that is, attains—great joy (*mudaṃ*) and rapture (*harṣaṃ*), being worthy of worship in the realms of *bhūr*, *bhuvar*, and *svar*. (GuSaPra, p. 96)
The Mahāyāna is that by which many great beings go to Buddhahood; it is the Mahāyāna path. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 73) The Mahāyāna path.
The Mahāyāna path, O Mañjuśrī, is the initiation of the vase, the secret, the wisdom, and the gnosis through the Vajra family. (Vi.pra., p. 22).
The Great Hero:
because he causes even the great wind (*mahaṭa*)—which is terrifying—to circulate within the lungs of the vajras at the navel, he is the Great Hero. (Va.ti.ṭī., p. 49).
"Mahāvīryā" means she whose great vigor (*mahadvīrya*) is aroused; thus she is Mahāvīryā. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 48) Right speech is Mahāvīryā. (Vajratilaka, p. 56)
The Mahāsattva is said to be "great being" because he is filled with the essence of great gnosis; [this is] great bliss (*mahāsukha*). (Hevajratantra 1.1.5)
Because its nature is infinite bliss, it is designated as "Glorious Great Bliss" (*śrīmahāsukha*).

The abode of great bliss (*mahāsukhāvāsa*) is the *dharmadhātu*, characterized by space, unmixed, the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), transcending worldly analogies, and all-pervadingly auspicious (*samantabhadra*). (Viṣamapada, p. 16) (Pradīpodyotana-vṛtti on the *Sekoddeśa*, 1.27)
The "mothers" (mātaraḥ) referred to as "the mothers" are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
or alternatively, the five sense-faculties are designated by such terms as "mother" and so forth.
One should satisfy them with the five qualities of sensual desire, namely sound, form, taste, and so forth.
This indeed is the unsurpassed worship. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, 67a) O Mother!

Above, because it carries the lungs like a mother (*mātṛ*), and because it generates longing for the mother and gives birth to the world at the navel, [it is called] *mātṛgṛha* (the mother’s house). (Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p. 45)

Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Rudrāṇī, Indrāṇī, Kauberī, Vārāhī, and Cāmuṇḍā are the seven Mothers of the World. Their abodes are in cremation grounds, empty houses, crossroads, solitary lingas, and solitary trees. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpa, p. 157).
This is the mental door.
The third door is mental, distinguished by the moon and the sun;
through entering and exiting, this indeed becomes the supreme door.
The primary and supreme gateway is proclaimed to be both below and above;
through the lower gateway comes discernment, and through the upper gateway, the elements.
The Buddhas, Vairocana and the others, abide in motion at the upper gate; their stationing is below, while their dismissal is by way of the upper [gate]. (Vajrāvalī, pp. 22–23).
Māmakī.
The gnosis of all Tathāgatas is considered by me to be my own; because they are mutually pervasive, she is therefore called Māmakī. (Jñānasiddhi 15.11) Māra.
Māra is the mind of sentient beings in saṃsāra, the impurity of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*); ... Māra is the defiled mind. (Vimalaprabhā, p. 23).
The Path.
In this context, there are indeed three paths: the path of light (*jyotirmārga*), the path of smoke (*dhūmamārga*), and the mixed path (*vimiśramārga*).
Among these, the path of light is the sun; the path of smoke is the moon;
and the mixed path has the nature of both day and night. (Viṣṇupurāṇa, p. 224)
The path is the recourse;
it is the path spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One. And that alone, and nothing else, is to be resorted to by me. (Sā. Mā., p. 56)
"Having resorted to the perfectly pure Jaina path, which is priceless even among those [paths] beginning with Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra... (*Sāṃkhyamīmāṃsā*, p.
117). "The path taught by the Tathāgata is such that it alone is to be followed by me, and no other" (*Sāṃkhyamīmāṃsā*, p. 202).
I take recourse in this path to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, namely, the Vajrayāna. (Sādhanamālā, p.
225) Mālatī-wood is the fuel; the seasoning is mālatī-wood. (Hevajratantra 2.3.58)
The *mālava* is the root of the upper arms (*bāhumūla*). (Vātulanātha-tantra, p.
32). That which is this pair of roots at the interior of the two arms;

The two aggregates (*skandha*) therein are *mālava*. It is called *mālava* because of the cutting (*lavana*), that is, the severing, of the "garlands" (*mālā*) of heterogeneous conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, p.
32). In *mālava*, however, the Mistress of the Jinas (*jineśvarī*) resides in the heart like the shade of a tree. (Vajrāvalī, p. 43).
The Māhendra-maṇḍala is the Māhendra-maṇḍala situated in the secret lotus.
At its rising, a yellow-colored ray issues forth and remains for half a watch (yāma).
Then one should perform the rite for prosperity. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana,
143) Furthermore, what is the nature of "joyful joy"?
It is the state of a joyful mind regarding the good conduct of sentient beings abiding in the three realms, as well as their enjoyments, sovereignty, and so forth. (Sā. Mā., p.

57) It is the [joy] characterized by a specific delight of the mind, which is "the joy of sympathetic gladness" (saṃmodikā). (Sā. Mā., p. 97) Likewise, it is "the intense joy" (pramuditā), which is the constant desire to endow them with virtuous qualities. (Sā. Mā., p. 100)
What is sympathetic joy (*muditā*)? It is a state of mental gladness regarding the roots of virtue produced by others, their enjoyments, sovereignty, and so forth. (*Sāratama*, p.

115) Sympathetic joy is the exultation arising from seeing the means for the successful accomplishment of one's resolve. (*Sāratama*, p. 138) Sympathetic joy is of the nature of intense delight. (*Sāratama*, pp. 172–173)

Sympathetic joy (*muditā*), however, is such delight; or rather, it is the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) that "I must establish all beings wandering in saṃsāra in Buddhahood, which is peerless, as well as in its means";
or else, it is the state of having one’s mind drawn toward whatever virtues belong to all [beings], as well as toward their enjoyments, sovereignty, and so forth. (Sā. Mā., p. 203)
Sympathetic joy (*muditā*) has the aspect of the certainty of never being separated from divine bliss; (Sā. Mā., p.
225) it has the aspect of "may sentient beings rejoice"; (Sā. Mā., p.
315) and it is the satisfaction in the happiness of others; (Sā. Mā., p. 385)
Muditā has the aspect of the certainty of the uninterrupted flow of divine bliss. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
13b) It is a mallet, because knowledge is not known by those submerged in the waters of saṃsāra.
For beings who follow the Buddhas, [the practice] involving striking is known as *mudgara*.
A *mudrā* is so called because it bestows joy (*muda*), that is, a particular kind of bliss and delight.

She is called *mudrā* because she constantly assumes joy (*muda*), characterized by the gnosis of supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha-jñāna*), through the yoga of immovability from her primordial state. (Se. Ṭī., p.
56) The crown, earrings, necklace, bracelets, and girdle—these five are proclaimed as the *prajñā-mudrās* due to their purity as the five Buddhas. (He. Ta. 1.3.14; 8.17)
The *mudrā* is said to be the five families for the sake of liberation;
it is called *mudrā* because one is sealed (*mudryate*) by means of this *vajra*. (HeTa 1.4.4) The *vajra* is indestructible gnosis (*jñāna*).
Because by this [seal] one is sealed (*mudryate*), it produces joy (*muda*), delight, and great bliss (*mahāsukha*);
for that reason, it is called a "seal" (*mudrā*). (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 18b) In the *vajra* there is the *ḍombī* seal, and likewise in the *padma* there is the *nartī*.
A washerwoman was declared [as the mother] for the act, and likewise a Brāhmaṇī for the Tathāgata.
In the *Ratna* [tantra], Caṇḍālinī is to be known; these are determined as the five mudrās.
(HeTa 1.4.6–7) Clapping the hands is a mudrā, as is the snapping of the fingers.
(HeTa 1.5.20) There are three kinds of mudrās: the Dharma-mudrā, the Cihna-mudrā, and the Mahāmudrā.
The syllables such as *hūṃ* are the dharma-mudrā;
the [hand] symbols such as the vajra are the cihna-mudrā; and the mandala of deities such as Akṣobhya is the mahāmudrā. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 42)
The *mudrā-samaya* is so called to declare that you are of the very nature of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). (*Abhidhānavyutpatti*, p. 38).
Urine.
Urine is the condiment. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, 191) Those who delight in false speech [regard] both the internal and the external as the locus of arising from conditions.
"They would be devoted to falsehood and engaged in an improper state of abiding" (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p.
47). "Meru is the skeletal frame of the body from the waist up to the shoulders; this is the rule" (Vimalaprabhā, p. 176). Mount Meru.
The most excellent mountain is Meru, which has the form of a skeleton.
And likewise, in the *Sampuṭa*:
"The Bhairava wind, shaped like a bow, resides at the soles of the feet."
It is situated at the region of the hips, and likewise, it is the extractor of the triangle.
Varuṇa, whose form is circular, resides in the three-petaled [lotus];
and the earth, which is square on all sides, is located in the heart.
For Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is like a skeleton staff; thus [it is said]. (Do. Ko. Vyā., p.

156) In this context, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is defined as an affection for all sentient beings that is characterized by a singular love for one's own son, exceeding [all other] benefit. (Sā. Mā., p. 57)

Friendship toward beings, characterized by equanimity and joy arising from regarding them as one's own only son; (Sūtrasamuccaya, p. 57); friendliness toward people, multiplied a thousandfold by the affection felt for a virtuous son; (Sūtrasamuccaya, p. 100); what is friendliness? It is the love for all sentient beings as if they were one's only son. (Sūtrasamuccaya, p. 115)
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is characterized by the affection one feels for an only son toward the entire world. (Sūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya, p.
138) "Loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, characterized by the affection one feels for an only son... (Sūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya, p. 172).
In this regard, what is this loving-kindness?
It is characterized by the love for all sentient beings as if they were one's only son, or else it takes the form of bringing about their welfare and happiness (*Sūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya*, pp.
202–203). [It is] loving-kindness toward all sentient beings that takes the form of bringing about their happiness (*Sūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya*, p. 225).
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the desire for others to possess happiness (*parasaukhyasampadicchā*). (Sā. mā., p.

315) Loving-kindness is the thought of the welfare of others (*parahitacintā*). (Sā. mā., p. 385) Loving-kindness is the mental aspect that brings about unsurpassed happiness for all sentient beings. (He. ta. ṭī., fol. 13a)
Delight in delusion (*moharati*): delusion is Vairocana; delight in him is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Delight in the purification of delusion is "delight in delusion" (*mohaviśuddhe ratiḥ moharatiḥ*).
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p.
25) Yakṣiṇīs are those who consume meat, liquor, blood, and so forth; yakṣiṇīs are devoted to sexual union. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 205) 3.
Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī is the abandonment of unwholesome states that have arisen; [she is] Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, [also known as] Yamadāḍhī. (Vajratārāsādhana, p. 57)
The production of unarisen wholesome states is Yamadāḍhī;
the protection of arisen wholesome states is Yamadūtī. (Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī, p. 57)
Yamamathanī is the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states; [thus] Yamamathanī is Yamāntaka. (Vajrāvalī, p. 57) Yamāntaka.

"Because he is liberated from the fear of death and so forth, he is the supreme one of all Tathāgatas; because his knowledge of subduing is preeminent, he is therefore known as Yamāntaka. (Jñānasiddhi 15.15).
[He is] the Maker of the End of Yama.
Yama is hell; because the Blessed One brings it to an end and destroys it through the samādhi of great wrath, he is Yamāntakṛt—this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Yama is the darkness of delusion, which is ignorance;
because he brings it to an end and destroys it by means of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), he is Yamāntakṛt—this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpa-ṭīkā, p.
26) 3. The request: "May the Blessed Tathāgatas teach the unsurpassed Dharma."
"May the Blessed Tathāgatas teach such unsurpassed instruction of the Dharma by which sentient beings may swiftly cross the bottomless ocean of saṃsāra" (Sā.

Mā., p. 56). "May the Blessed Tathāgatas teach such unsurpassed instruction of the Dharma by which transmigrating sentient beings are instantly liberated from the bonds of existence" (Sā. Mā., p. 202).
The single, natural body (*svābhāvikakāya*) is the union (*yuganaddha*), the non-duality of emptiness and compassion;
it is known as "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) and in some places as "union" (*yuganaddha*). (Sā. Mā., p. 505)

The body of union (*yuganaddhakāya*) is indeed the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), consisting of the ultimate truth (*parārthasatya*): the assembly of deities such as Vairocana—who are the forms of the supreme, pure radiance and the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*)—and the maṇḍala of the supporting palace and so forth.
That very [reality] is proclaimed in all the kings of tantras as the supramundane maṇḍala.
Because it is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all the qualities of a Buddha, this very state—whose nature consists in the two truths being in union—is called "the union" (*yuganaddha*).

Therefore, the body of union (*yuganaddhakāya*) alone is the *dharmakāya*, which is distinct from both the *sāmbhogika* and *svābhāvika* [bodies], and is to be personally realized by the yogi. (Se. Ṭī., 57) Yoga.
Yoga is meditative absorption (*samādhi*). (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
43a) The deity-yoga is the mind in the form of the deity, beginning with the going for the three refuges. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
44a) The innate yoga (*sahajayoga*) is the state of one-pointedness of mind. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 44a)
Yoga should be known as threefold: the foundational, the imagined, and the perfected; this yoga of the mental image has been described by the Buddhas.
The union with the ego-sense of the mere substratum is called the "substratum";
however, the purification of the bodhicitta is the great arising of the seed-mantra.
But the form accomplished through the sequence, which is fashioned by the assembly of mudrās, is called "imagined" (kalpita);
thus, the yoga is said to be "imagined."

"Endowed with the excellence of all aspects, performing emanation and reabsorption, the yoga that is instantaneously perfected through gnosis is called 'perfected' (*niṣpanna*). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p.
119). Furthermore, the word "yoga" does not denote the meaning of "means" (*upāya*) nor the meaning of "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
The word "yoga" denotes the meaning of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*):
"Yoga would not exist through the body of means alone, nor through wisdom alone;
the union of wisdom and means is called 'yoga' by the Tathāgatas. (Viṃśatividha-vajrayoginī-sādhana, p. 18).
Yoga is the state of purity, the pure mind, which is inseparable from emptiness and compassion (*Vi.pra.*, p.
222). Yoga is the mutual union of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths (*Vi.pra.*, p. 229).
Yoga is the unification of inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*), which is retention (*kumbhaka*) (*Vi.pra.*, p. 230).

The yoga (consisting of six limbs) and the six-limbed yoga have been taught by the Blessed One in the *Samājottara* as the means for achieving the supreme accomplishment characterized by perfect enlightenment, through [the methods of] brief statement (*uddeśa*), detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*), and further exposition (*pratinirdeśa*), as follows...
"Pratyāhāra, as well as dhyāna, prāṇāyāma, dhāraṇā, anusmṛti, and samādhi—this is called the six-limbed yoga. (Se. Ṭī., p. 30).
A brief explanation of these verses is now stated. (Se. Ṭī., pp. 31–34).
However, the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) has been stated very clearly by the venerable Mañjuśrī in the *Kālacakrottaratantra*: "... [as follows]. (Se. Ṭī., p.
34) It is also mentioned in the *Śrīkālacakra* and explained in detail in the *Vimalaprabhā*. (Se. Ṭī., pp.
35–36) In both the Mantra Vehicle and the Pāramitā Vehicle, there is a twofold practice of yoga.

...In the *Samāja* and other [tantras], it was taught by the Blessed One through the yoga of night; in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, it was taught through the yoga of day and by means of intentional terminology (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*). (Se. Ṭī., p.
37) The six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) was also taught by the venerable Vajrapāṇi. (Se. Ṭī., p. 38)
Furthermore, the instruction on the initial cultivation (*ādibhāvanā*) of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is stated in other tantras;
here, in the *Śrīsamājottara*, it is [described] as service (*sevā*), near-accomplishment (*upasādhana*), accomplishment (*sādhana*), and great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*). (Se. Ṭī., pp. 39–45).
Now, Haṭhayoga is discussed... the practice of sound (*nādābhyāsa*) is mentioned right here. (Se. Ṭī., p. 45).
The four limbs of yoga constitute *sevā* (service);

it is called *sevā* because it is served—that is, practiced—by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). From the stage of smoke up to the vision of the *bimba*, there are the limbs of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditation (*dhyāna*).
Indeed, that supreme service must be performed by means of the nectar of knowledge alone, through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) itself. (Sevārthabodhinī-ṭīkā, p.
31) The cultivation of signs such as smoke and so forth is "service" (*sevā*). (Sevārthabodhinī-ṭīkā, p.
36) At the time of service, one should diligently visualize the form of Mahoṣṇīṣa.
But at the time of the secondary practice (upasādhana), one should [visualize] the image as Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
One intent on yoga should meditate upon the form of the deity during the *sādhana*;
however, at the time of the *mahāsādhana*, one should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord Buddha as the image.
Here, in another *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language), it refers to the image of the *uṣṇīṣa*—the image of the Buddha that is the entirety of the three realms.

Having established the mind-vajra in the space of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), one should meditate upon it during the stage of service (*sevā*)—that is, at the first stage—by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), and stabilize it by means of the limb of meditation (*dhyāna*).
Thus, the limb of service is said to consist of withdrawal and meditation. (Se. Ṭī., p.
39) [This is] the near-attainment (*upasādhana*).
By the designation of the *amṛtakuṇḍalī* image, according to the terminology of the *sandhyābhāṣā*, the vital wind (*vāyu*) is expressed.
...In this way, the breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained in the form of a mass (*piṇḍa*) at the location of the *bindu*.
By that very means, its retention (*dhāraṇā*) is described.
Thus, the *upasādhana* [accomplishment] is performed by means of the two limbs, namely the form of the *Amṛtakuṇḍalī*.
That very *upasādhana* is called the "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajāpa*). It is also called the *upasādhana* of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*). (Se. Ṭī., pp. 41–42)
Regarding the statement "the means of accomplishment is the image of the deity within the accomplishment":

here, by the power of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), the yogi perceives the Caṇḍālī blazing at the navel— free from all obscurations, resembling a *pratisenā* [magical reflection], and emitting clouds of infinite rays of light from the Buddhas, which is the Mahāmudrā.

He describes that recollection (*anusmṛti*), which is resplendent with a halo of light, as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*); [this is] the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 42)
At the conclusion of *dhāraṇā*, the yogin should meditate upon the *caṇḍālī*; this is the rule.
Then, by the flame of her gnosis (*jñānārcis*), the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and so forth, are incinerated and become unified as a single mass.
The consciousnesses and the elements, such as earth and the rest, which reside in the left and right channels and possess the nature of the mandalas, enter the lunar mandala at the forehead.

Then, when the moon has been melted by the flame of gnosis (*jñānārcis*) of the Caṇḍālī, that bodhicitta which has descended in the form of a drop (*bindu*) through the nature of joy (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), and cessation (*viramānanda*) at the throat, heart, navel, and secret lotus,

and subsequently reaches the vajra-jewel with the nature of innate joy (*sahajānanda*)— or alternatively, with the nature of the distinct characteristics of the stages of variety (*vicitra*), maturation (*vipāka*), dissolution (*vimarda*), and the signless (*vilakṣaṇa*)— when it bestows bliss within the jewel, being full of the sixteen digits (*kalā*) by the power of meditation; [that is the state].
The phrase "resembling *surata*" is merely an illustration;
in its essential nature, the pleasure born of the two organs does not equal even a thousandth-millionth part of the supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*).
Here, that state of imperishable bliss which consists of innate joy (*sahajānanda*) is an indescribable state for novice yogins;
it is called the "samādhi of emptiness" by the Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, it does not follow the meaning of nihilism merely according to worldly convention.
In this way, through the yoga of six limbs, Buddhahood is accomplished for yogins. (Sevārthasamgraha-ṭīkā, p. 42). Yoga Tantra.
In this context, one who possesses yoga (yoga) is a yogī; likewise, one who possesses it is a yoginī.
Therefore, there exists the Yoga Tantra and the Yoginī Tantra.
...Therefore, the *yogatantra* is a tantra whose nature consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). (Vi.pra., p.
18) The four seats of yoga (*yogapīṭha*)—known as the seats of self, other, mantra, and reality—are, respectively, the navel, heart, throat, and head. (Va.ti.ṭī., p. 6)
The practice of yoga is threefold— the practice of yoga being: the intellectual (bauddha), the demonic (āsura), and the material (bhautika).
In that regard, the Buddhist yoga consists of emptiness and compassion;
the demonic yoga is characterized by conceptual construction;
and the materialistic yoga is of two kinds: eternalist and nihilist.
Among them, the arising of knowledge for Buddhist yogins occurs during the day;
for Asura yogins, it occurs during the night;
and for Buddhist yogins, the arising of knowledge occurs at a time devoid of the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*). (Vi.pra., p. 222) [Thus speaks] the yogin.

Yoga is the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) that has reached the ultimate limit of excellence; those who possess this yoga are *yogins*, having attained the state of the Great Vajradhara. (Se. Ṭī., p.
60) Yoga is the mutual union of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths.
He who possesses that [yoga] is a yogin. (Vi.pra., p. 229) *Rajas* refers to black dust, namely the charcoal from a cremation ground.
The white powder is made from powdered human bone;
the yellow powder from yellow orpiment;
the red powder from bricks from cremation grounds.
With yellow pigment, powdered human bone, and *cauryapatra* [a type of leaf],
she is proclaimed as a washerwoman, a washerwoman, a daughter, and a dancer. (Hevajra Tantra 1.2.20)

Because she delights all sentient beings, she is likewise known as the "Dyer" (*rajakī*). (HeTa 1.5.17) She is the Dyer because she delights [beings] with unsurpassed bliss. (HeTa Ṭīkā, p. 20a) [The dust-mandala]
The dust-mandala is to be known as the body of the Blessed One (*se.

ṭī.*, p. 17). It is called a "jewel" (*ratna*) because it extends (*tanoti*) delight (*rati*), which is infinite bliss; thus, the fourth joy (*caturthānanda*) is to be understood as the jewel (*ca. ko. vyā.*, p. 133).

But the jewel is even more difficult to obtain. (Jñānasiddhi 15.24) The "jewel" is the supreme, untainted great bliss that persists throughout cyclic existence. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 78) The bearer of the jewel.
He is "Ratnadhṛk" because he holds the jewel that fulfills all hopes; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
He is "Ratnadhṛk" because he holds the jewel of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 24)
Ratnavajra is so called because of the emergence of yellow-colored pus from the secret place; [this is] Ratnasambhava. (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, p. 49)

"Since the jewels, beginning with the Buddha, certainly arise from it, and since knowledge associated with the welfare of sentient beings arises therefrom, it is called Ratnasaṃbhava. (Jñānasiddhi 15.7).
Ratnasaṃbhava is the jewel of existence. (Sādhanasamuccaya 2.7).
Ratnasambhava is the jewel of all the Tathāgatas; it is the conventional bodhicitta,
and because he arises from that, he is called Ratnasambhava— this is the interpretable meaning (neyārtha).
The jewel of all the Tathāgatas is the ultimate bodhicitta;
because he arises from that, he is Ratnasambhava—this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 24)

The path of space is the gnosis of equality; that which proceeds from, is produced from, and arises from that is the one who dwells on the path of space, Ratnasambhava. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana, p. 51).
Because the two jewels—the Enjoyment Body and the Emanation Body—arise from this, he is called Ratnasambhava. (Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p. 85).
Ratneśa is Ratneśa because he is the locus of all the jewels of the Buddhas. (He. Ta. Ṭī., p. 19b) Rasanā.
In the right nostril, the *rasanā* channel is situated by way of the nature of the sun of skillful means (*upāya*).
And so it is said in the *Hevajra*: “The *rasanā* is established as skillful means” (*Hevajra Tantra*, commentary on verse 2.4.40, p. 151). This is passion (*rāga*).

Because one takes delight in all sentient beings by preventing the entire flood of suffering from arising from its causes, compassion is therefore proclaimed as "attachment" (*rāga*). (PVSV 1.15) This is the joy of attachment (*rāgarati*).
"Passion is Amitābha; delight in that is 'delight in passion'—this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Delight in the purification of passion is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)" (Guhyasamāja-pañjikā, p. 25).
Attachment and detachment: attachment is the white side of the bodhicitta, and detachment is the black side. (Se. Ṭī., p. 26) The King.
A *rājā* is so called because he shines (*rājate*) and gleams like vermilion powder (*cīnapiṣṭa*) through conjunction with the sun. (Va. Ti. Ṭī., p. 82).
Rāmeśvara is likewise renowned as being located between the eyebrows. (Va. Ti., p. 32).
The two *rāme*s are the eyebrows, which possess the nature of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of a beautiful woman (*lalanā*).
Between those two is that which has sovereignty (*īśvaratva*) as its flame of knowledge; that is the space between the eyebrows, the sheath of the *ūrṇā* hair.
As for the channel well-known as *kharvarī* in Rāmeśvara, it is that very one. (Vajratārā-ṭīkā, p. 32)
For the arrangement of the garland of bones remains established by virtue of its solid nature. (Vajravārāhī-tantra, p.
42–43) It is "possessing form" (*rūpiṇī*) because it gives form to and purifies wind and space. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 41)
The application of mindfulness to the mind is Laṅkeśvarī, who possesses form; Laṅkā is the city of the body. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 51)
In that [context], Īśvarī is the mistress, the sovereign, the Mistress of Laṅkā. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
47) Smṛtīndriyā is Laṅkeśvarī. (Vajratilaka, p. 54) Lampāka.
"Lampāka" refers to the middle of the throat. (Vajratilaka, p. 33).
The tongue (*rasanā*) is "Lambikā," being greedy for the tasting of the nectar of the lower [cavity]; due to its connection with that, the throat is "Lampāka. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 33).
Subhadrā is indeed proclaimed to reside in the abdomen in Lampāka (Vajratilaka, p. 45). Lalanā resides in the left nostril; Lalanā exists by way of the nature of the moon of wisdom.

And likewise in the *Hevajra*: “Lalanā is by nature Prajñā” (*Dohakośavyākhyā*, p. 151). Lāmā is so called because she shines (*lasana*) in the space of the water element (*abdhātu*). (*Vimalaprabhā-ṭīkā*, p. 41). Lāmā is the application of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanānusmṛtyupasthāna*). (*Vimalaprabhā*, p. 51).
The characteristic, the characteristic—this is conventional truth; [it is] supramundane truth. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 67)

Supramundane truth is the accomplishment of the Mahāmudrā-siddhi through the signless non-conceptual mind by means of smoke and other signs, according to the stage of generation (*utpannakrama*). (Vi.pra., p.
20) Locanā is form—subtle and gross—which is permeated by the three times.
Because she is seen abiding in all fields, she is called Locanā. (Jñānasiddhi 15.10) Regarding the mundane and supramundane consecrations: first, the mundane ones consist of water, and so forth.
The crown, the ribbon, and the vajra-bell.
The Great Vow,
by name,
the authorization.

The vase, the secret, and the wisdom-knowledge— these are the ten initiations for those born from a womb according to worldly convention, [performed] because of the impurity of body, speech, mind, the elements, the aggregates, the sense bases, and the action faculties.

The eleventh is supramundane, and the fourth is likewise; by this rule, it is characterized by the gnosis of the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*) Mahāmudrā. It is the "mouth of the Guru" (*guruvaktra*), which purifies through the removal of obstructions of body, speech, and so forth.
(Vi.pra., p. 21) The mundane initiations are seven: water, crown, ribbon, vajra-bell, great vow, name, and authorization.
Likewise, the higher [initiations]—the Vase, the Secret, and the Wisdom-Knowledge—are the eleventh and the fourth, which is the supramundane initiation. (Vi.pra., p. 51) This is mundane truth.

The cultivation of conceptualizations of the mandala circle is mundane truth; it is the means for achieving mundane siddhis through the generation stage (*utpattikrama*). As for the *vajra*, just as with Akṣobhya-mudrā, the primary [knowledge] is the principal [wisdom], while the other is secondary. (Vimalaprabhā, p. 20)
Likewise, by means of the Vajrasattva-mudrā, consciousness (*vijñāna*) would also be the back [of the hand], while the primary [hand] would be the *vajra*.
And it is said in the *Vajraśekhara*:
"It is firm, essential, indestructible, and characterized by being uncuttable and impenetrable."
"Neither burning nor subject to destruction, it is called the emptiness-vajra. (Abhidhānavajrasamuccaya, p. 23, 37).
"By a measurement of twelve finger-breadths, the vajra [is established] through the purification of the twelvefold dependent origination...
'The vajra is indivisible,' so it is said in the Hevajra[tantra]. (Abhayapaddhati-saṃgraha, p. 37).
The "supreme primordial" vajra:
it is supreme because of its excellence,
and primordial because it is the primary cause of bliss.
That very vessel, because it is the support of bliss, is designated as the lotus of knowledge (*vidyāpaṅkaja*).
When the *bodhicitta* has entered the *avadhūtī*, it is then designated as the *vajra*. (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p. 7)
Bodhicitta is the vajra; (Jñānasiddhi 15.24) bodhicitta is the vajra;
they say that the syllable *vaṃ* is the vajra.
(From the *Abhayapaddhati-vivaraṇa-siddhi*, p.

218) The semen (*śukra*) of these [energies] is the thunderbolt (*vajra*). (From the *Hevajra-tantra* 2.3.63) The thunderbolt is indestructible gnosis (*jñāna*). (From the *Hevajra-tantra-ṭīkā*, fol. 18b)

The vajra-bell (*vajraghaṇṭā*)—which, according to the previous intention, measures twelve finger-breadths and possesses a downward-facing lotus and vajra—is intended to demonstrate that the nature of all phenomena is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). To awaken [the practitioner] to the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) as the expression of indivisible gnosis, it is adorned with two rows of vajras, one above and one below. (Abhidhānavatārasaṃgraha, p. 37)
The first [stage] is the fourfold vajra; the second is the awakening to emptiness;
the third is the accomplishment of the image; and the fourth is the placement of the syllables.
By these four vajras, service (*sevā*) has its general characteristic.
(Guhyasamāja-tantra 18.133; Seva-ṭīkā, p. 29) Vajrajaṭila.
Because the bile constituent (*pittadhātu*) is generated from the two breasts of the one whose form is Vajrajaṭila, he is called Vajrajaṭila. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
49) Vajrajāpa is breath control (*prāṇāyāma*); thus, it should be recited as "Vajrajāpa" because it is an inseparable limb of wisdom (*jñāna*). (Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā, p. 33)
That very *upasādhana* is called *vajrajāpa*. (Se. Ṭī., p.

42) *Jāpa* is the observation of the coming and going [of the breath] through the channels of the left and right nostrils (*āli* and *kāli*), and the retention of those very [breaths] according to the teacher’s instruction.
That very [practice] is expressed by the term "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajāpa*).
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 20a-b) Vajraḍākinī.

The *vajra* is the *saṃvara* situated at the door of the unstruck (*anāhata*) eye, which is itself unstruck; it is of one flavor with the face of the sky (*khagamukha*), emitting flowing nectar and releasing waves like those of the ocean of milk. Because it flies—that is, moves—it is the *Vajraḍākinī*.
(From the *Vajratilaka-ṭīkā*, p. 7). [This is] the *vajra-body*.
One whose body is as firm as a *vajra*, with its core extending from the base of the arms to the heart, is the *Vajradeha*. (*Vajratilaka-ṭīkā*, p.

48). Here, *Vajradhara* refers to the entry of the apprehending mind into the apprehended mind; this non-engagement with external objects is called the sixfold yoga consisting of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), retention (*dhāraṇā*), and immersion (*majjana*).

Therefore, from that immersion comes the bliss of nirvāṇa, which is unchanging, innate, and indeed the fourth imperishable bliss; it is beyond the vibrations of the child, the mature, and the [yogic] movement; it transcends worldly analogies; its meaning is that it is free from the conduct of the three worlds;

it is devoid of laughter, gazing, touch, embracing, and the union of hands; it is free from the causes of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*); and its characteristic is the manifestation of all forms within emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

This is the Buddha’s mouth, the mouth of gnosis, which has entered the heart of the master and been cultivated; it exists at all times for the purpose of imparting to disciples that which has become his own experience and has reached the state of bliss. Such a guru is Vajradhara—this is the meaning. (Se. Ṭī., p.
45) He is called Vajradhara because he holds the vajra-substance, namely, the human skull-cup together with the *madana* [intoxicant].
...He is called Vajradhara because he holds the vajra, which is non-dual gnosis. (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p.
9) The syllable *e* is said to be the *bhaga*; the syllable *vaṃ* is remembered as the *kuliśa*.
"By me" (*mayā*) is declared to be the shaking; such is the characteristic of Vajradhara.
The Blessed One takes the form of semen (*śukra*); that bliss is known as the *kāminī*.
The nature of the enjoyment of the Dharma is the characteristic of Vajradhara.
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 2a) "Vajradhara" means one who holds the vajra (the literal meaning).
He is Vajradhara (the Samastāṅga) because he maintains the fivefold cognition beginning with the mirror-like [cognition] through being identical with that;
he is Vajradhara (the Garbhī) because he maintains the mind-made body (*manomayadeha*);
and he is Vajradhara (the Kōlika) because he maintains the vajra—non-dual gnosis—through being identical with it.
(Vajrasattvasādhanavidhi, pp. 55–56) [End of page 150, gross page 106] The heart of Vajradhara is the vajra, which is indivisible gnosis.
He who holds that [essence] is Vajradhara, the Perfectly Awakened One; because its heart is not revealed, it is designated as Dharmodaya. (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p. 6). Vajradhātreśvarī.

The Great Goddess abiding in the heart, who conveys the yoga of yogins, is known as the Mother of all Buddhas, the Sovereign Lady of the Vajra Realm (Vajradhātvīśvarī). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 48, 202) Vajradhātvīśvarī.
Among these [Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, and Tāriṇī], the leader is Vajradhātvīśvarī, whose nature is *Āli* and whose form is that of Vajrasattva.

This very Blessed Lady is designated as suchness (*tathatā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and selflessness (*nairātmya*). (Abhidhānavatārasaṃgraha, p. 43)
"Vajradhṛk, Vajradhṛk" indicates the fivefold manifest enlightenment (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*).
He holds the vajra, thus he is "Vajradhṛk"; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
One who holds the vajra-wisdom, which consists of the two truths, is called Vajradhṛk; this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 23).
This is the "vajra-word" (*vajrapada*).
Vajra is Hevajra;
his *pada* consists of the *mālīḍha*, *pratyālīḍha*, the maṇḍala stance, the even-footed stance, the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), and so forth.
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 22a) In this Mantra system, the *vajrapada* is twofold: one according to worldly convention (*laukika-saṃvṛti*).

The second [is] from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). Of these two, according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), the vajra-word bestows the accomplishment of the commitments (*samayasiddhi*) in rites such as slaying;
by way of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), the vajra-word bestows the fruit of the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā (*mahāmudrāsiddhi*). (Vi.pra., p. 19)
Vajraprabha is so called because his radiance is like that of a diamond-jewel; he is Vajraprabha because, abiding in the eye, he causes the liver (*bukka*) to function. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 48)
Vajrabhadra is so called because he sets in motion [the wheel] from the throat to the belly;
for by means of the throat and the belly, he sets in motion the vajra-like Wheel of Dharma that is auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end. (Vajrāvalī-nibandha-ṭippaṇī, p. 49)
"Vajra" means that which is indivisible, indestructible, and great.
That itself is the vehicle—the system of Mantra and the system of Pāramitā—which consists of both fruit and cause, and has become unified as one. (Vi.pra., p. 163)

Vajrayoga is the union (*saṃyoga*), the merging (*mīlana*), of the two natures of the conventional and ultimate truths; it is non-dual, known as the "yoked pair" (*yuganaddha*), and is imperishable (*akṣara*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 70)
By means of vajra-yogas whose nature consists of pure phenomena, mantras, and forms;
by means of the meditative absorptions of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and lack of volitional effort;
and by means of the sublime abodes of compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
...by way of the forms of the innate, enjoyment, and emanation bodies.
In that regard, it is "empty" because of the absence of intrinsic nature;
the state of that emptiness is "emptiness."
...Emptiness is profound and vast;
it is profound because of the non-existence of the past and the future,
and it is vast because of the vision of the past and the future.

The cognition characterized by that [emptiness] or the cognition which apprehends it is the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*). Purified by that, there is the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) of the fourth state, imperishable and indestructible. Because it restrains (*runddhi*) pleasure (*kaṃ*), it is the gnosis-vajra (*jñānavajra*) characterized by compassion (*karuṇā*).
That very innate body (*sahajakāya*), whose nature is wisdom and means, is called the pure yoga.
The conceptual mind—such as [the notions] "Buddha," "enlightenment" (*bodhi*), and so forth—is the cause.
Precisely because of emptiness, there is an absence of cause.
Therefore, that for which no sign (*nimitta*) exists is the signless (*animitta*); this signless knowledge is the liberation from signs.

By means of that, the mind—which is purified through the exhaustion of deep sleep, free from the duality of permanence and impermanence and so forth, characterized by loving-kindness, performing the welfare of the world through the radiations of the two bodies, and non-conceptual in nature—is the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*).
That itself is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), consisting of wisdom and skillful means, the essence of phenomena, and is called Yoga.
From the signless (*animitta*) itself comes the absence of discursive reasoning (*atarka*);
from the absence of discursive reasoning comes the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
That which lacks such aspirations as "May I become a perfectly awakened Buddha" and so forth is the liberation of the wishless (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*).
Purified by that, the inexhaustible and unassailable sound—which consists of the voices of all sentient beings and is characterized by the joy of mantra—is the Vajra of Speech (*vāgvajra*).
Because it gladdens all sentient beings through their own voices and because it serves as a mental refuge, it is called mantra.
This very [Vajra of Speech] is the Saṃbhogakāya; consisting of wisdom and means, it is termed Mantrayoga.

Because there is an absence of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), there is no volitional formation (*abhisaṃskāra*) characterized by the white and red vital winds (*prāṇāyāma*) and consciousness; this is the liberation of non-formation (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣa*).

Purified by that, through the exhaustion of the waking state, he is the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), whose nature is equanimity, unmixed with forms such as fierce passion or tranquility, and who, by means of infinitely extended emanation-bodies, brings forth the path that is the antidote to the afflictions.
That very emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), consisting of wisdom and means, is the "configuration yoga" (*saṃsthānayoga*).

As it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā* in the commentary on the first verse: "That very innate body (*sahajakāya*), purified by the liberation of emptiness, is the gnosis-vajra (*jñānavajra*), the omniscient one, consisting of wisdom and means, and is the 'pure yoga' (*śuddhayoga*)."

That very Dharmakāya, purified by the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokṣa*), is the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*), the Gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*), whose nature is wisdom and means (*prajñopāyātmaka*), and which is joined with the Yoga of the Dharma-nature.

That very [Dharmakāya], purified by the wishless liberation (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*), is the Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*), whose form is like the sun, whose nature is wisdom and means, and which is called the Mantra-Yoga.

That very [Dharmakāya], purified by the unconditioned liberation (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣa*), is the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, whose nature is wisdom and means, and which is the Saṃsthāna-Yoga. (Se. Ṭī., pp. 5–6)
In the six chakras from the secret place to the uṣṇīṣa, he is sequentially named Vajrasattva, Mahāsattva, Bodhisattva, Samayasattva, Vajrayoga, and Kālacakra.

He alone is called Vajrayoga because his union (*yoga*) with the bodies and other vajras—through the consort (*prajñā*), the image (*bimba*), and the immutable drops (*akṣara-bindu*)—is a state of oneness;
and because he has conquered anger, he is taught as Mahākrodha, and because he has triumphed over Māra, he is the enraged enemy of Māra. (Se. Ṭī., p. 73)
Transcending existence and non-existence, the exhaustion of being and non-being, non-dual,
inseparable from emptiness and compassion, vajrayoga is great bliss.
Transcending the nature of atoms, devoid of empty phenomena, liberated from eternalism and nihilism, the vajrayoga is without lineage. (Vimalaprabhā, p. 44). Thus, reality is sixteen-fold in aspect.

That very same [nature] is the *sahajakāya*, purified by the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*), the wisdom-vajra (*jñānavajra*), the omniscient one, whose essence is wisdom and means (*prajñopāyātmaka*), called the "pure yoga" (*viśuddhayoga*).

That very same [nature] is the *dharmakāya*, purified by the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokṣa*), the mind-vajra (*cittavajra*), the body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*), whose essence is wisdom and means, called the "dharma-yoga.

That very same [nature] is the *saṃbhogakāya*, purified by the wishless liberation (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*), the speech-vajra (*vāgvajra*), whose form is like the sun, whose essence is wisdom and means, called the "mantra-yoga."

That very emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), purified by the liberation of non-conditioning (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣa*), is the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), with eyes as broad as lotus petals, consisting of wisdom and means, and is called the yoga of form (*saṃsthānayoga*).
Thus, this fourfold Vajrayoga... (Vi.pra., p. 45).
This Vajrayoga is to be explained in detail in the Chapter on Gnosis (*jñānapaṭala*) (Vi.pra., p. 46).
Vajrayoginī:
"Vajra" is non-apprehending gnosis;
she is so called because she possesses yoga together with that. (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p. 4)
The heart of the Vajra Lady is gnosis; that very [gnosis] is the Vajra Lady, because her intrinsic nature is indivisible wisdom (*prajñā*). (Jñānasiddhi, p. 139)
Vajrarati: Vajra is Amoghasiddhi; delight in him is Vajrarati—this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
It is delight in vajra-gnosis (*vajrajñāna*).
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana, p.

25). The Vajra-vow initiation (*vajravratābhiṣeka*) is the complete purification of the sense objects such as form and the sense faculties such as the eyes; because it brings about the attainment of the *mahāmudrā* siddhi by means of the restraint of ordinary objects, it is the fifth [initiation], the Vajra-vow initiation. (Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā, p. 21).
Vajrasattva: by "vajra" emptiness is expressed, and by "sattva" mere gnosis;
the identity of these two is established through the nature of Vajrasattva.
The distinction between emptiness and compassion is like that between a lamp and its light;
the unity of emptiness and compassion is like that between a lamp and its light.
Emptiness is not other than phenomena, nor do phenomena exist without it;
they are inseparable, just like the relationship between "produced" and "impermanent.
That which is called indestructible vajra is the oneness of the being of the three realms.
"By means of this wisdom and logic, he is known as Vajrasattva" (Hevajra Tantra 1.1.24).
The *vajra* is the sign (*cihna*) arising from the seed produced by the union of the moon and sun, whose natures are wisdom and method;
the *sattva* is the seed situated within its interior.
Vajrasattva is the being endowed with the vajra. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.

45b). Here, the five-syllable great emptiness, the collection of vowels, the semen, and the moon are so called; the six-syllable emptiness of the bindu, the collection of consonants, the menstrual blood, and the sun are so called.
In this context, semen is the moon, represented by the syllable *vaṃ*, which is the vajra;
passion is the sun, represented by the syllable *e*, which is the lotus.
The unification of these two, the vajra and the lotus, is Vajrasattva.
The *vajra* is the gnosis (*jñāna*) of supreme bliss; the *sattva* is the semen (*śukra*), the knowable (*jñeya*), the image of wisdom (*prajñā*) in all its aspects, and the sun.

When conjoined with gnosis and consciousness, rendered free from obscuration and unified into a single mass, this reality (*tattva*) brings about the welfare of the world. This is the *vajrasamaya*. (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, p. 49)
From this point forward, in order to make you understand that you are the unconditioned, indivisible, yoked-in-pair (*yuganaddha*) Bodhicitta-samaya, there is the Vajra-samaya. (Abhisamayamañjarī, p.
38) Vajra-samaya is the union of the two organs; it is the embryo (*garbha*).
Vajra-samaya is the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*).
The *kolika* [nature] (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p.
22). The Vajra-lion-throne (*vajrasiṃhāsana*) is the mandala of moon, sun, and fire; it is uncuttable and indivisible.
The letter *E* is the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), the vajra-lion throne (*vajrasiṃhāsana*). (Vi.pra., p.
16) Vajra-hūṃkāra is so called because, unlike [the breath] at the tip of the nose, it causes the opening of the gates. (Va.ti.ṭī., p. 49)

Veneration (*vandanā*) consists of seeing the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas—who have pervaded all regions of space by means of the rays of light issuing from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, who are intent solely on compassion and the performance of deeds for the benefit of the world through the process of emanation and reabsorption—and then, by means of the very rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, emitting clouds of divine perfumes, flowers, and so forth; preceded by the [mental] maṇḍala, with palms joined and head bowed at the lotus feet of the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, it is the act of prostration. (Sādhana)

Having worshipped [the deity] (Mā.pṛ. 115–116), the yogin, possessing supreme compassion and bowed with devotion, should pay homage through body, speech, and mind; this is *vandana* (salutation). (Sā.mā., p.
373) [He who holds] the excellent *vajra*.
"Vara," "vara," and "kuliśadhara"—[these form] "varakuliśadhara.
...These three would be designations for emptiness (*śūnya*).
By the designation of the first "vara," the second emptiness is expressed.

That is to say: the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), the wind element (*vāyudhātu*), olfactory contact (*ghrāṇasaṃsparśa*), the faculty of speech (*vāgindriya*), and the excretion of feces (*viṭsrāva*).

The absence of obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*) regarding these, their state of equal flavor (*samarasatva*), and their being unified into a single mass (*ekalolībhūtatva*) is the "excellent" (*vara*); this is the void of the second syllable.
Its symbolic sign (*saṃjñācihna*) is a mere stroke in the shape of a staff located to the east of the central unstruck symbol (*anāhatacihna*); it is not to be articulated.
The second excellent state is said to be the fifth void (*śūnya*).
It is as follows: the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), odor (*gandha*), the anus (*pāyu*), and speech (*ālāpa*).

The excellence (*vara*) of these is their state of being unobscured (*nirāvaraṇatā*), their being of equal flavor (*samarasatva*), and their becoming unified as one (*ekalolībhūtatva*); this is the fifth syllable-void.
Its symbolic sign (*saṃjñācihna*) is the shape of a plow to the west of the sign of the *anāhata* [cakra], and it is unutterable (*anuccārya*).

Thus, according to the sequence described, through the five [elements] having become one, the five-syllabled *mahāśūnya*, the syllable *vaṃ*, Vajrasattva, is called the *mahāsukha-vajra*. [The term *vajradhara* should also be understood here. (Vi.pra., p. 48)
Vasanta... is the Unstruck (anāhata) because the syllable *huṃ* cannot be uttered;
he is the Hero (vīra) because he has emerged from all conceptual constructions and fears.
He alone, because he generates joy in the hearts of all embodied beings like the spring season, should be known as the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka, the "Spring" (*vasanta*). As it is said:
"He is renowned as 'Spring,' the delighter of the hearts of embodied beings" (*Vasantatilaka*, p. 38). This is the *Vasantatilakā*.

This fire of gnosis, which resembles the fire of speech, kindled by the wind of ritual action characterized by the union of the churning stick and the churning base, blazing forth from the region of the navel and ascending through the upper path, touches that Hero situated in the heart with a torrential downpour of the stream of his nectar—
likewise melted— and because it thus abides in the state of non-dual union (*samāpatti*), it is called the "Spring Season" (*vasantatilakā*) (Vasantatilaka-ṭīkā, 38).
"This hero Śrī Heruka is known as Vasantatilakā" (Vasantatilakā, p.
38). "The well-known Vārāhī is known as Vasantatilakā" (Vasantatilakā, p. 86).
"Spring (vasanta) [is] like a tilaka-mark (tilaka) consisting of the syllable HŪṂ and so forth" (Vasantatilakā-ṭīkā, p. 86).
The Vasantatilakā yoga:
"The Nāda, nourished by this [yoga], shall attain the state of perfect bliss;
this indeed is declared to be the Vasantatilakā yoga. (Vasantatilakā-ṭīkā, p. 64)
The syllable *vaṃ*, the syllable *vaṃ*, is known as the vajra; [it is] the syllable *vaṃ*. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 2a) *Vaṃ*-kāraḥ.

Among the designations of the mind purified by the gnosis of the reality of the *bindu*—the innate supreme syllable [consisting of] the great passion and great bliss of the syllable *vaṃ*—the single designation "syllable *vaṃ*" is preeminent, because it establishes the great mudrā, the innate joy, and the immutable bliss. (Vi.pra., p.
34) *Vaṃ* is the Vajrī, Vajrasattva, Vajrabhairava, and Īśvara.
"Heruka and Kālacakra are [designated] by names such as Ādibuddha and others" (Vi.pra., p. 40).

Thus, the syllable *vaṃ* is the five-syllabled Great Void (*mahāśūnya*), whose nature is objectless compassion; it transcends the reality of atoms (*paramāṇudharmatātīta*), resembles a reflected image (*pratisenārūpa*), and is accessible only to the yogin. (Vi.pra., 48) This is the Wheel of Speech (*vākcakra*).
"Thus, all the countries are established within the wheel of speech; they are declared to be the [abodes] of the Bhūcarīs, who take the form of specific locations. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p.
34) "The channels situated in the wheel of speech are established as the Bhūcarī messengers. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 45)
In the [cakras] known as kṣetra, upakṣetra, chandoha, and upacchanda, there are eight channels belonging to the earth-dwelling [goddesses] in the wheel of speech.
The other fourfold door of speech is known as the vocal door. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 45)

The Āgneya, Vāyavya, Māhendra, and likewise the Vāruṇa [breaths]—from these very [gateways of speech], which are joined with the apertures of the left, right, and middle channels, the Blessed Lady, the Mother of Phonemes (Varṇamātṛkā), arises. (Vātūlanāthasūtra-vṛtti, pp. 20–21; Vātūlanāthasūtra-ṭīkā, p. 21).
At the eastern vocal gate, there are four kinds of ḍākinīs. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p.
48) Or, at its arising, she is Vāmanī; she is called Vāmanī because she produces the element of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) in the form of a dwarf, or because she carries the sinews.

Or, upon its arising, by means of vomiting after eating, [one should touch] the left ear; the left hand is the hand whose function is holding. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 44) The hand is the instrument for the act of supporting.
Due to its similarity to that [left side], the wind is "Hand" (*hasta*);
it is the breath situated in the left nostril (*vāmanāsikāpuṭasthita*). (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p.
11). Because it carries the full flesh of the "Dwarf" (*vāmana*) itself, it is "Left" (*vāmā*) on the back. (Vimalaprabhā-ṭīkā, p. 44).
The wind mandala:
the wind mandala is situated in the navel lotus.
At its arising, a ray of dark-blue color emerges and remains for half a watch (three hours).
At that time, one should perform the raudra-karman. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 143) The wind exiting through the nose is the recaka breath.
Entering [the breath] is inhalation (*pūraka*); having filled the interior, it is retention (*kumbhaka*);
having entered and become motionless, it is the tranquilized state (*praśānta*). (Hevajra-tantra-ṭīkā, 42a)
The wind-maṇḍala is situated on the soles of the feet; the Vairambha wind is bow-shaped. (Vajrāvalī-nāma-maṇḍalopāyikā, p. 61).
[She is] Vāyuvegā.
Vāyuvegā is she whose speed and velocity extend below, above, and in the ten directions like the wind; in both the Vajra-tantra-alaṃkāra and its commentary (p.
47), the power of water is Vāyuvegā (Vajra-tantra, p. 55).
Vārāhī is so called because she brings forth (*āhinoti*) the excellent *bodhicitta*; for the root *hi* means "to go."
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the prefix *āṅ* in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), and the substitution of *ā* [for *āṅ*] occurs by virtue of its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
The meaning is that it follows the Blessed One who abides in great bliss (*mahāsukha*). (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p. 2)
His very innate wisdom (sahajā prajñā) remains assuming that very form.
Blazing, driven by the winds of karma within the circle of the navel, she is well-known as Vārāhī... (Vajravatī-tantra, p.
86). She is called Vārāhī because she impels—that is, causes to flow—by means of the syllables *vā* and *ra*, and by the two mothers who are fire (*hu*) and wind (*ya*). (Vajravatī-ṭīkā, p. 86).
The Vāruṇa-maṇḍala is located within the heart-lotus.
At the time of its rising, a white-colored ray of light emerges and remains for half a watch (ardhayāma).
Then one should perform the great propitiation (*mahāśānti*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p.
143) "Vikaṭadaṃṣṭra" means one whose back has a formidable (*vikaṭā*) fang—that is, a fang consisting of flesh; thus he is Vikaṭadaṃṣṭra. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 48)
There, "transformation" refers to the transformation of the body by means of the *ālīḍha* stance and so forth, as well as the crushing [of the enemy];
the transformation of speech is the utterance of mantras with a roar like the clouds at the time of dissolution.
The mental transformation that takes emptiness as its object destroys all [obstacles] (*sarvaghna*).
Vighnāntaka is liberated from obstacles and the like; his gnosis accomplishes all aims. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 191)
"Because he is accomplished as consisting of all Buddhas, he is known as Vighnāntaka. (Jñānasiddhi 15.18).
He is "Vighnāntakṛt" because he brings about the end—that is, the destruction—of obstacles; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
The four elements are obstacles;
they are obstacles because they afflict the body through their increase and decrease.
He is the "Destroyer of Obstacles" (Vighnāntakṛt) because he brings about their destruction through the arising of knowledge regarding the means [to counteract them].
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, pp. 26–27).
"Variegated" (*vicitra*) means diverse, known as embracing, kissing, and so forth. (Hevajra-tantra 2.3.7).
In the *vicitra* [cakra], there is the first bliss (*prathamānanda*). (HeTa 2.3.9). *Viṭ* means food (*anna*). (GuSaPra, p. 191).
Knowledge (*vidyā*).

In this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), that which is knowledge regarding worldly conventions is ignorance with respect to the object of ultimate reality. ... "Knowledge" refers to non-conceptual inner knowledge, emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects.

"...Vidyā is without objective support and consists of untainted bliss. Vidyā consists of both cause and fruit, being unified as cause and fruit, like the light of a fire which is unified with its burning power. (Viśva-prakāśa, p. 258). [Thus says] the Vidyādhara.
The *samayas* are those of the *ḍākas*, *ḍākinīs*, and so forth;
the *vidyā* among them is the mantra for their accomplishment.
One who holds that is a *vidyādhara*. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 113)
The Knowledge-Person (vidyāpuruṣa) consists of the mantras of all the Tathāgatas, beginning with the syllable Oṃ;
Mahāvajradhara is the one who has perfected the pledge (samaya) through them.
That very reality for those devoted to mantra is the Vidyā, the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).
The person arisen from that is the Vidyāpuruṣa. [This is] the group of eight Vidyās.
The mother, the sister, the daughter, the sister’s daughter, as well as the wife of the maternal uncle, and one’s own mother’s sister; these are [the women who must not be approached].
Likewise, the father's sister—these eight are proclaimed as the Vidyās. (He. Ta. 2.5.59) These are not connected to the world.
"The Mother" refers to the teacher’s beloved wife.
She alone is the mother of the disciple;
her friend is his sister;
and the preceptor’s female disciple is his daughter.
The sister’s daughter is his disciple;
she is the wife of his maternal uncle’s dear friend;
she is the sister of his mother and the friend of his teacher.
"Sister" (*svasṛkā*) refers to the beloved of the disciple; "father's sister" (*piturbhaginī*) refers to the sister of the teacher. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p.
65a): Through the purification of the impure mind, she becomes the eye, the sister.
The sister's daughter is indeed the ear, and the mother is said to be the nose.
The tongue is the daughter, and likewise the mind shall be the wife;
these six excellent sciences are the bestowers of Mahāmudrā. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, 67a-b).
The branches of knowledge.
The auxiliary sciences, the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā,
the extensive Nyāya, the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstras— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.

Thus is the position of other schools; furthermore, the sciences of grammar and logic, as well as that of inner science, and the two sciences of medicine and the arts—these are the five branches of knowledge. (Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī-ṭīkā, p. 72)

The maturation (*vipāka*) is that which has matured; it is the enjoyment of the knowledge of bliss, which is the reversal of that [maturity]. (Hevajra Tantra 2.3.7) Supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) arises from maturation (*vipākaja*). (Hevajra Tantra 2.3.9)
Vimarda is said to be the contemplation of the dissolution [of the object], thinking, "I have experienced pleasure.
And Viramānanda occurs during Vimarda. (Hevajra Tantra 2.3.8–9)
Vimalā is the left ear, the space between the eyebrows, the eyes, and the base of the arms;
"upapīṭha" means near to the pīṭhas.

That very [nature] is "stainless" (*vimalā*), because the stains of conceptual construction have been burnt away by the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*); it is "separation" (*viyoga*). (Vajrayoginī-ṭippaṇī, p. 28)
Generally, due to the consumption of meat, there is [affliction] in the anus, either through separation or by generating conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). (Vajravatī-ṭīkā, p.
46) Virūpākṣa is so called because he is the initiator of the three-eyed one at the boundary of the penis. (Vajravatī-ṭīkā, p. 49)
Vilakṣaṇa means distinct from the three [states], other than them, and free from both passion and dispassion. (Hevajra Tantra 2.3.8). This is purity.
That by which all phenomena become faultless is purity (*viśuddhi*).
The universal lotus belongs to that Meru (which is synonymous with *kaṅkāla*).

That which is this head, in the center of which are the thirty-two indestructible channels (*nāḍīs*) and so forth—these alone are to be understood as the universal lotus (*viśvapadma*), the seat of the Blessed One. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 62) The "universal image" (*viśvabimba*) is that image which, by being suspended in the intermediate space, is perceived by the yogi’s direct perception like a dream—an unconstructed image in the void of space, free from subject and object, with eyes half-open.
The universal vajra is known as the "universal vajra" because it is non-dual in its mutual pervasion. (Jñānasiddhi 15.27) (Se. Ṭī., p. 48)
"Viṣṭhā" refers to that which carries what is called "pitta" (bile); thus, it is *viṣṭhā* in the two breasts. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 44).
This is the *vīrakrama*.
The *vīrakrama* is not external; indeed, it is said to be the exhaustion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the body (*Viṣamapadaprakāśikā*, p.

7). The vow of the hero’s conduct (*vīracaryāvratam*) is itself called the practice of the vow of universal sovereignty (*yaurājyavratacaryā*) and the practice of the vow of the Vajra-Kāpālika, as stated in the *Śrīsampuṭatantra*.
(Vajrāvalī, p. 219) Vīramatī:
she is called Vīramatī because a hero exists as her progenitor.
"Because of the statement, 'The Hero resides in the center of the navel' (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 47);
the faculty of faith is Vīramatī (Vajratilaka, p. 54); [and] the Heroes."

Those lords of yogins, by whom [reality] has been realized in its stainless form through the lotuses of wisdom, are heroes in this circle of existence because they crush the enemies that are the sense-objects. (Candrakīrti-vyākhyā, p. 70) The twenty-four elements are the heroes; they are the feet of the Moon. (Vimalaprabhā-ṭīkā, p. 89) Virya.

And vigor [is so called] because it endures the affliction of the eight worldly dharmas (*aṣṭalokadharma*). The faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*) is that which inspires enthusiasm for those dharmas produced by the faculty of faith; such is the faculty of vigor. (Avaivartikacakra-sūtra, p. 3)
And that is of four kinds: the vigor of undertaking,
the vigor of non-retrogression,
and the vigor of discernment.
