And there is the vigor of practice (*pratipattivīrya*). (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p.
54) The application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanānusmṛtyupasthāna*):
Feeling, consisting of the pleasant and so forth, is eighteenfold because it is based upon the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍvijñānakāya*).

That [foundation] is also called the "application of mindfulness to feelings" (*vedanānusmṛtyupasthāna*) because it is the application of mindfulness within one's own mind, [realizing] that feelings such as pleasure are empty due to their non-existence through distinctions such as past and so forth. (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p.
52) Vemacitrī, Vemacitrī is the lord of the asuras. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 64a)
Vaibhāṣya (or Vaibhāṣika): *vibhāṣā* is the exposition for the sake of detachment; that itself is *vaibhāṣya*.
And that Śrāvakayāna consists of works such as the *Avadānaśataka* and the *Tridaṇḍakamālā*. (He. Ta. Ṭī., p.
67b) Vairambha is so called because it has the shape of a bow and because of its distinguished exertion (*viśiṣṭārambha*). It is precisely that which is Vairambha.

The suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*). Furthermore, the action consisting of the movement of the feet, like that of Vairocana, is called *vairambha*. (Vaiśeṣika-tattvopaplava-ṭīkā, pp. 61–62). [The term] *vairocanam*.
Locanā is the [wisdom] of the Vajrasattvas, blazing by her very nature;
that pure Tathāgata wisdom is called Vairocana. (Jñānasiddhi 15.5) Vairocana is the Tathāgata. (Sampuṭa-sādhana 2.7)
Vairocana is so called because he consists of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
Through the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of hardness arises from contact;
since hardness is of the nature of delusion (*moha*), delusion is considered to be Vairocana. (Hevajra Tantra Ṭīkā, p. 19a; Hevajra Tantra 2.2.53)
The mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is the knowledge of the body that is like space;
from that, Vairocana is produced, because he consists of that very nature. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 51)
Vairocana is so called because he brings forth the white-colored shield (*kheṭa*) with his two thumbs; (Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p. 49).
Because he constructs [reality] in the form of self-cognizable awareness, he alone is Vairocana; (Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p. 85).
The prophecy regarding the vow.

The bestowal of the *vajra-vrata* is for the purpose of abolishing external observances (*bāhyavrata*). The prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) is for the purpose of indicating that [the elements] such as earth have the nature of the [mantras]. For instance, the meaning of "bhūrbhuvassvaḥ" is: "May the earth (*bhūḥ*), etc., be its own nature (*svaḥ*)," which is to say, "may it become its own true form (*svarūpa*). (Avaśiṣṭasamaya, p. 38)

The fourfold power consists of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and the third, the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), which effects the entry of the world into one's own mind, the illumination of phenomena, and the attainment of the object through the realization of essential identity.
"Furthermore, the fourth is renunciation; she who is bowed to by the three worlds is indeed non-dual.
In due order, among those [powers], the Vajrī swallows nothing at all, nor does she ever release. (Kālacakra Tantra 2.90).
"In this context, the powers of the mind are characterized as waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state. (Vimalaprabhā, p. 219).
Śamatha is indeed a specific type of cultivation characterized by one-pointedness of mind;
it is attained through gradual practice. (He. Ta. Ṭī., 43b)
He performed the practice after making the gift of his body;
as it is said: "Having given the gift of his body, he should thereafter undertake the practice" (Hevajra Tantra 1.6.19).
Because of this statement:
"The gift is given until the end of the body" (*Abhayapaddhati-saṃgraha*, p. 3).
[This refers to] the mandala of the body.

This has been explained in the complete eighth chapter [of the *Vimalaprabhā*] through such passages as, “The body is the beautiful mandala with four gates, as previously described,” and “It is considered a mandala because it grasps (*śarati*) and protects (*lāti*)”; therein, the body itself is the mandala. (Vimalaprabhā, pp.
60–69) In that context, the body is indeed the mandala.
Because it is the locus for the channels (*nāḍī*) and elements (*dhātu*) that take the form of the maṇḍalas of mind, speech, and body, as well as for the yoginīs and vīras. (Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p.

60) Just as this body has a certain measurement from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), so too, when the arms are extended, it possesses that same measurement; thus, the squareness of the body-maṇḍala is established. (Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p. 65)
"Everything mentioned here, such as the mandala and so forth, is to be understood exactly as it was taught [in the Vimalaprabhā] (Vatī, p. 69).

This means that whatever mandalas and other implements for the mandala were not explicitly stated here—such as the taking up of the thread and colored powders, the invocation, the installation, the dismissal, the mandala-sādhana, the consecration, the ritual bathing, the offering of bali, and so on—are to be known in that very same context of the body-mandala."
For instance: the central channel is the thread;
here, the consecration [is performed]. The tasting of the tongue is the oblation for those who are its outflows. (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, pp. 69–70)

Because it induces the sleep of great bliss within the garlands of entrails at night, it is called *śarvarī*; and because it generates conceptual construction at the tip of the nose, it is [also so called]. (*Vajrayoginī-ṭippaṇī*, 45).
It is peaceful.
It is free from the transformations of the eighteen elements. (Se. Ṭī., p.
60) Here, "the state of Śiva" refers to the semen-drop being devoid of differentiation, characterized by the state of bliss beyond emission.
That itself is the state of Śiva. (Viṣṇupurāṇa, p.
258) Śītadā remains, having enveloped the intestines with a network of veins, channels, fat, and marrow.
The river carrying it is "cool-giving" (*śītadā*), because it bestows the sensation of cold upon the mouth; this is its nature (*śīla*). (Vajrayoginī-ṭīkā, p. 45) Śīla.

Ethical discipline (*śīla*) consists in the restraint of body, speech, and mind for the sake of all sentient beings (*Avaśyakasūtra-vṛtti-saṃgraha*, p. 3). *Śukra* [is derived from] *sug*, meaning "well" (*sukha*), and thus it is *śoka*.

That which splits like a saw is *śukra*, which is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). (Guhyasiddhiprakaraṇa, p. 71) That which fells or destroys grief (*śuca*) and sorrow (*śoka*) like a saw is *śukra*, which is wine (*madya*). (Guhyasiddhiprakaraṇa, p. 190) It is pure (*śuddha*).
Untouched by the stains of the afflictions (*kleśamala*).
Pure,
pure, and perfectly established (*pariniṣpanna*).
The pure body (*śuddhakāya*) is that which is designated as great bliss (*mahāsukha*), known as non-abiding nirvāṇa; it is the pure body.
... That which is the drop of the body (*kāyabindu*) opposite to the pure body designated as great bliss is the pure body due to the exhaustion of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*).
The Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Emanation-bodies radiate from the Pure Body. (Se. Ṭī., p.
55–56) Śūkarāsyā is Right Mindfulness; she is Śūkarāsyā. (Va. Ti., p. 56)

At the end of the death of living beings, due to the abandonment of the aggregates and the subsequent grasping of the aggregates pertaining to the portion of rebirth, there is an intermediate interval characterized by emptiness; that single vision of the three worlds, which has the nature of emptiness, is called "the Void" (*śūnya*).

The aggregate of knowledge (*jñānaskandha*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), the element of knowledge (*jñānadhātu*), the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), mind (*manas*), ear (*śrotra*), sound (*śabda*), the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the divine faculty (*divyendriya*), the emission of the female organ and urine, and the discharge of semen— their state of being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*), their state of having a single flavor (*samarasatva*), and their state of being unified into one (*ekalolībhūtatva*)—
do not mean their total non-existence, because they are to be personally realized by the yogi.
That very [sound] is called the Unstruck (*anāhata*) by the Victors.

The symbolic sign of this Unstruck is a mere line in the shape of a curved knife (*kartikā*), situated in the middle between the right, left, front, and back; it is unutterable and is the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*) of the first syllable. (Vi.pra., p. 47).
This is the tetrad of voids (*śūnyacatuṣṭaya*).
The four leaves [are] by way of the nature of the four voids: void, extreme void, great void, and universal void. (Do. Ko. Vyā., p. 151).
Voidness is characterized by the voidness endowed with the excellence of all aspects. (A. Va. Saṃ., p. 40).

The thorough knowledge of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas through the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Furthermore, the *saṃbhogakāya* also has emptiness as its characteristic.

And emptiness, established by being endowed with the excellence of all aspects, is realized as having a nature comparable to an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a reflection, an echo, the moon in water, and a magical creation.
(a. pra. vi. si., pṁ.

216) The awakening to emptiness consists in taking all phenomena as objects with the mind [and realizing]: "This is merely mind; when external forms do not exist, the form of an object appears through delusion."
"Just as in a dream":

one should perceive even that [dream]—which is the very nature of appearance—as the mind, devoid of the intrinsic nature of being either one or many, free from appearances, and consisting of luminosity. (This is the awakening to emptiness; *Hevajra Tantra Commentary*, fol. 13b).
Emptiness is the reality (*tattva*).
I, too, am empty, because I am within the domain of conceptual construction;
the world, too, is empty, being nothing more than mere conceptual construction.
Even the three worlds are empty. In the stainless, immaculate, and innate great bliss,
neither sin nor merit exists.
And so it has been said:

"In that stainless, great gnosis, radiant with the form of light, auspicious and beyond the sphere of conceptual construction—wherein could there be any talk of sin or merit? (Dvayasamvaratattvasaṃgraha-vyākhyā, p. 71).
Śauṇḍinī is so called because of her intoxication with *surā* liquor and *āsava*; (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
48). The awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is Śauṇḍinī; (Vajratilaka, p. 55).
By this reasoning—that it "breathes" (śvasati) corpses—it is called *śmaśāna*;
according to etymological analysis (*nairukta*), there is an elision of syllables in the term meaning "the abode (*vasati*) of corpses (*śava*). (Hevajra Tantra 1.3.16)
The meaning is "the abode of corpses.
...How is the body a cremation ground?
It is designated as a "cremation ground" by this reasoning: because it breathes (*śvasati*). (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 15b)

Śyāmādevī: because of the arising of intense love (*prema*), she is *śyāmā* (dark-complexioned); and because she sports within all the *cakras*, she is *devī* (goddess)—thus she is Śyāmādevī. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 47).
The power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is Śyāmādevī. (Vajravārāhī-tantra, p. 55).

The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is faith; it is the mind’s conviction regarding that which is to arise in the supramundane path, or regarding the Three Jewels and so forth—that is the faculty of faith (*va. ti. ṭī.*, p. 54).
"śrāyaḥ śavaḥ śrāyaḥ" (HeTa 2.3.56); [the forms] śrvākāḥ.
Those who attain the state of an Arhat by means of the realization of the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) are the Śrāvakas.
The Glorious One is Śrī; Śrī is Locanā. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana, p. 204)

He who possesses [it] is the Glorious One (*śrīmān*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 121) *Śrī* is Pāṇḍaravāsinī; he who is joined with her is the Glorious One. (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 121)
The dog-faced [mudrā] is the correct exertion; it is the dog-faced [mudrā]. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 56).
The six organs of action.
At the end of sixteen years, the divine faculty arises within the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*); this is the rule for the six organs of action. (Vi.pra., p. 168).
The six families are the imperishable bliss, the element of gnosis.
Consciousness is the element of space, mental formations are the element of wind,
and feeling is the element of fire.
Perception is the water element and form is the earth element; these are with obscuration for those born from a womb, but without obscuration for the Buddhas. (Vimalaprabhā, p. 20)
These elements are the six families of the six sense faculties.
Thus, the families of body, speech, and mind, together with the family of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), become four families.
The three bodies (*kāya*) become the four bodies.
The three states become four states;
thus, for those born from a womb, the five families of the aggregates (skandhas), together with the aggregate of gnosis (jñānaskandha), become six families.
[This occurs] at twelve years of age for a girl.
For a man, [the lineage extends] up to sixteen years;
for a girl, it should be understood as the three families or five families until the time of her menses.
For a man, it should be understood as the three families or five families until the time of the emission of semen.
At the time of the arising of the *jñānadhātu*, there are four families for both [the body and speech], and six families until death.
Thus, the Blessed One said in the *Mūlatantra*: "The three families, the five families, and indeed the single nature—there are one hundred families. (Vi.pra., p. 50).
[There are] the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakrāṇi*).
The *uṣṇīṣa* is in the element of space for gods and humans, and the secret [place] is in the element of gnosis;
the heart-lotus is in the element of wind, while the throat-cakra clearly shines in the element of fire.
In water is the lotus between the eyebrows with sixty-four petals, and the navel-cakra is in the element of earth.
The six joints of the feet and hands are threefold among earth, water, fire, and wind. (Kālacakratantra 2.15).
Regarding the eighteen wheels, it is the rule that twelve wheels will be described in what follows. (Vimalaprabhā, p. 169).
In the guhya, uṣṇīṣa, and navel, the body of the Sahaja Jina is of a nature devoid of intrinsic existence.
O King, the Dharmakāya indeed resides in the heart-cakra; the Sambhogakāya of the Jina resides in the throat-cakra;
and by the power of its qualities and through the sequence of the presiding deities, the Nirmāṇakāya resides in the drop (bindu).
Thus, the heart-cakra, the throat-cakra, and the lotus at the head are respectively the pure Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Śuddhakāya.

At the navel, throat, secret place, head, and likewise at the heart and the center of the uṣṇīṣa, there are the threefold vajras of body, speech, and mind belonging respectively to the mother and the father.
These are the six families joined with the vajra: the wheel, the jewel, the sky-lotus, the water-born [lotus], and the excellent sword.

These six transformations of the mind— jealousy, hatred, and so forth— occur within the excellent body in the space of the element of gnosis, having entered the threefold paths of the upper and lower channels through the divisions of moon, sun, and fire. (Kālacakra-tantra 2.27–28) Jealousy arises in the element of gnosis, and the mind of hatred in the sky.

For the mind of envy is manifest in air, the mind of passion likewise in fire; the glorious mind of pride in water, and the mind of delusion in earth, by the power of the qualities of nature. (Kālacakratantra 2.23). [The thirty-six elements and aggregates].

By way of division of the body, the aggregates (skandhas) and sense faculties (indriyas) are phenomena consisting of short vowels and consonants; the elements (dhātus) and objects (viṣayas) are phenomena consisting of long vowels and consonants.
Through the division of the modifications of the elements, the six tastes become thirty-six elements.
The six aggregates become thirty-six aggregates through the division of the six sense faculties and so forth;
namely, the six tastes and the six elements.
The six sense faculties, the six objects, and the six organs of action.
The six objects of the organs of action are the six transformations of the taste-element;
the six consciousnesses, such as auditory consciousness and so forth,
are likewise the six formations.
Six feelings, six perceptions, and six aggregates of form.
The six aggregates of knowledge (*jñānaskandha*) are transformations of the [five] aggregates (*skandhavikāra*). (Viṣṇupurāṇa, p. 49):
Generosity is cow dung mixed with water; ethical discipline is sweeping; patience is the removal of small ants; and vigor is the performance of the ritual act.
Meditative concentration is the making of the mind one-pointed at that very moment, and wisdom is the brilliant, well-drawn lines;
having constructed the maṇḍala of the Sage, one obtains these six perfections alone.
He becomes golden-hued, liberated from all diseases, distinguished among gods and men, with a radiant splendor like the moon;
he is born into a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold.
Having performed bodily actions in this supreme abode of the Sugata,

the six beings (the *skandhas*)— who are themselves this very non-dual, immutable, and upward-streaming [vitality]— obtain the four names beginning with Vajrasattva, respectively, by proceeding through the secret place, the navel, the heart, and the throat.
The one located in the forehead is called the fourfold yoga beginning with Viśuddhi as previously described;
the one located in the uṣṇīṣa is named Kālacakra—these are the six beings (*ṣaṭsattva*). (Se. Ṭī., p.
29) In the six cakras from the secret place to the uṣṇīṣa, they are respectively named Vajrasattva, Mahāsattva, Bodhisattva, Samayasattva, Vajrayoga, and Kālacakra.
The explanation of this is as follows: "Vajra" refers to the primordial vajra, the image of emptiness (*śūnyabimba*).

Because it is indivisible, it is of great significance. Regarding the designation of *Haṃ*: that being who is called the unity of body, speech, and mind in the form of the desire realm and so forth is designated as the supreme unchanging; thus, he is Vajrasattva.

Alternatively, "vajra" refers to the indestructible gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), which is the single essence of body, speech, and mind; "sattva" refers to the unity of the three realms of existence. The oneness of these two is the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*). Because he is great due to being full of great bliss, he is designated as "Great Passion" (*mahārāga*). Furthermore, because that *sattva* is full through the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), he is designated as "the one who brings joy to all beings"; thus, he is the "Great Being" (*mahāsattva*).
Alternatively, by the word "great" (*maha*) here is meant the supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*).
A being (*sattva*) or a stage (*bhūmi*) that is filled with this is a "Great Being" (*mahāsattva*).

Because he is established immovably in the Wheel of Dharma—which consists of awakening characterized by emptiness and compassion—and because he has conquered the hosts of hatred in the form of the afflictions and so forth, he is designated as "Great Hatred" and the "Great Foe."
Therefore, "sattva" refers to the Bodhisattva.

Since he is the one who, by conquering delusion (*moha*), performs the "eating"—which consists of the non-emission of bliss—of the seminal essence (*śukra*) known as the moon-nectar (*candrāmṛta*) at the time [of union], and since he is designated as "Great Delusion" (*mahāmoha*) because he destroys the delusion of those with deluded minds, he is thus "equal in essence" (*samasattva*).
This is because his yoga is a state of oneness with the vajras of body and so forth, together with the Prajñā’s reflection and the imperishable drops (*bindu*).
Because he has conquered anger, he is the Great Wrathful One (*mahākrodhin*); because he has conquered Māra, he is designated as the enemy of the enraged Māra; thus is the Vajrayoga.
Since that Time is great bliss, for that reason the Blessed One, through that means, does not abandon the internal wheel called *cakra* for the sake of sentient beings.
For this very reason, he is called Kālacakra because, having liberated sentient beings, he is the Great Lust who destroys perishable lust.
In the six-spoked wheel consisting of the six channels, these [deities] such as Vajrasattva and the others are each of six types.
Among them, at the spoke below in the form of Śaṅkhinī is imperishable gnosis (akṣara-jñāna).
On the southern spoke in the form of the *rasanā* is imperishable sensation (*vedanā*);
on the upper spoke in the form of *avadhūtī* is imperishable consciousness (*vijñāna*);
and on the western spoke in the form of the *viṇṇāḍī* is the imperishable form (*rūpa*).

The six aggregates (*ṣaṭskandha*) are as follows: the refinement of syllables (*akṣarasaṃskāra*) in the eastern spoke in the form of the urinary channel (*mūtranāḍī*), and the designation of syllables (*akṣarasaṃjñā*) in the northern spoke called *lalanā*. These are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 73)
The six sense bases are Khaṇḍakapāla and the others, who are the six universal monarchs (*ṣaḍ-cakravartin*). (Vajrāvalī-ṭīkā, p. 67).
The six destinies (*ṣad-gati*) are the destinies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, asuras, and gods. (Viśuddhiprakaraṇa, p. 256).
The six philosophical systems (*ṣaḍdarśana*) are said to be the six systems: Brahmanism, Īśvaravāda, Arhatvāda, Bauddhavāda, Lokāyata, and Sāṃkhya. (Do. Ko. Vyā., p. 72).
The six mudrās.
The wheel, earrings, necklace, bracelet, girdle, ashes, and sacred thread—these are the six mudrās (Vi.pra., p.
186). The sixth Jina, the sixth Victor Vajrasattva, is designated as the substance.
Therefore, because it arises from that,
[it is so called] by metaphorically applying the name of the effect to the cause.
...The sixth is Vajrasattva.
Because it is the cause of its arising, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) itself is designated as Vajrasattva, by way of metaphorically applying the name of the effect to the cause.
By means of that [thought], which serves as a defining characteristic—
But the bodhicitta should not be directed toward the arising of the lotus of wisdom,
for in that case great bliss would not occur.
And so it is said in the Ādibuddha:

But when the bodhicitta, the treasury of all accomplishments, has fallen, and when the consciousness of the aggregates has fainted, how can there be irreproachable accomplishment? (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p. 6). The sixteen compassions.
The bright fortnight is the moon, which is skillful means.
...Compassion is threefold: that which has sentient beings as its object, that which has phenomena as its object, and that which is without an object.
Among those, the five lunar days beginning with the eleventh, up to the full moon, have sentient beings as their object.
Between the end of the full moon and the entry into the first day of the dark fortnight lies the sixteenth, Karuṇā. (Vi.pra., p.
21) These are the sixteen principles (*ṣoḍaśatattva*).
the emanation body, the emanation speech, and the emanation mind.
the wisdom of emanation;
the enjoyment body,
and the enjoyment speech;
the enjoyment mind,
the enjoyment gnosis;
the dharma body;
The speech of Dharma, the mind of Dharma,
and the knowledge of Dharma together constitute the body.
Innate speech,
innate mind,
and innate gnosis— these are the sixteen principles categorized according to the divisions of bliss, supreme, cessation, and the innate.
For those born from a womb, [the cakras] possess obscurations because they release sixteen half-and-half drops (*bindu*).
For the Buddhas, they are without obscuration because they maintain sixteen half-and-half drops. (Vi.pra., pp. 20–21).
These are the sixteen emptinesses (*śūnyatā*).
emptiness of the internal,
emptiness of the external,
and emptiness of the internal and external;
great emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness,
and the emptiness of the ultimate truth;
emptiness of conditioned phenomena, emptiness of unconditioned phenomena,
and absolute emptiness;
emptiness without beginning or end, emptiness of non-dispersal,
and emptiness of specific characteristics;
emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of all phenomena, and emptiness of non-existence;
The emptiness of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*). (He. Ta. Ṭī., p.
36a) The dark fortnight is the sun, which is wisdom (*prajñā*).
... There are three divisions of emptiness: emptiness (*śūnyatā*),...
Great emptiness and ultimate emptiness.
Therein, the emptiness of the five aggregates corresponds to the five lunar days beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight.
Great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) consists of the fivefold emptiness, which are the five lunar days beginning with the sixth;
ultimate emptiness (*paramārthaśūnyatā*) consists of the emptiness of the five sense faculties, which are the five lunar days beginning with the eleventh.
Thus, there are fifteen lunar days, corresponding to the fifteen emptinesses, extending up to the new moon (*amā*).
Between the conclusion of the new moon day and the entry into the first day of the bright fortnight, there is the sixteenth emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in all its aspects (*sarvākārā*).
There are sixteen joys (*ānanda*), and those joys are sixteen according to their divisions. (Vi.pra., p. 21)
In that context, "desires" refers to the bliss of the body; "bliss" refers to the bliss of speech; and "trembling" refers to the bliss of the mind.
By the designation "syllable" (akṣara), there is the bliss of gnosis (jñānānanda).
Thus, by this group of four, the yoga of bliss is one.
Likewise, "full" (pūrṇā) refers to the supreme bliss of the body (kāyaparamānanda).
Here, the triad beginning with *paramānanda* (supreme bliss) corresponds, respectively, to speech, mind, and gnosis-vajra (*jñānavajra*).
Therefore, *paramānanda* is the supreme bliss of speech;
that which arises from it is the supreme bliss of mind (*cittaparamānanda*).
"Power" (śakti) is the supreme bliss of knowledge;
this is the second yoga.
"Flame" (jvālā) is the cessation-bliss of the body.
"Viramānanda" refers to the cessation-bliss of speech;
"ghūrṇa" refers to the cessation-bliss of mind;
and "bindu" refers to the cessation-bliss of gnosis.
Thus is the third yoga: likewise, *oṃ ṇṭrā* is the innate bliss of body (*kāya-sahajānanda*); *sahajānanda* is the innate bliss of speech (*vāk-sahajānanda*);
and *nidrā* is the innate bliss of mind (*citta-sahajānanda*).
"Nāda" refers to the innate bliss of gnosis (*jñānasahajānanda*).
Thus, the body is fourfold;
the body is divided into four types by way of the distinction between the emanation, enjoyment, dharma, and essential bodies (*nirmāṇa-sambhoga-dharma-svābhāvika-bheda*).
Speech is fourfold,
mind is fourfold, and gnosis is fourfold.
Thus, the sixteen varieties of bliss are to be seen in detail in the *Śrītantra* (*Se. Ṭī.*, p. 27).
The two truths: first, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
And the second is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Thus, there are two truths: namely, conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 71)
The seven precious gems (Dharmasaṃgraha, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya, Vol. 1, p. 335).
The seven jewels are ruby, sapphire, lapis lazuli, emerald, diamond, pearl, and coral. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p.
78). The seven ornaments, the five topics, the introduction, and the fourfold logic.
The explanation has six points, and the narrative is fourfold.

The fifth has two divisions, the sixth possesses five divisions, and the seventh should have two divisions; such, in brief, are the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*). (Guṇasārasaṃgraha, p. 2) 1. Introduction (*upodghāta*; fivefold).
What is the name of this treatise, for what purpose was it composed,
who is its author, what is its authority, and what is its purpose?
The name of the tantra shall be its designation; the sign is for those people possessed of passion;
Vajrasattva is its author, and its extent is now proclaimed.
Furthermore, it consists of four types— pariccheda, kalpa, khaṇḍa, and paṭala— and these may also be distinguished by their length in terms of both textual content and number.

The purpose, moreover, is mathematics, the ritual procedures for pacification and so forth, the eight supernatural accomplishments (*siddhis*), and even supreme Buddhahood. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 2).
2. Logic (*nyāya*, fourfold).
Continuity, the causal basis, etymological derivation, and also the cause.
Birth among humans is called "origination," while the departure from the midst of the harem is the sequence of the causal basis.
Restraint as taught in the Vinaya is called "etymological definition" (nirukti);
one who practices the Dharma while desiring its fruit is said to be "the cause."
This fourfold method is intended for the doctrine of detachment;
now, for the sake of clarifying the meaning, I shall explain it according to the system of passion.
The arising of the five Buddha families is called the "continuum" (santāna);
furthermore, the state of being of a single family and its causal basis have been demonstrated.

The inclusion of the *vajra* and so forth is called "etymological explanation" (*nirukti*); the practice through the erotic and other aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) is designated as the "cause" (*hetu*). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, pp. 2–3). 3. The Explanation According to the Six Parameters (*ṣaṭkoṭika-vyākhyāna*).

Because the mantras consist of mind, because they are purified from the body, and because they are carried by yoga, one should enter the six points after gradually understanding the meanings of the five clusters. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 1)
And there is the six-cornered exposition (*ṣaṭkoṭika-vyākhyāna*). Furthermore, the third ornament is the determination of the six-cornered words;
it is taught in the system of Yoga Tantra and awakens the meaning that was previously sealed.
Through the distinctions of intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*), non-intentional language, provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), and definitive meaning (*nītārtha*),
as well as literal expression (*yathāruta*) and non-literal expression, it is proclaimed as having six points (*ṣaṭkoṭi*).
The Jina speaks with provisional meaning for those who are obscured and unfortunate;
he speaks again with definitive meaning to reveal the reality that truly exists.
The revelation of the reality of phenomena to beings of superior inclination through the employment of contradictory speech— that is what is called "intentional language" (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*).
In the ritual manuals for mandalas and the like, as well as in the various modes of conduct,
the explicit explanation of the meaning according to its respective context is that which is spoken according to the literal expression (*yathāruta*).
Words such as *koṭākhyaka* and others, which are excluded from both worldly usage and the treatises, are the conventions of the Tathāgatas; that is proclaimed to be non-ordinary speech (*naruta*).

"For the sake of awakening sentient beings with dull faculties, the very clear exposition of reality is called 'the manifest' (*vyakta*), not 'intentional speech' (*sandhyā-bhāṣita*). (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p.
3) "It is neither intentional speech nor that which is expressed in intentional language; it is neither the interpretable meaning nor that which is to be interpreted."
"In the Yoga Tantra, there are indeed six points: that which is according to the literal word (*yathāruta*), and that which is not according to the literal word. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p.
10). 4. The fourfold explanation: the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*), the complete member (*samastāṅga*), the hidden (*garbha*), and furthermore, the ultimate (*kolika*).

The first [type] should be only one, while the second has two varieties consisting of all its constituent parts (*aṅga*). The *garbhin* is known to be threefold, and the *kolika* is considered to be twofold.
Many who know the external scriptures are devoted solely to the literal word.
In order to illuminate the method for its mastery, the literal meaning is now being declared.
For those who have taken refuge in the sūtras and other scriptures, this is revealed as the complete set of limbs, through the removal of regret and by means of the yoga of the generation stage.
It is called "the womb" because it contains within it the revelation of the dharma of passion;
it is the discernment of the three types of knowledge regarding the realization of the truth of conventional reality.
The luminous radiance and the awakening to the union (*yuganaddha*): these two are declared to be the *kolika* [level]. *Kola* signifies the ultimate limit (*paryanta*). (Guhyasiddhiprakāśa, p.
3). 5. Exegesis (*vyākhyāna*) [is twofold].
The speaker may wish to cause [the teaching] to be heard further through two types of divisions:
the first is designated as the "sacrificial exposition" (satravyākhyāna), and the second is the "exposition for disciples" (śiṣyākhyāna).
One should not apply literal meaning, nor intentional terminology, nor even the interpretable meaning;
rather, the explanation of the tantra is said to consist of the literal sense of the syllables together with all its constituent parts.
The literal meaning, the definitive meaning, as well as the intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā),
the hidden meaning, and the collective meaning— these are intended for the explanation to disciples.
Relying upon the two stages, the various explanations were demonstrated by the Tathāgatas for those to be trained, in accordance with the explanatory tantras. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p.
4) 6. The Fivefold Typology of Persons (The Sixth Ornament).
In this world, there are always five types of persons who, born of destiny, seek to hear [the Dharma]; they are equalized by virtue of their diverse mental dispositions.
The *ratnacandana*, the *padma*, the *puṇḍarīka*, and likewise the *utpala*—
these are designated by different names by their very nature, and they have been so described by the Omniscient One.
One who is skilled in retention may forget everything they have heard in an instant, as was the case with the well-known person Utpala.
Having heard much and abundant scripture to be grasped, the person named Puṇḍarīka is unable to manifest it further, like a small water-pot or cotton.
One who possesses faith, compassion for living beings, and an expansive heart through learning is a person renowned as a "lotus-like" individual, being as permeable as a jointless bamboo reed.
One who has heard little, yet is full of ego and speaks much without foundation—
the person known as "sandalwood"— is unable to bestow grace.
Virtuous, pure, skillful, wise, and single-minded;
having heard [the teaching], he proclaims it correctly—such is the renowned jewel-like person (ratnapudgala).
He is like the white lotus, the blue lotus, the red lotus, and the sandalwood tree.
For these four individuals are persons who provide discourses and explanations on the sūtras.
Capable of the yoga of the completion stage and adorned with virtuous conduct,
this person named Ratnapudgala is a worthy vessel for the explanation of the teachings to disciples.

Having thus examined who is a worthy recipient and who is not, by means of the distinction of knowledge regarding individuals, the wise Vajrācārya should provide a twofold explanation. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p.
4) 7. The Seventh Ornament.
Through these six ornaments, there is the determination of the two truths;

this is indeed the seventh ornament, which is the accomplishment of the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 5) This is the application of equanimity (*samatāyoga*).

The yoga of equality for the Lord of Yogins is indeed the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) which possesses a single nature. (Candrakīrti’s *Vyākhyā*, p. 158). *Samaya* refers to the commitments (*samaya*) consisting of mantra, tantra, mudrā, and so forth.
(Vajrāvalī, p. 180):
Pervasion in all directions through the yoga of radiation is the *samaya*.
Proceeding through the three realms by means of various forms according to the needs of those to be trained is the *samaya*. (Hevajra-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 3b)
The fourfold commitment (*samayacatuṣṭaya*) refers to the four commitments stated in the fifth chapter (pp. 47–48), beginning with: “And living beings are to be slain by you” (16.59).
This is to be understood through the explanation of the *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (twilight language). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p.
193) The vow beginning with "the seizing of another's property" (16.95) is found in the ninth chapter (p. 84).
This has been explained in the *Sandhyābhāṣā* (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 202):
"The *samaya-maṇḍala*—the *samaya* is Mahāvajradhara."
Its essence is the core ritual procedure (*vidhi*);
because it takes up or grasps that, it is called the *samayamaṇḍala*. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 94). [This refers to] the *samayamudrā*.

The manifestation of Vajradhara in the form of Heruka for the sake of sentient beings—by way of the nature of the *sambhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, and by way of a transparent form—is designated as the *samayamudrā*.

Having taken up that *samayamudrā* in the form of a wheel, one should conceptualize the fivefold gnosis in five ways: through the mirror-like, the equality, the discerning, the all-accomplishing, and the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu* [wisdoms].

The masters meditate upon the wheel of the pledge-mudrās (*samayamudrā*) by means of the initial yoga (*ādiyoga*), the glorious king of the mandala (*maṇḍalarājāśri*), the glorious king of activity (*karmarājāśri*), the yoga of the drop (*binduyoga*), and the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*). (Abhisamayamañjarī, p. 35) The pledge-vajra (*samayavajra*) is Amoghasiddhi.
In this context, however, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, who is absorbed in reality (*tattva*), is intended by the term "Samayavajra" (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p.
17). A *samayasattva* is so called because he is constantly engaged in the commitment (*samaya*) (Hevajratantra 1.1.5).
In the vow of the *samaya*, one should consume the *samaya* substance there while remaining concentrated,
[uttering] "Nādi," "Gādi," "Hādi," "Antaśva," and "Mādiśva" (Hevajra Tantra 1.11.8).
Whatever one performs is his *samaya*;
whatever one does not perform is his *saṃvara*. (HeTaṬī, p. 23a). Regarding *samaya*, [it refers to] the consumption of cow-flesh and so forth. (HeTaṬī, p. 67a).
"Samarasa" is said to mean equal, uniform, and identical; its essence is known as the Wheel (*cakra*).
However, "samarasa" is also spoken of in the sense of having a single state of being (*ekabhāva*). (Hevajra Tantra 1.8.40; Samāja-siddhi 2.4)
The meaning of the word *samāja* is the union of the two; this is the literal sense (*akṣarārtha*).
The union of the moon and the lotus is the *samāja* (assembly), which is the complete body (*samastāṅga*).
The union of wisdom and means is the *samāja*, which is the embryo (*garbha*).
The union of the conventional and ultimate truths is the *samāja*; it is the *kolika* [meaning]. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, 21–22) *Samāja*.
"In brief, the mind has the form of an assembly (*samāja*).

In brief, because all phenomena have a single form—that is, the form of great bliss—the mind is the *bodhicitta*; thus, it is said that the mind "has the form of an assembly. Alternatively, knowledge (*jñāna*) in the form of the *dharmamudrā*, the *mahāmudrā*, and the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is truly designated as "assembly" (*samāja*). (Ārya-va-jra-saṃgraha, p. 35)
Through the meditative absorption of wisdom and means, one should briefly withdraw all phenomena into a single mass and visualize the image in the center.
The instantaneous perfection of gnosis is called *samādhi* (Se. Ṭī., p. 31). Through mastery over *samādhi*, there arises a state free from obscuration (Se.

Ṭī., p. 31). By means of the union of wisdom and method, through the sequence beginning with the generation stage (*utpannakrama*), when the lotus of the void has arisen, by virtue of immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*), one becomes unified with the object of knowledge and the knowing subject; thus, in the state of stainless purity, all phenomena appear as mere reflections.

Having briefly and concisely withdrawn—that is, dissolved—all stationary and moving beings into a single form consisting of the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) whose nature is supreme untainted great bliss (*paramānāśrava-mahāsukha*), just as the essence of all metallic ores and minerals is transformed into a single form of perfected elixir (*siddhirasa*), one should meditate upon—that is, visualize—the image (*bimba*) whose nature is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) within that luminosity which has the single flavor of supreme untainted great bliss. ...The instantaneous accomplishment and realization of gnosis (*jñāna*), which is the non-duality of the two truths, is called "samādhi. (Se. Ṭī., pp. 33–34)
In this context, the imperishable bliss that arises from the oneness of the mind of the apprehended and the apprehender is called "samādhi.
Mastery over that [bliss], immovability from it, and consequently, the state of being free from obscurations would come to be.

The meaning is that from the mere mastery of the luminous gnosis (*prabhāsvara-jñāna*), which is characterized by the supreme unchanging gnosis (*paramākṣara-jñāna*), the state of being free from obscurations (*nirāvaraṇatā*) occurs.

At a time subsequent to that, the realization of meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—which consists of the true method (*bhūtanaya*) characterized by the non-duality of the two truths—becomes the fruit. (Se. Ṭī., p.
34–35) Meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is so called because one is concentrated (*samādhīyate*) or established within the mind. (Gu. Sa. Pra., p. 115)

The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) is that which, having brought forth those phenomena through the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), establishes them in the mind by setting aside all other internal essences;
that is the faculty of concentration. (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p. 54)
Superimposition (*samāropa*) is the cultivation of Mahāmudrā, which is unstained by the blemish of all conceptual constructions; this is superimposition. (Se. Ṭī., p.
48/3) This is the path of accumulation (*saṃbhāramārga*).
In that regard, what is the path of equipment? It consists of twelve factors.
What are the twelve?
The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases of psychic power (va. ti. ṭī., p. 51).
The sambhogakāya is the sixteen-petalled lotus located in the middle of the throat; the throat-cakra is the sambhogakāya. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 78)
Moreover, because they bestow the enjoyment of the nectar of the Dharma and because of their extreme delight [in it]—(Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
78)—the Sambhoga [body] resides in the sixteen-spoked [wheel]. (Vajratilaka, p.
78) In the center of the Saṃbhogacakra, however, is the syllable Oṃ, the illuminator of all phonemes.

Surrounded on all sides by the four digits (*kalā*), when the moon resides in the throat in the form of Great Passion (*mahārāga*), that is declared to be the *saṃbhoga* body, the supreme body of the Buddhas. (Vajra-tantra, pp. 79; 81–82)

Regarding the natural purity of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaprakṛtipariśuddhatā*): immediately after the cultivation of the four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one should contemplate the natural purity of all phenomena— bringing to mind such thoughts as, "All these phenomena are pure by nature in their own essence," and "I, too, am pure by nature."

One should reinforce this very purity of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaprakṛtipariśuddhatā*) by means of the mantra: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho 'ham*. (Sā. Mā., pp. 57–58).
Following the cultivation of the four divine abodes (*caturbrahmavihāra*), one should cultivate the purity of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
All phenomena whatsoever are pure by their very nature and by their own essence.

One should bring to mind [the realization] beginning with "I too am naturally pure," and should consecrate this natural purity of all phenomena with this mantra: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho 'ham* ("Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature").
This is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*).
Having brought to manifestation the intrinsic purity of the nature of all phenomena, one should meditate on the emptiness of all phenomena.
In this regard, this is emptiness: all this is merely mind, appearing as various forms whose essence is luminosity;
just as in a dream, there exists nothing external to the mind that can be grasped by the mind.
Due to the absence of an object of apprehension, the mind as the subject of apprehension also does not exist.
Consequently, all phenomena have the nature of the mind;
their reality is the emptiness of the entire conceptual proliferation consisting of the duality of subject and object, and so forth.
This refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The meaning is as follows: one should contemplate that the entire world, including all moving and stationary beings, consists solely of the light of non-duality (*advaita-prakāśa-mātra*).

One should then consecrate this very emptiness (*śūnyatā*) with the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako 'ham* ("Oṃ, I am of the nature of the diamond of the wisdom of emptiness"). (Sā. Mā., p. 58)
Having contemplated the natural purity of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaprakṛtipariśuddhatā*), one should contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*).

In this regard, emptiness is as follows: one should reflect that the entire universe, including the moving and the non-moving, consists solely of the manifestation of variegated non-duality, which is free from the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of all imaginings such as the grasped and the grasper.
One should empower this very emptiness with the following mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* ("Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness"). (Sādhanamālā, p. 204)
Then, having grasped all phenomena with the mind, one should investigate them:
"This is merely the mind appearing deluded in various forms;

just as in a dream there is no object external to the mind because of the absence of apprehended and apprehender, so too the mind itself becomes the apprehender. Therefore, all phenomena have the mind as their essence."

Having ascertained with absolute certainty that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of these [phenomena] is the emptiness of the grasped and the grasper, one should abandon the forms of all phenomena—which are the signs of delusion superimposed by error—and perceive their very nature alone:
characterized solely by non-dual representation (*advaya-vijñapti*), resembling pure crystal, like the cloudless midday sky in autumn, infinite.
This is called supramundane knowledge of emptiness, free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).
Then one should empower it with the mantra: *oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness*.
She herself is the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā; she herself is the supreme protection. (Sādhanamālā, pp. 225–226). [The mustard seed.]
With mustard seeds, which are drops of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p.
192) That which is innate (*sahaja*), being real, is designated as "innate" because it conforms to the shadow of the innate.
The shadow of the coemergent (*sahaja*) brings about knowledge that resembles the coemergent. "Coemergent" refers to the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*).
For this very reason, there is no arising of the coemergent from wisdom-knowledge.
Because that which is called "the innate" (*sahaja*) is the uncontrived intrinsic nature of all phenomena—that is to say, their specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
... The masters, having attained the wisdom of insight through their skillfulness and considering that they have experienced the innate, give rise to satisfaction.
Even those who are contented and virtuous do not know even the news of the *dharmamudrā*.
Without knowing the *dharmamudrā*, how can unartificial knowledge known as the *sahaja* arise through the mere artificial *karmamudrā*?
From a cause of the same nature, only an effect of the same nature arises.
But not from a heterogeneous cause;
just as a rice sprout arises from a rice seed, but not one of *kodrava* grain.
Likewise, from the uncontrived *dharmamudrā*, the uncontrived innate (*sahaja*) arises.
...The lotus of the *karmāṅganā* is a jewel-mine of the mass of blisses.
When that clear abode, through the union of the essences of the *bola* and *kakkola*, becomes contained within the *maṇi* of the conventional bodhicitta via the *avadhūtī*, [the innate arises].
Then, another knowledge called "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) and known as "innate" (*sahaja*) arises. (A.V.S. pp.
32–33) Having cast the *bolaka* into the *kakkola*, the observer of the vow produces the *kunduru*;
in that [state], the camphor arising from yoga is remembered as the innate (*sahaja*). (Do. Ko. Vyā., p. 69)

"Indeed, the stabilization of the mind in the *mahāsukhacakra* through the cultivation of the *caṇḍālī-yoga* is the cause for the manifestation of the innate (*sahaja*). In the thorough knowledge of the innate, there is no other liberation whatsoever. ...
All those various collections of liberations imagined separately by others are nothing other than the innate itself. (Do. Ko. Vyā., p. 71)
...and not knowing the innate (*sahaja*), they wander in saṃsāra like a water-wheel.
And that [innate] is attained by one who has taken refuge in a true guru.
In that regard, within the innate, there are the signified and the signifier.
They are not obtained—
the innate [nature] does not exist within the three [realms] due to the relationship between the signified and the signifier;
it was established by the Blessed One in certain places through the application of the stages of teaching.
While the book is being observed for the sake of sentient beings, there is no consciousness [of it as such];
whatever object one may see is merely a conceptualization of the form of error and so forth.
"That respective object would not be seen as non-delusory through the lineage of the Guru.
... Whatever commentary on the scriptures, Purāṇas, and so forth is composed, all of that pertains only to the *sahaja* (the Innate), and not to anything else. (Dohākoṣavyākhyā, pp. 86–87)
"There is one supreme reality that is innate" (*Dohakośavyākhyā*, p. 155).
"From that [reality], the innate has a twofold nature" (*Hevajratantra* 1.8.27; *Sampuṭa-sādhana* 1.5).
"The innate is fourfold because of the perspective of the Arisen Stage" (*Hevajratantra* 1.8.30; *Sampuṭa-sādhana* 1.8).
"Spontaneously born [reality] is devoid of these. (HeTa 1.8.34) "The spontaneously born is not described by another, nor is it found in anything else;
it is known by oneself through merit and service to the lineage of gurus. (HeTa 1.8.36; SaSi 1.15)
The innate (*sahaja*) is the nature unmarked by the stains of defects in both *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa* (HeTaṬī p. 31b).
"Innate" refers to the awakening that is innate bliss (HeTaṬī p.

39a). That which is produced through the internal *prajñā* and *upāya*, which are themselves innate, and which possesses the characteristic of being free from outflows—that is the innate, expressed by the term "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*) (HeTaṬī p. 41a).
Emptiness has the characteristic of non-arising, and that itself is supreme wisdom (*prajñā*).
That which is inseparable from these two, characterized by luminosity, is expressed by the term "ultimate bodhicitta" (*pāramārthikasambodhicitta*). (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 41b)
The "intrinsic nature" (*prakṛti*) of phenomena is a synonym for the "innate" (*sahaja*).
"There is neither passion nor dispassion, nor is a middle state perceived;
by the very avoidance of these three, the innate is called awakening. (Hevajra Tantra 1.10.17)
"Variegated, known as the waveless and the innate" (Hevajra Tantra 1.10.34).
"The waveless one is the self of the essential nature; it is established throughout the entire body...
that which is produced within the innate state is proclaimed as the 'innate' (*sahaja*)."
"Intrinsic nature is said to be innate (*sahaja*), the single vow of all aspects" (Hevajra Tantra 1.10.41).
"Therefore, the entire world is innate; innate is what is called one's own true nature" (Hevajra Tantra 2.2.44). This is the Innate Body (*sahajakāya*).

That very Blessed One, in the system of Mantra characterized by the fruit, is called Sahajānanda and Sahajakāya; free from subject and object, transcending the nature of consciousness, and non-abiding in either cyclic existence or nirvāṇa, he is the assembly (*samāja*) of the Buddhas and the enclosure (*saṃvara*) of the Goddesses—the body of the innate (*sahaja*). (Vi.pra., p. 43)

Inner knowledge is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), naturally luminous, the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) whose form is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); this state, full of the outflow of the *dharmadhātu*, is called the "innate body" (*sahajatanu*).
The drop (*bindu*) becomes emptiness. (Se. Ṭī., p. 69)
And that drop, being unemitted, is called the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*).
The supreme syllable is also the letter *A*.
The Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), who arises from the letter *A*, is Vajrasattva, whose nature is wisdom and means; he is called the neuter state, the Innate Body (*sahajakāya*).
"And that Blessed Kālacakra is the supreme immutable state of bliss" (Se.
Ṭī., p. 69). "Saṃvara is the gathering of all elements, the meeting, the assembly; thus it is 'saṃvara'" (Se. Ṭī., p. 26).

The restraint (*saṃvara*) of those external and coarse [elements] which a yogi would determine to have entered within himself—because they are restrained (*saṃvṛta*) and because they are gathered together (*saṃkṣepa*)—is the consecration (*seka*). (He. Ta.
Ṭī., p. 6a) Restraint (*saṃvara*) is the consecration (*seka*). (He. Ta. Ṭī., p. 7a)
Conventional reality is inquiry;
conventional reality is the proliferation of speech. (A.K. 64, 78)
Similarity is similarity; just as the reflection of a face cast upon a mirror is not the face itself,
it was not established previously, nor is it established now.
That very reflection of the face produces only a semblance;
nevertheless, people, thinking "I have seen my own face," become satisfied through delusion. (Avataṃsaka-sūtra, pp. 32–33).
Sādhumatī.
The cremation ground is on the back of the fingers and feet, because it is the nature of all sacred seats (pīṭha) and because of the experience of the states of conceptual construction.
That very [ground] is Sādhumatī.
Because selflessness (*nairātmya*) exists therein for the practitioner (*sādhū*). (Vi. Ti. Ṭī., p.
28) Because it carries the phlegm that is the equilibrium of the elements (*dhātusāmya*), it is common to the secret place. (Va. Ti. Ṭī., p. 46)
"Sālijam mahāmāṃsam" means that which is produced from *sāli* is called *sālija*. (He. Ta. 2.3.60).
It is accomplished.

The production of sweat is established in all cases during meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). Because it flows through them, it is established in the two calves; or rather, it is so called because they have jurisdiction over the production of the signs of accomplishment (*siddhinimitta*). (Vajrayoginī-ṭīkā, p. 46). Accomplishment (*siddhi*).
"Worldly accomplishment" (*laukikasiddhi*) refers to sovereignty extending as far as the Akaniṣṭha realm.

"Supreme accomplishment" (*uttarasiddhi*) refers to the state of perfect buddhahood (*samyaksaṃbuddhatva*), attained through the realization of the twelve stages (*dvādaśabhūmi*) by means of abandoning all obscurations of the afflictions, the knowable, and meditative absorption, along with their latent predispositions (*savāsana*).
Accomplishment (*siddhi*) is the state of being the lord of the three realms (*traidhātukeśvaratva*). (Se. Ṭī., p. 3; Se., p. 47)
Accomplishment is threefold: superior, middling, and inferior. Among these, invisibility is the superior, and the sight of treasures buried in the earth is the middling.
Subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) is the lowest accomplishment (*siddhi*). (Guṇabhadra’s *Siddhasārasvata-prakriyā*, p. 222). The eightfold group of accomplishments consists of:
collyrium, pills, sandals, efficacious herbs, jewels, mantras, yakṣīs, and the power of entering another's body. (Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p. 27).
"Sindhu" refers to the back of the foot. (Vajratilaka, p.
25). Because the *bodhicitta* pulsates from the back of the foot to the big toe, "Sindhu" is the back of the foot. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 34).
In Sindh, she is known as Mahābalā, and as Śaśokā and Aśruvāhinī (Vajratilaka, p.
47). Sihlakam is [the name of] Svayambhū; sihlaka is to be understood [as such] (Hevajra Tantra 2.3.59).
The bliss born of the two organs is known as the reality of the passionate gods;
the bliss of the Buddhas is imperishable and free from the conduct of the three worlds.
Released from laughter, glances, and the like; free from all dualities;
devoid of cause and effect; appearing as the three worlds yet non-dual; ...
non-abiding like space, all-pervading, and devoid of defining characteristics.
Thus has been described that supreme reality, the unsurpassed Vajra-knowledge:
non-abiding like space, all-pervasive, devoid of defining characteristics,
indefinable, and formless— this is the characteristic of reality.
That which is like the pure sky is perceived by the Victors as if it were covered by objects, due to those clouded by the cataract of ignorance—just as [the sky] might be obscured by moons.
Bliss is black; bliss is yellow; bliss is red; bliss is white.
Bliss is dark, bliss is blue; bliss is the entire world of the moving and the unmoving.
Wisdom is bliss, the means is bliss, and likewise the *kunduru* is bliss;
existence is bliss, non-existence is bliss, and Vajrasattva is known as bliss. (Hevajra Tantra 2.2.32–33) Suḥkhāvatī.

The buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitābha is called Sukhāvatī; here, however, the "blisses" (*bhaga*) of selflessness and so forth are the "abbreviations of Sukhāvatī," because they protect unsurpassed bliss. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 46b)

"I shall dwell in Sukhāvatī, within the bhaga of the true Vajra-woman, in the form of the letter E, in that jewel-casket of the Buddha. (HeTa 2.2.38) "In the bhaga of the woman, in Sukhāvatī. (HeTa 2.2.41)

In the Sukhāvatī of the female *kakkola*, which has the nature of the syllable *evaṃkāra*, it is called "Sukhāvatī" precisely because of the protection (*rakṣaṇa*) of bliss. (Hevajra Tantra 2.4.30–31) —
Sucandra.

To the north of the Śītā River, in the great realm of Śambhala consisting of ninety-six million villages, dwells the sovereign lord, whose lotus feet are saluted by the lords of millions upon millions of villages— born from the lineages of ninety-six great royal families of gods, asuras, and nāgas, and bound with crowns of great jewels— and who, through the abandonment of the sixteen kalās of obscuration, acts as the listener to all Tathāgatas by means of gathering the Dharmas spoken by the Tathāgatas in the various languages of all sentient beings.
Because he possesses the radiance of the stainless moon, he is both beautiful and the moon; thus, Sucandra is the Lord of Secrets, the illustrious Vajrapāṇi, who dwells in Āḍhakavatī.
King Sucandra, his emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), makes this request.
As it is said in the Root Tantra:
The Bodhisattvas, gods, and others, seated upon their respective thrones, sought to hear the meaning of the Mantra Vehicle from the Buddha, the leader of the three worlds. ...
That teaching of the Mantra Vehicle which was previously given by Dīpaṅkara...
Today, that duty which ought to have been performed has indeed been accomplished for us by the virtuous Gautama.
Now, therefore, Sucandra the king— known as Śambhala and emanated by Vajrapāṇi— arrived at the Dharmadhātu of the glory of the True Dharma.
First, having performed a circumambulation of the Teacher’s two lotus-feet,
and having worshipped them with jewel-flowers, one should prostrate again and again.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he stood before the Perfectly Awakened One; there, Candra was the requester of the Teacher and the compiler of the collection. (Se.
Ṭī., p. 2) In the Vajrayāna, the Great Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the lord of great yakṣas residing in Aḍakavatī, is the requester of the Tathāgata and the compiler of the collection.

How is it that Sucandra, born from the womb of Queen Vijayā, became the requester [of the teaching] for Sūryaprabha, the sovereign of the village of Kalāpa in the realm of Sambhala? (Vi.pra., p. 22, 24).
Sudurjayā is the mouth and the throat; these are the two *chandoha* sites.
Because the activity of desire proceeds toward the enjoyment of flavors;
that very [desire] is extremely difficult to conquer, since it is impossible to turn one away from flavors. (Vasubandhu’s Commentary on the *Triṃśikā*, p. 28)
Subhadra is so called because he causes the wick of the qualities that provide nourishment through happiness to proceed; thus, Subhadra. (Vṛtti-Ṭippaṇī-Ṭīkā, p. 49) Subhadrā.
Subhadrā is she whose satisfaction is beautiful, auspicious, and beneficial. (Vajracchedikā-ṭīkā, p. 47) Subhadrā is the power of wisdom. (Vajracchedikā, p. 55) She is well-minded.
She is *sumanā* because she produces mental well-being (*saumanasya*) for yogins through her saliva (*kheṭa*), [as stated in] the *Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā*, p.
46. She is *surābhakṣī* because she consumes *surā*, that is, nectar (*sudhā*).
The fire of knowledge (*jñānolau*). (Vajravatī-ṭīkā, p.
47) The power of memory (*smṛtibalaṃ*) is Surābhakṣī. (Vajravatī, p. 55) [She is] Surāvairī.
The enemy of the gods (*surāṇām*) is the enemy of the sinews (*snāyūnām*); it proceeds from the left ear and is thus the "enemy of the gods" (*surāvairī*). (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
48) Suvarṇadvīpa:
This pair of shanks is like an island (*dvīpam*) for the gold—that is, for the mind (*citta*) which possesses a very white luster. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 34)
The two shanks are renowned as Suvarṇadvīpa (the Golden Island). (Vajratilaka, p.
35) The channel that carries perspiration is situated in Suvarṇadvīpa;
she is considered to be Cakravarmiṇī, whose limbs are agitated and intensely radiant. (Vajratilaka, p. 46)
*Suvīrā* is so called because she originates from the excellent (*su*) act of heroism (*vīra*). (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 48).
*Suvīrā* is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*). (Vajratilaka, p. 55).
"Sūkṣmā" means subtle, because it carries the extremely fine hairs of the head; it is of a subtle form at the crest [of the flame]. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
44). "Sūtrānta" refers to a follower of the Sūtra school (Sautrāntika).

"Sūtrānta" refers to those sūtras that are not extremely profound; these are the Sūtrāntas such as the *Ekagāthā*, *Caturgāthā*, *Upadhāraṇī*, *Ṣaṇmukhī*, *Bhadracaryā*, *Lalitavistara*, *Daśabhūmika*, and so forth.
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 67b–68a)
The sun, the sun is the non-dual gnosis arising from production. (Candrakīrti’s *Commentary on the Madhyamakāvatāra*, p. 49).
The sun.
By the word "sūrya" is meant the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*). (Vi. Pra., p.
196) Here, the *prāṇa*—the lord of the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*—is the *sūrya* that flows upward from the navel. (Vi. Pra., p.
196) The solar channel (*sūryanāḍī*) is the *rasanā*.

The channel that rises upward from above the navel and rests in the middle of the throat is proclaimed to be the carrier of blood. This is the channel called Rasana, which is on the right side. (Vajratilaka-tantra, p. 80)
With its opening facing upwards, it carries blood from the navel up to the throat. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p.
80) It is called *sekha* because by means of it, the body and so forth are sprinkled (*sicyate*) and rendered stainless and free from obscurations; thus it is *sekha*. (Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā, pp. 2–3)

In the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara* as well, only eleven consecrations (*seka*) are taught. For it is said: "First by the water-consecration, second by the crown-consecration, third by the ribbon-consecration, and fourth by the vajra and bell."
The fifth is the name-empowerment by one's own master alone, while the sixth is the empowerment of the Buddha’s command; the seventh empowerment is that of the vase.
The ninth [empowerment] is by means of the secret empowerment, and the tenth is from the wisdom empowerment;
through the application of the reality-vajra, one should bestow all the vajra-words.
"The Teacher himself explains this procedure for consecration;
the preceptor must not be disparaged, nor should one transgress the command of the Sugata. (Se. Ṭī., p. 27).

Thus, because of the Lord’s explicit statement that "the eleventh consecration is the principal one through the application of the Vajra of Reality," scholars should not understand the fourth or the eleventh consecration as being separate [from it].
(Se. Ṭī., p.
28) The names of these four, beginning with *kumbha*, are respectively *kṣara*, *akṣara*, *spanda*, and *niṣpanda*, together with their etymologies;
likewise, they are designated as *bāla*, *prauḍha*, *vṛddha*, and *prajāpati*.

The experience of bliss consisting of physical bliss (*kāyānanda*), verbal bliss (*vāgānanda*), mental bliss (*cittānanda*), and gnosis-bliss (*jñānānanda*), which occurs through the arrival of a stream of white nectar from the four-petaled *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus into the pericarp of the sixteen-petaled lotus at the forehead—
that is the "child" (*bāla*). Because he has received the first consecration, the yogi who is consecrated by the breasts is called a "child."
Then, through the slight vibration of the vajra within her bhaga, the *bodhicitta* descends.

From the thirty-two-petaled lotus of the hands, it reaches the pericarp of the eight-petaled heart-lotus; the experience of bliss consisting of the supreme bliss of body (*kāyaparamānanda*), the supreme bliss of speech (*vākparamānanda*), the supreme bliss of mind (*cittaparamānanda*), and the supreme bliss of gnosis (*jñānaparamānanda*)—because this exceeds the former [stages], it is the "mature" secret initiation (*proḍhau guhyābhiṣeka*).

Then, through intense swinging, having attained vibration (*spanda*), the semen-moon— having traveled from the navel-lotus of sixty-four petals to the secret-lotus of thirty-two petals, and having reached the end of the hollow of the *vajra*-jewel as the clear fluid moving at the tip of the fifteenth lotus known as *spanda*— experiences an intense bliss consisting of the bliss of cessation of body, the bliss of cessation of speech, the bliss of cessation of mind, and the bliss of cessation of gnosis; this is the "mature" (*vṛddha*) initiation of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*).
"Mahāmudrā" is the image arisen from space.

From the passion (*anurāga*) known as the cultivation of its own natural flavor and external [objects], there arises "the motionless" (*niṣpanda*); thus, the external movement of the vajra-jewel is restrained within the *bhaga* by way of non-emitted bliss (*acyuta-sukha*). That lunar nectar (*candrāmṛta*), which consists of the innate joy of body, the innate joy of speech, the innate joy of mind, and the innate joy of gnosis, is the fourth consecration called "Great Gnosis" (*mahājñāna*).

He is the *prajāpati* because, like an accomplished elixir (*siddharasa*), he brings about the transformation of the obscured aggregates, elements, and so forth—into the nature of the five Tathāgatas, the five deities, and so on—just as copper and other metals are transformed into the state of gold by means of the realization of unobscured supramundane gnosis (*nirāvaraṇa-lokottara-jñāna*). (Se. Ṭī., p.

28) It is called *sekha* (consecration/empowerment) because one is sprinkled (*sicyate*) by it for the purpose of washing away the stain of ignorance (*avidyā-mala*), just as external impurity is washed away by external water. (A.V.Saṃ., p. 36)
Vow is initiation.
And so it will be said:
"Initiation is known to be fourfold for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings."

That by which one is sprinkled or bathed is called *seka* (consecration). (He. Ta. Ṭī., p. 7a) *Seke*: [The term] *seka* refers to the two armpits (*bāhumūla*), because it sprinkles the hearts with the essence of nectar (*sudhārasa*). (Va. Ti. Ṭī., p. 44) *Sevā*:
*Sevā* is the taking of refuge in the *bodhiliṅga*. (Gu. Sa. Pra., p. 115)
"Service" (*sevā*) is so called because it is served by those seeking liberation and practiced [by them] (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p.
116). For those established in the supreme means, however, there is the "fourfold vajra," which is the fourfold emptiness;
by means of that, service should be performed (Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā, p. 120).
There is no bliss other than the bodhicitta; there is no other bliss in the three realms.
The bliss consisting of bodhicitta is the source from which all bliss flows forth. (Jñānasiddhi, p. 141)
Saurāṣṭra is the thighs; it is called Saurāṣṭra because it is the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*) of bliss (*saukhya*). (Vajratilaka, p. 34) It is the realm of happiness.
And in the vision of the distinguished time, it is indeed the two thighs [that face] one another. (Vajratilaka, p.
34) In Saurāṣṭra, she who is called Lohitā is considered to be the Ḍākinī Śauṇḍinī. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 46) Stambha.

Stambha (stiffening) is the state of remaining motionless like a piece of wood through a state of stillness, having first removed the ordinary ego-sense of the recipient by means of the possession by a deity. (Guṇasāraprakaraṇa, p.
171) Stobha (shock) consists of leaping, trembling, and whirling. (Guṇasāraprakaraṇa, p. 171)
An elder is one who has reached ten years [of seniority]; [this is] the faculty of mindfulness. (Abhidharmakośavyākhyā, p. 84)

The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) is that by which the dharmas brought forth by the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*) are repeatedly brought before one's mind and are not forgotten. (Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī-ṭīkā, p. 54)
The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are the four foundations of mindfulness named after the recollection of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. However,

the distinction in the Śrāvaka view is that the four foundations of mindfulness are characterized by impermanence, impurity, suffering, and non-self, serving as the antidotes to the four perversions of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self.

In the Mantradarśana, however, the ḍākinīs, whose nature is self-awareness (*svasaṃvid*), should be understood as the *dharmatā* of the body and so forth. (Vajraṭīkā, pp. 52–53) The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are the tongue; the moon of the heart is of the nature of the *lalanā*. (Vajraṭīkā, p. 67)

The *lalanā* and *rasanā*, situated on the left and right [channels], are to be known respectively as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles because they carry substances downward (*adhodravyavāhitvāt*). (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 67).
"Intrinsic nature" and "intrinsic nature itself" are neither real nor false, being unarisen from the beginningless past.
...it is established that the fivefold aspects, being dependently originated, have the nature of the five Tathāgatas;
and since that nature is non-different from emptiness and compassion, it follows that the world is non-different from emptiness and compassion. ...
Precisely because they arise dependently, [all things] are clearly like a city of Gandharvas.
The universe does not abide in intrinsic nature; it is like a lotus in the sky.
And it is said in the *Hevajra* (II.4.34):
"These phenomena are indeed nirvāṇa, yet through delusion they take the form of saṃsāra. (*Abhisamayālaṃkāravṛtti-saṃcaya*, pp. 26–27).
This is the *svabhāvakāya*.
A lotus with thirty-two petals is situated in the center of the head;

this is the head-wheel (*śiraścakra*), which is the Great Gnosis (*mahājñāna*) and the Svabhāvakāya, because its essential nature is that of the ultimate *bodhicitta*. (Vajratilaka, p. 78; Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 78)
Likewise, within the thirty-two-petaled [lotus], the great bliss and great gnosis are established all around. (Vajra-tantra, p.
78) In the great wheel of great bliss, the syllable *haṃ* takes the form of a drop (*bindu*). (Vajra-tantra, p. 79)
Self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*): Self-consecration is the vision of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). (Se. Ṭī., p.

40) The vision of the remaining aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth as being unconstructed—like an illusion, a dream, a city of Gandharvas, or a reflected image—is called the vision of conventional truth and is termed self-consecration. (Se. Ṭī., p. 57)
"Self-consecration" is the vision of the three realms within emptiness (*Viśeṣastava-prakaraṇa*, p.
7). "Svāhā, svāhā" is the consolation of the mantra-deity (*Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana-ṭīkā*, p. 164).

Now, Haṭhayoga is described. In this context, when— despite the bimba having been perceived through withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) and other means— the moment of the imperishable (akṣarakṣaṇa) does not arise because the vital breath (prāṇa) remains unrestrained, then, by force (haṭhena) through the practice of the inner sound (nāda), one should cause the prāṇa to flow through the central channel (madhyamā).

By means of non-vibration (*niṣpanda*), one should accomplish the imperishable moment through the cessation of the drop of *bodhicitta* within the jewel-vajra situated in the lotus of wisdom; this is *haṭhayoga*.
The practice of *nāda* is also taught in this very context. (Se. Ṭī., p.
45). [This is] Hayakarṇā.
She is Hayakarṇā because she emerges through the right ear like a horse; (Va. ti.
ṭī., p. 47) Hayakarṇā is the limb of enlightenment that is concentration (samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga); (Va. ti., p. 55) [He is] Hayagrīva.
Hayagrīva [is so called] because of the flowing forth of powerful blood from his two thighs (*urubhyām*).
Hariṇī is so called because she takes away—that is, she shatters—the six objects of the senses which are the graspers of existence (*bhava*). (Vajratārā-ṭīkā, p. 49)
In the *Sandhyābhāṣā*, that very [mudrā] is the Jñānamudrā (*Caryākoṣavyākhyā*, p.
21). This skull-bowl of the head is called the vessel for the oblation (*Vajratilaka*, p. 67).
This skull-cup on the head—that very cranial bowl—is the vessel for the sacrificial oblation because it serves as the support for the moon-butter offering, and nothing else. (Vajratārā-ṭīkā, p. 34).
Furthermore, she whose face is like a bird dwells in the center of the Sīmānta region in the Himalayas. (Vajratārā, p. 45).
The syllable *hūṃ* indicates the unsurpassed reality (*niruttara-dharmatā*) of the middle way; its meaning is as follows: *ha* signifies being free from causes (*hetu-viyukta*).
*Ū* means free from conceptual construction (*ūha*);
*aṃ* means that all phenomena are without foundation. (Avalokiteśvara-vrata-saṃgraha, p. 37).
This is the heart-vajra.

"The five aggregates are here declared by the Victors to be all the Tathāgatas; that which consists of their body, speech, and mind is the Heart-Vajra, the Great Bliss. (Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana, p. 13).
[She whose] face is joyful.

The *sīmanta* [is located] in the middle of the *varaṭaka* because it carries that; in the face, because of its joyful appearance; and in the hands, because of the touch of the hands. Because of the state of being blissful and intensely blissful through wisdom and means, it is in the *meḍhra*. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 45). The *hetudāyikā* is in the toes of the feet because fat (*medas*) alone is the cause for the nourishment of the limbs, and she carries that cause. (Vajratilaka-ṭīkā, p. 46).

"Heruka is indeed the non-empty emptiness; Heruka is the non-empty emptiness because wisdom and means are of the nature of a single flavor. (Hevajra Tantra 2.5.70) "Non-empty emptiness" [is so called] because wisdom and means possess the form of a single flavor.
This very gnosis is what is expressed by the term *Heruka*, because it is the non-dual nature of emptiness and compassion.
(Hevajra Tantra Commentary, fol. 66a-b)
Heruka is indeed the form of all; Heruka is [the essence] of all [the five aggregates]. (Vajra-tīkā, p.
15) All [of the five aggregates]...
He who possesses form as his innate nature is "possessed of all forms" (*sarvarūpī*), the pervasive Lord Śrī Heruka, the sixth Mahāvajradhara;
he is to be known as having the nature of *dharmatā*—this is the remainder [of the sense]. (Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p.
15) But Heruka, the Supreme Lord, is the source of all sense-bases and elements (*sarvāyatanadhātu*). (Vajra-tilaka, p. 16)
This skeleton in the form of a staff is Heruka, the supreme support;
he is called the stūpa of the Buddhas of the aggregates, elements, and so forth. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p.
19) The Blessed One Śrī Heruka is perfect meditative absorption. (Vajravārāhī-tantra, p. 56)
This hero Śrī Heruka is known as Vasantatilakā (The Tilaka of Spring). (Vasantatilakā, p.
38) Therein, in the nirmāṇacakra at the navel, he himself is spring, in the form of the short vowel *a*.
In the heart, in the dharmacakra, he has the form of the syllable *hūṃ* joined with *nāda* and *bindu*.
In the enjoyment wheel at the throat, that very same [syllable] consists of three morae and is protracted; it takes the form of the *praṇava*.
Due to the curvature of the channels (*nāḍī*), it undergoes three revolutions because of the entry and exit of the *caṇḍālī*.
In the forehead, the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), is the syllable *haṃ*, the unstruck sound (*anāhatākṣara*) adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*.
That very [deity] in reverse order is Śrī Heruka, whose form consists of the head, throat, heart, and navel, and who is the embodiment of the mantra. (Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p.
38–39) Because he causes the fat—which is of the nature of the indestructible syllable *HŪṂ*—to flow from the toes of his feet, he is Śrī Heruka. (Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p.
49) The Blessed One Śrī Heruka has the three bodies (*trikāya*) as his intrinsic nature. (Vajra-tilaka-ṭīkā, p. 86)
In *Hevajra*, the syllable *he* signifies great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), while *vajra* is said to be wisdom (*prajñā*).
Thus, the tantra consists of the nature of wisdom and means (*prajñopāyātmaka*)... (Hevajratantra 1.1.7).
The syllable *he* is great compassion;
the *vajra* is the emptiness of all phenomena. (Hevajra Tantra Commentary, p. 60b) This is the fire offering (*homa*).

Because of the sharpness of the blazing Caṇḍālī within the fire of wisdom (*prajñā*), this offering (*homa*) should be understood as a blaze of burning. (Vajravārāhī-tantra-ṭīkā, p. 66) By means of the internal oblations of semen and so forth, as well as the external oblations of form and so forth, the offering is performed in the greatly blazing fire of wisdom. (Vajravārāhī-tantra, pp. 66–67)
